New Brunswick Court of AppealCitation: New Brunswick v. Estabrooks Pontiac Buick Ltd.Date: 1982-12-31Hughes C.J.N.B., Stratton and La Forest JJ.A.Counsel:R. P. Burns, for appellant.Edmund E. Tedford, for respondent,
Estabrooks Pontiac Buick Ltd.Douglas L. Smith, for respondent, Brunswick
Bottling Ltd.[1] Hughes C.J.N.B.:— I have perused the reasons for judgment
prepared by my brother La Forest J.A. and
I agree with the conclusion which he has reached, namely, that the special lien
created by s. 19(1) of the Social Services and Education Tax Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. S-10, does not apply to any of the items
concerned in these appeals.[2] The difficulty encountered in interpreting s. 19(1) lies in
determining the scope to be given to the words "a special lien . .. upon
all the property used in or in connection with . . . the business of the
vendor". When considered in isolation and apart from its legislative
history, the subsection would appear to create a special lien on property other
than property of the vendor since the words which precede the quoted words
already create such a lien on the vendor's entire estate and the quoted words
would therefore be superfluous.[3] The reasoning of my brother La Forest, based on the legislative
history of the subsection is, however, persuasive of a different interpretation
which incidentally is consistent with the French version and supports the view
that "the property used in or in connection with . . . the business of the
vendor" is restricted to property of the vendor by the use of the words
"sur tous ses biens".

[4] Counsel for the appellant submitted that the English version best
expresses the intention of the Legislature. I am not convinced that such is the
case. Counsel also submitted that the court should avoid any construction
having the effect of reducing the quoted words to "futility". I think
as a general rule there is merit in the submission that such an interpretation
should be avoided where possible. When applied to the instant case, however, it
is apparent that the French version is incapable of including any property
other than that of the vendor whereas the English version may not be so
restricted. The Official Languages of New Brunswick Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. O-1, provides that in construing any
statute both versions in the official languages are equally authentic. While
the words of both versions respecting the property used in or in connection
with the business of the vendor may be redundant, the French version is to be
preferred for its clarity and because it avoids results which the Legislature
probably did not anticipate or intend.[5] I agree with the disposal of the appeal as proposed by my brother
La Forest.[6] Stratton J.A.:—I
have had the benefit of reading the reasons for judgment prepared by the Chief
Justice and Mr. Justice La Forest and agree with them that these appeals should
be dismissed.[7] It has long been settled that an intention to take away the
property of a subject without giving him a legal right to compensation for the
loss of it is not to be imputed to the Legislature unless that intention is
expressed in unequivocal terms: see E. A. Driedger, The Construction of
Statutes (1974), p. 138. Where, as here, the expression of
the legislative intent is unclear and the statute is susceptible of two
meanings, it is my opinion the court must make a choice on the assumption that
the Legislature did not intend to disturb existing rights.

property owned by persons other than the vendor.[11] The facts of the first case may briefly be stated as follows.
Estabrooks Pontiac Buick Ltd. carried on the business of retailing automobiles
at 92 Lorne St. in Sackville. Being engaged in retail sales it was registered
as a vendor as required by s. 12 of the above Act. Other sections of the Act
require a vendor to collect the tax imposed by the Act on behalf of the
province. By s. 19, the tax so collected is deemed to be held in trust for the
province and the amount so collected forms a lien on certain property described
in the section.

[12] On March 19, 1981, an audit was carried out on behalf of the
province which, according to counsel for the province, established a tax
liability in the amount of $16,350.17, being the amount collected by the
company as vendor and not remitted to the provincial Minister of Finance as
required by the Act. (This latter fact is disputed by counsel for the
respondents but this is not material for present purposes.) As a result of the
audit a notice of assessment dated April 16, 1981, was issued requiring the
company to remit the amounts owing by it under the Act for the period from
November, 1978 to December, 1980. On default by the company, judgment was
obtained pursuant to s. 38 of the Act on behalf of the province. The judgment
not having been satisfied, a certificate was issued under s. 19.1 of the Act
authorizing the sheriff to seize the property subject to the lien created by s.
19(1). Acting on this authority the sheriff seized the property at 92 Lorne St.
which, it is alleged, was used in connection with the company's business as a
car dealer.[13] The property seized included the real property at that address
but it was not owned by the company. It belonged to Mr. Larry N. Estabrooks,
the secretary-treasurer and a part owner of the company. The company held the
land from him under a one-year renewable lease dated April 28, 1980. The lease
had been terminated at the time of the audit, but this factor is of no
significance in light of the view I take of the issues.

(b) a soft-drink dispenser, claimed to be owned by Brunswick
Bottling Ltd., but subject to a conditional sale under which title is retained
by the seller made by Grandale Company Limited as seller to Jack Jardine (not
Fisherman's Wharf despite Dickson J.'s statement to that effect);(c) a stand-up cooler owned by McKay's Dairy Ltd. on loan to
Fisherman's Wharf under an oral arrangement which provided that the latter
would handle the former's products; and(d) a cigarette machine owned by Mr. William D. Cook which was
installed on the premises of Fisherman's Wharf pursuant to an oral arrangement
under which the latter was paid a commission on merchandise purchased through
the machine.[16] On an interpleader action by the sheriff seeking a resolution of
the validity of the various claims in respect of the above-listed property,
Dickson J. held that the lien created by s. 19(1) of the Social Services and
Education Tax Act did not apply to this property and directed that it be
released to its owners.[17] In his view, s. 19(1) was not worded sufficiently clearly to
warrant seizure of property not owned by the vendor. If that result had been
intended the section would have spoken of property "regardless of
ownership" or used words to like effect. He noted that s. 19(1) only gave
the lien priority over "a claim, privilege, lien or encumbrance",
words denoting third party claims rather than ownership, and that s. 19(5),
which gave some protection to persons other than the vendor whose property was
affected by the lien, was limited to persons like mortgagees and other encumbrancers. In his view, s. 19(1), if interpreted
as applying to property of persons other than the vendor, would in effect
amount to confiscation of private property by the Crown without compensation.
The statute being a taxing measure and encroaching on private rights should be
restrictively interpreted. Finally, as a corollary ground, he relied on the
broad rights of the individual guaranteed by the recently proclaimed Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

appeals.The problem[19] The English and French versions of s.
19(1) read as follows:19(1) Every vendor who collects any
tax under this Act shall be deemed to hold the tax in trust for Her Majesty in
right of the Province and for the payment over of the tax in the manner and at
the time provided under this Act, and notwithstanding subsection 72(2) of the Workers'
Compensation Act, the amount shall, until paid, form a special lien upon
his entire estate, on the entire assets of his estate in the hands of any
trustee, and upon all the property used in or in connection with or produced in
or by the business of the vendor, in priority to every claim, privilege, lien
or encumbrance, whenever created, subject only to taxes levied under the Real
Property Tax Act.19(1) Tout vendeur qui
perçoit une taxe en vertu de la
présente loi est réputé la détenir en fiducie pour le compte de Sa Majesté du
chef de la province, dans le but de lui remettre cette taxe de la manière et à
l'époque prévues en vertu de la présente loi; et, par dérogation au paragraphe 72(2) de
la Loi sur les accidents du travail le montant de cette taxe constitute, tant qu'il n'a pas été remis, un privilège spécial sur tout
son avoir, sur tous les actifs de celui-ci qui sont confiés à un fiduciaire et
sur tous ses biens utilisés directement ou indirectement dans ses affairs ou
qui y sont produits, en priorité sur toute réclamation droit, privilège ou
charge quelle que soit l'époque de leur création sous la seule réserve des
taxes perçues en vertu de la Loi sur l'impôt foncier.

[20] Both versions make it clear that the
lien on property other than that "used in or in connection with or
produced in or by the business of the vendor" (which latter property I
shall for ease of reference at times refer to as the business property) is
restricted to property owned by or held in trust for the vendor. But there is
an important difference between the portions of the English and the French
versions dealing with the business property. The English version speaks of the
property; the French speaks of his property ("ses biens").
Since by virtue of the Official Languages of New Brunswick Act, R.S.N.B.
1973, c. O-1, the two versions are equally authoritative, both must be examined
to determine the intention of the Legislature. As we saw, Leger J. came to the
conclusion that the English version being ambiguous, the clear words used in
the French version should determine the issue.[21] Counsel for the province argues,
however, that to limit the business property to property owned by the vendor
makes that portion of the section entirely redundant, and the use of
unnecessary words is not to be imputed to the Legislature. The language of the
Act, he argued, is clear and explicit; that being so it must be given effect
whatever the consequences. Within its legislative jurisdiction, the Legislature
is supreme and may enact provisions that have the effect of destroying vested
rights. Section 19(1) was consistent with other provisions in the Act. It had
been enacted to create a "special lien" to ensure collection of the
tax, and the legislative history of the section revealed that the Legislature
has given it a continually expanding scope. Though taxing statutes were once
subject to restrictive interpretation that approach has now been displaced by
s. 17 of the Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, which provides
that all statutes should be construed as remedial.

General principles[22] There is no doubt that the duty of the
courts is to give effect to the intention of the Legislature as expressed in
the words of the statute. And however reprehensible the result may appear, it
is our duty if the words are clear to give them effect. This follows from the
constitutional doctrine of the supremacy of the Legislature when acting within
its legislative powers. The fact that the words as interpreted would give an
unreasonable result, however, is certainly ground for the courts to scrutinize
a statute carefully to make abundantly certain that those words are not
susceptible of another interpretation. For it should not be readily assumed
that the Legislature intends an unreasonable result or to perpetrate an
injustice or absurdity.[23] This scarcely means that the courts
should attempt to reframe statutes to suit their own individual notions of what
is just or reasonable. However, legislative supremacy is not all there is to
the Constitution. In determining whether a statute is just or reasonable, the
courts can derive considerable assistance from the nature and origins of our
political organization as a parliamentary democracy. Those who struggled to
wrest power from the Stuart kings and placed it in the hands of the elected
representatives of the people were not of a mind to replace one despot by
another. Rather they were guided by a philosophy that placed a high premium on
individual liberty and private property and that philosophy continues to inform
our fundamental political arrangements — our Constitution. Indeed, for a time
after the English Revolution, the English courts appeared to be prepared to
hold statutes that invaded rights of this kind invalid; for an account, see
Corry, "The Interpretation of Statutes" reproduced as app. I in E. A.
Driedger, The Construction of Statutes (1974), p. 203 at p. 212 et
seq.

[24] With the complete realization of the
implications of parliamentary supremacy, this type of judicial approach, of
course, disappeared. But the original foundations of our governmental
organization remained as a legacy in a number of presumptions designed, as
Driedger notes at p. 137, "as protection against interference by the state
with the liberty or property of the subject". "Hence", he adds,
"it was 'presumed' in the absence of clear indication in the statute to
the contrary, that Parliament did not intend to affect the liberty or property
of the subject": see also D. L. Keir and F. H. Lawson, Cases in
Constitutional Law, 3rd ed. rev. (1948), pp. 3-4.[25] This approach of the courts to
legislative action permitted them to exercise an important role in the protection
of individual liberties even in the absence of an entrenched Bill of Rights.
If the legislation is clear, of course, the intent of the Legislature must
be respected. But what these presumptions ensure is that a law that appears to
transgress our basic political understandings should be clearly expressed so as
to invite the debate which is the life-blood of parliamentary democracy.[26] One of these presumptions is that a
statute should not, in the absence of clear words, be construed as taking the
property of an individual without compensation. This, of course, frequently
arises in expropriation cases but it is not limited to these. Thus, in Manitoba
Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen (1978), 88 D.L.R. (3d) 462, [1979] 1 S.C.R.
101, [1978] 6 W.W.R. 496, the Supreme Court of Canada applied the principle
under the following circumstances. The plaintiff company had for many years
been engaged in buying fish from fishermen who fished in various lakes in
Manitoba and in processing and selling the fish to customers in other provinces
and in the United States. In doing so it had built up a clientele in what had
become a highly competitive business. In 1969 the Fresh Water Fish Marketing
Act, a federal statute, gave a statutory corporation exclusive rights to
export fish from Manitoba to provinces that participated in the scheme set up
by the Act. The effect was to put the plaintiff out of business and it sued the
federal government for its loss of goodwill. The Supreme Court of Canada held
that the plaintiff was entitled to compensation.

[27] Ritchie J., giving the judgment of the
court, relied heavily on the leading case of Attorney-General v. De Keyser's
Royal Hotel, Ltd., [1920] A.C. 508, and particularly the judgment of Lord
Atkinson. In that case Lord Atkinson had this to say at p. 542:The recognized rule for the
construction of statutes is that, unless the words of the statute clearly so
demand, a statute is not to be construed so as to take away the property of a
subject without compensation. Bowen L.J. in London and North Western Ry. Co.
v. Evans, [1893] 1 Ch. 16, 28, said: "The Legislature cannot fairly be
supposed to intend, in the absence of clear words shewing such intention, that
one man's property shall be confiscated for the benefit of others, or of the
public, without any compensation being provided for him in respect of what is
taken compulsorily from him. Parliament in its omnipotence can, of course,
override or disregard this ordinary principle ... if it sees fit to do so, but,
it is not likely that it will be found disregarding it, without plain
expressions of such a purpose."[28] If the courts lean against confiscation
of property without payment of compensation when the fact of taking is clear,
it follows that they will in an appropriate case lean against the taking: see Attorney-General
ex rel. Whitechapel Board of Works v. Homer (1884), 14 Q.B.D. 245, where
Brett M.R. refused on this basis to construe a statute as interfering with the
plaintiff's property rights to a market; affirmed 11 App. Cas. 66. At times, a similar
approach is expressed in terms of a presumption against interference with
common law rights: see Turton v. Turnbull, [1934] 2 K.B. 197 at p. 201,
and East Coast Amusement Co. Ltd. v. British Transport Board ("Re
'Wonderland' Cleethorpes'"), [1965] A.C. 58 at p. 71, per Viscount
Simonds. That is not surprising because these cases are all merely special
applications of the same general principle: see Maxwell on the
Interpretation of Statutes, 12th ed. (1969), pp. 251-2 and Keir and Lawson,
p. 4.

[29] A recent Supreme Court of Canada
decision, Board of Industrial Relations v. Avco Financial Services Realty
Ltd. et al. (1979), 98 D.L.R. (3d) 695, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 699, 33 C.B.R.
(N.S.) 34, provides a convenient example in the present context. There the
court was asked to interpret s. 5A of the British Columbia Payment of Wages
Act. Subsection (1) provided that wages certified as having been unpaid by
an employer constituted a lien "payable in priority over any other claim
or right. .. including . . . every mortgage of real or personal property"
and s-s.(2) went on to say that a certificate of such unpaid wages "shall
constitute a lien and charge under s-s.(1) from the date wages were
earned". In an action to determine the priority of the lien in relation to
mortgages registered against the employer's land before the wages were earned,
the Supreme Court held that in the absence of specific statutory indication of
the property to which the lien attached, s. 5A "should not be construed in
a manner which could deprive third parties of their pre-existing property
right".[30] In coming to this conclusion, the court
stressed the inequitable results that would flow from an interpretation that
included property other than the employer's. It quoted from the judgment of
Robertson J.A. in the British Columbia Court of Appeal words that are apt in
the present context. The section, if broadly interpreted, would, he said,
"confiscate in order to pay wages owing by an employer, not only land in
which he might have an equity, but also, for example, land of which he was only
a lessee for years": see 81 D.L.R. (3d) 289 at p. 294, 5 B.C.L.R. 289, sub
nom. Homeplan Realty Ltd. v. Avco Financial Services Realty Ltd. et al.

[31] The principle I have described is
fundamental. It is a constitutional principle in the British sense: see Keir
and Lawson, p. 4. The Legislature may modify or even abolish it in certain
circumstances, but it is not to be readily assumed that it has done so.[32] Like other constitutional principles,
its precise content will vary over time and the Legislature undoubtedly has the
major burden of adjusting its application to changing circumstances.
Accordingly, the courts must in applying it do so with great caution to ensure
that its application conforms to changing social values and affords the
Legislature the widest possible scope in the performance of its task of
adjusting private rights to meet evolving social realities.[33] The courts should not, for example,
place themselves in the position of frustrating regulatory schemes or measures
obviously intended to reallocate rights and resources simply because they
affect vested rights. For legislation almost inevitably affects vested rights.
They must similarly have great deference for legislative schemes establishing
priorities among creditors and encumbrancers and, in particular, those that
favour the Crown over other creditors; indeed the common law itself has always
recognized certain Crown priorities flowing from the prerogative: see The
Queen v. Bank of Nova Scotia et al. (1885), 11 S.C.R. 1.[34] It is probably to avoid difficulties of
this kind that the security of property was not expressly protected by the Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms. But when we are asked to construe a statute
as taking the property of one person to pay the debts of another, as we are
here, it is our duty to scrutinize the legislation with great care to see
whether the Legislature really intended to do this. That has always been an
important role of the courts and the Charter, by s. 26, carefully provides that
it is not to be construed "as denying the existence of other rights and
freedoms that exist in Canada".

[35] In performing this duty, the courts
should not be looked upon as being at odds with the Legislature. Rather they
are working along with the Legislature to ensure the preservation of our
fundamental political values. All branches of government have an interest and a
duty in doing so. Lord Radclife in Belfast Corp. v. O. D. Cars Ltd., [1960]
A.C. 490 at p. 523, put it this way:On the one hand, there would be the
general principle, accepted by the legislature and scrupulously defended by the
courts, that the title to property or the enjoyment of its possession was not
to be compulsorily acquired from a subject unless full compensation was
afforded in its place. Acquisition of title or possession was
"taking." Aspects of this principle are found in the rules of
statutory interpretation devised by the courts, which required the presence of
the most explicit words before an acquisition could be held to be sanctioned by
an Act of Parliament wihout full compensation being provided, or imported any
intention to give compensation and machinery for assessing it into any Act of
Parliament that did not positively exclude it. This vigilance to see that the
subject's rights to property were protected, so far as was consistent with the
requirements of expropriation of what was previously enjoyed in specie, was
regarded as an important guarantee of individual liberty. It would be a mistake
to look on it as representing any conflict between the legislature and the
courts. The principle was, generally speaking, common to both.

[36] It may be that some of the
beneficiaries of the principle in the present cases may not appear deserving of
protection or that some of the interests involved are of small consequence. But
a jewel does not lose its value by being placed in a trivial or unworthy
setting. For if, for example, we were to apply the lien to property of a
landlord whose identity might, if we were to pierce the corporate veil, be
found to be the same as the owner of a company to which he has leased the
property, we would have to apply it to any landlord who leases premises to a
vendor though he had no other relationship with the landlord. If the
Legislature wishes to include landlords (and others for that matter) who are
not at arm's length with the vendor, it has many legislative techniques
available by way of inclusion or exclusion or by resort to ministerial or
official discretion. And if it really wishes to override the interests of an
owner who has no connection with the vendor apart from a landlord-tenant
relationship and thereby make him pay the tenant's liabilities under the tax
system, it can say so expressly, as it appears to have done in s. 72(2) of the Workers'
Compensation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. W-13.[37] I might add in passing that s. 17 of
the Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, which deems all statutes
remedial and requires "a fair, large and liberal" interpretation of
all statutes, has nothing to do with this principle. That provision was enacted
to correct an earlier but vanishing distinction between the "strict"
approach of the courts to penal and taxation statutes and the
"liberal" construction given other statutes: see Driedger, p. 148 et
seq. The courts, be it noted, still require that a penal or taxation
statute clearly bring within their ambits those made subject to a penalty or
tax either on the theory that Parliament intends to act reasonably or because
it is difficult to determine a purpose beyond the words of the statute. In any
event, the former dichotomy between strict and liberal construction was something
quite separate from the presumption referred to earlier.

Analysis of the section[38] Apart from the application of the
principle I have described, there is considerable evidence that the Legislature
did not by the provision here in question intend to attach the property owned
by persons other than the vendor. To begin with, there is the equally
authoritative French version of the statute which is clearly limited to the
vendor's property. And though, as we saw, this raises some problems of
redundancy this version cannot be ignored. Especially is this so in this
instance, since the English version, too, gives some indication that the
application of the lien created by s. 19 was limited to property of the vendor.
Thus the section gives the lien priority over "every claim, privilege,
lien or encumbrance whenever created", words that ordinarily comprise
third party claims, mere security interests rather than ownership.[39] It is true, as counsel for the province
argued, that "claim" is a broad general word that is capable in
certain contexts of including ownership. But words, particularly broad,
flexible words like this one, are coloured by the context in which they appear
and all the other associated words refer to claims against goods owned by
another: see Driedger, pp. 85-6. What is more the section refers to s. 72(2) of
the Workers' Compensation Act which gives a lien for assessments levied
against an employer against "property . . . used in or in connection, with
or produced in or by the industry . . . though not owned by the
employer". With that section clearly in contemplation, one would think
the draftsman would have used similar words if it was desired to attach
property other than that owned by the vendor.

Legislative history[40] But it is the legislative evolution of
the section that most strongly militates against the view that the Legislature
intended to cover property owned by a person other than the vendor under the
Act. Resort to legislative history is, of course, a well-known device for
determining the intention of the Legislature: see R. v. Popovic and Askov (1975),
62 D.L.R. (3d) 56, 25 C.C.C. (2d) 161, 32 C.R.N.S. 54 (S.C.C.).[41] Though counsel for the province argued
that the legislative history of the section clearly established an
ever-widening ambit of the lien created by s. 19(1), I cannot so view it. What
it shows, rather, is a somewhat confused picture. Let us begin with the section
as it originally appeared in the 1973 revision in which form it had existed
since its enactment in 1955, as s. 17A (1955, c. 75, s. 3). That revision read
as follows:19. Every vendor who collects any
tax under this Act is deemed to hold the same in trust for Her Majesty in right
of the Province and for the payment over of the same in the manner and at the
time provided under this Act, and the amount shall, until paid, form a lien and
charge on his entire estate or on the entire assets of his estate in the hands
of any trustee, and such lien or charge has priority over all other claims of
any person.

One would have thought the vendor's
"entire estate" would cover "the entire assets of his estate in
the hands of any trustee", so the latter words seem surplusage, but it
appears to show a clear intention on the part of the Legislature to limit the
section to the property owned by the vendor whether at law or in equity, and it
is in respect of such property that the lien takes priority over the claims of
others.[42] In 1978 [c. 55, s. 6], the section was
repealed and substituted by the following:19. Every vendor who collects any
tax under this Act is deemed to hold the same in trust for Her Majesty in right
of the Province and for the payment over of the same in the manner and at the
time provided under this Act, and the amount shall, until paid, form a lien and

[46] Far from indicating an ever-expanding
ambit, s. 19, as enacted in 1979, was clearly reduced in its application to
what I have described as the business property. Counsel for the province
argued, however, that it would include the property of persons other than the
vendor. But this proposition runs counter to Crown Trust Co. et al. v.
Workmen's Compensation Board et al. (1975), 55 D.L.R. (3d) 498, 7 O.R. (2d)
466, where Houlden J. of the Ontario High Court confined the application of a
very similar section in the Ontario Workmen's Compensation Act to the
property of the employer.[47] Even in the absence of authority, I
would have come to the same conclusion. Quite apart from the presumption I have
already discussed one would not, in the absence of a clear indication of such
an intention, construe a provision that creates a lien for the purpose of
satisfying a debt owing by one person as applying to the property of another.
It is trite knowledge that a legislative provision must be interpreted in
context in the light of its purpose.[48] This natural assumption is confirmed by
the French version which, by speaking of "ses biens", expressly
confined the operation of the lien to the property of the vendor. It is worth
underlining that it was in this context — when the ordinary reading of the
English version would also confine the lien to the vendor's property — that the
expression "ses biens" ("his property") appeared in the
French version.

[49] Nor is this all. The English version contains other clues that
tend to confirm this interpretation. It is in this 1979 version of s. 19 that
the reference to s. 72(2) of the Workmen's Compensation Act first
appeared and the lien in that section, then as now, expressly provided that it
applied to non-owners. The section reads as follows:72(2) The amount of an assessment including provisional
amounts and any judgment with respect to the assessment is a first lien upon
all the property, real, personal or mixed used in or in connection with or
produced in or by the industry with respect to which the employer is assessed, though
not owned by the employer, subject only to taxes levied under the Real
Property Tax Act, and the amount levied under execution upon ay such
judgment to the extent of the amount due upon that execution shall forthwith be
paid by the sheriff or the deputy sheriff to the Board.(Emphasis added.) The draftsman would have known that this
related section would be referred to in clarifying any doubts there might be
about the interpretation of s. 19(1).[50] As already mentioned, the types of property made subject to the
lien on the vendor's property appear to be various kinds of encumbrances and
security interests. These, it is true, would include the interest of a
mortgagee, who though technically the legal owner, in fact really owns an
encumbrance, for s. 19(5), which was enacted at the same time, clearly
contemplates that interest. (This might have been debatable before: cf.,
Crown Trust Co. v. Workmen's Compensation Board, supra; Dinning v. Workmen's
Compensation Bd., [1932] 1 D.L.R. 373, [1932] 1 W.W.R. 136, 13 C.B.R. 256;
and Workmen's Compensation Board v. Sumas Oil & Gas Co., [1933] 3
D.L.R. 489, [1933] 2 W.W.R. 121, 47 B.C.R. 12.) I am inclined to think the lien
would extend to other situations where the vendor is the owner in a practical
sense, if not in abstract legal theory, as for example where the vendor is a
purchaser under a conditional sale.

[51] But that is a far cry from making the lien apply to property that
is really owned by another person. And s. 19(5), by providing express remedies
for mortgagees and other encumbrancers whose property is made subject to the
lien, appears not to contemplate property owners other than the vendor.[52] The lien under the 1979 version of s. 19(1), therefore, clearly
appears to have been limited to property owned by the vendor although, of
course, it took priority over other claims to that property. When to the
reasons already given one adds the presumption that the Legislature does not
intend to take the property of one person to pay for the debts of another, that
interpretation becomes irresistible.[53] The 1979 version was then amended by 1980, c. 52, s. 5(a):(a) by adding immediately after the words "special
lien upon" where they appear in subsection (1) thereof the swords
"his entire estate, on the entire assets of his estate in the hands of any
trustee, and upon";By doing this, we get the present s. 19(1).[54] The 1980 amendment, it will be noted, is expressly confined to
property of the vendor; it applies only to "his estate". But by
adding this additional portion of the vendor's property to the 1979 enactment
which, we saw, is also limited to the vendor's property, we are asked to come
up with the result that the property of a third person is now included, and
this in the face of clear words in the French version expressly restricting the
lien to the vendor's property. This proposition appears wholly untenable. Had
the reverse taken place — if to all the property owned by the vendor the
business property had been added — a different issue would have been raised. It
would be difficult to explain why the Legislature thought fit to add extra
words unless it intended them for a different purpose.

Surplusage[55] But it is said that the words that were in the section in 1979
become surplusage when the new words are inserted into the section unless one,
in effect, stretches their original meaning to include, because of the new
context in which they appear, property other than that of the vendor. While
counsel rightly asserted that one must attempt to give meaning to every word in
a statute, the fact is, as I have already pointed out, that surplusage does not
appear to be new to the section. There was some from the beginning, and it
continues to exist in the very words added in 1980. As already mentioned, I am
unable to see what is comprised in "the entire assets of the vendor's
estate in the hands of any trustee" that is not covered by "his entire
estate".[56] The probability is that when the 1980 amendment was enacted the
Legislature intended nothing more than to bring back within the scope of the
section property that had been covered by the section as originally enacted in
1955 and that it overlooked the fact that this made superfluous some of the
words enacted in 1979. That is at least as probable as the idea that the
Legislature was, probably for the first time, attempting to cover property of a
person other than a vendor in this covert manner, a device I would not lightly
impute to the Legislature. And I do not think this possibility is made more
persuasive by the fact that the 1978 enactment may have included property owned
by a person other than the vendor, especially so when the Legislature had moved
to retract this step in 1979.

[57] Whatever might have been the result had the whole section been
enacted at one time, the least that can be said in the light of its legislative
history is that one is left in considerable doubt about the intention of the
Legislature. Under those circumstances, it seems clear that one should exercise
the presumption against a gratuitous taking by the Legislature of property
owned by a person other than the person directly aimed at by the Legislature.[58] But what of the surplusage? There is no magic in this. Though
courts do try to give meaning to all the words of a statute, they will ignore
excess verbiage where doing so appears to be more consonant with the
legislative intent: see Driedger, pp. 72-3. In Salmon v. Buncombe et al. (1886),
11 App. Cas. 627, for example, the Privy Council in effect deleted the last
nine words from a short section to arrive at what otherwise appeared to be the
intention of the Legislature. Such a course is especially likely to be required
in the case of amendments, for in these circumstances the draftsman and the
Legislature may not have squarely focused on all the words used in the
pre-existing statute. In such cases, the courts have sometimes ignored some of
the words or in effect read some in: see Driedger, at pp. 105-6. We need not go
that far here. All we need do is treat the surplusage as just that — merely
repetitive.

Workers' Compensation Act cases[59] Counsel for the province relied on several cases relating to the Worker's
Compensation Act and particularly on two cases decided by this court, Workmen's
Compensation Board v. White Motor Co. of Canada Ltd. et al. (1971), 19
D.L.R. (3d) 551, 3 N.B.R. (2d) 565, and Le Gassick et al. v. Continental
Automotive Inc., supra, which deal with the predecessor to s. 72(2) of that
Act cited above. That section, it will be remembered, also applies to property
used in or in connection with the industry.[60] It must be said at the outset that these cases are of very
limited use for present purposes. They are based on a statute that is
completely different, both in its wording and legislative history, from the one
in question here. What is more there is such a wide diversity in the opinions
of the judges who sat on these cases that they can only be considered as
binding authority on the specific questions decided.[61] In the White Motor case, supra, the Workmen's
Compensation Board claimed a lien on equipment sold under a conditional sales
contract by the defendant to an employer who used it in connection with his
business. The case really turned on whether the lien attached in respect of
assessments made against the employer to support the workmen's compensation
fund during the year when the contract was made or whether it also attached in
respect of arrears from previous years. On that question, a majority decided
that the lien extended to property used by the employer during the year of
assessment.

[62] But the court also had to deal with the ambit of the lien. Hughes
J. A. (now C.J.N.B.) in dissent was of the view that the lien attached to all
property at any time used by the employer regardless of ownership. Limerick
J.A., however, while agreeing that the lien extended to a conditional buyer and
other situations where the employer was a joint owner with others, was of the
view that for the lien to attach the employer had to have some property, right
or interest in the reversion at the time the assessment was made. The other
majority judge, Bugold J.A., held that the lien attached to "the property
of the employer only which is used in or in connection with the
industry" the year the employer is assessed.[63] Taking the view of the case most favourable to the province's
position, it should be noted that both Hughes and Limerick JJ.A. based their
decisions that the lien extended to the interest of a person other than an
employer on the effect of s. 68(2) of the Act which provided that where such a
person had an interest in property on which the lien attached, the property was
to be deemed that of the employer only. Hughes J.A., for example, had this to
say [at p. 564]: "Without the provision contained in s. 68(2) the Board in
enforcing its judgment for an assessment could not levy upon property now in
the employer's industry unless it was owned by the employer or was property in
which the employer had an exigible interest." There is no provision
similar to s. 68(2) in the Act under consideration in the present case, so I
find it difficult to see how counsel for the province can draw comfort from the
White Motor case.

[64] In the Continental Automotive case, supra, the
court, again by majority, held that the lien under the Workmen's
Compensation Act extended to the property owned by the employer at the time
the assessment was made though subsequently sold under a conditional sales
contract to a third party. The majority this time consisted of Hughes C.J.N.B.
and Limerick J.A. with Bugold J.A. in dissent. But there was no change in their
previous views of the law; each maintained his original position. Accordingly,
this case affords no support for the province's position either.Subsidiary arguments[65] Counsel for the province also relied on the fact that the lien in
s. 19(1) is referred to as a "special lien". I do not know what is
special about it except the fact that it ranks in priority to the "first
lien" created by the Workers' Compensation Act.[66] The attempt to equate the lien to that attaching under
legislation respecting municipal rates does not impress me either; it is well
known that municipal rates are taxes on property rather than on a person and
the major subject of municipal rates is land, which creates a context wholly
different from a lien that applies to the entire estate of a vendor.Conclusion[67] For the above reasons I do not think the lien created applies to
any of the items of property concerned in these two cases. Though, as I
mentioned, I would be inclined to think it would apply to the property of a
buyer under a conditional sales contract, the vendor was not the conditional
buyer under the conditional sales contract in question in the Fisherman's
Wharf appeal.

this case affords no support for the province's position either.Subsidiary arguments[65] Counsel for the province also relied on the fact that the lien in
<legislation><fragment>s. 19(1)</fragment></legislation> is referred to as a "special lien". I do not know what is
special about it except the fact that it ranks in priority to the "first
lien" created by the <legislation><title>Workers' Compensation Act</title></legislation>.[66] The attempt to equate the lien to that attaching under
legislation respecting municipal rates does not impress me either; it is well
known that municipal rates are taxes on property rather than on a person and
the major subject of municipal rates is land, which creates a context wholly
different from a lien that applies to the entire estate of a vendor.Conclusion[67] For the above reasons I do not think the lien created applies to
any of the items of property concerned in these two cases. Though, as I
mentioned, I would be inclined to think it would apply to the property of a
buyer under a conditional sales contract, the vendor was not the conditional
buyer under the conditional sales contract in question in the <decision><title>Fisherman's
Wharf </title>appeal</decision>.

are fixed at $600 in respect of the Estabrooks appeal and at $600 in respect of
the Fisherman's Wharf appeal.[69] Appeals dismissed.

affiliated bargaining agents represented by the employee bargaining agency. The

constituent element of various employer bargaining agencies for various trades
currently engaged in collective bargaining in the construction industry and
affected by the picketing.

3. It was agreed that all of the affiliated
bargaining agents or locals of the United Association in Ontario in the ICI
sector are engaging in a lawful province-wide strike and that Local 663 in
Sarnia is picketing all of the sites that the employees it represents were
working on prior to the strike. As a result of the said picketing, other craft
employees such as electricians, ironworkers, insulators, teamsters, operating
engineers, labourers, carpenters, and cement masons employed by contractors who
are members of the applicant, Sarnia Construction Association, have refused to
report for work as they were normally scheduled to do. It was agreed that the
electricians, ironworkers, insulators, teamsters, and operating engineers were
not in a strike position at the time such employees refused to report to work. Labourers
and cement masons were in a strike position but had not called the
province-wide strike pursuant to the legislation at the times relevant to this
application. And, finally, carpenters were not in a strike position at the
time of the application but have since arrived at this position although a
province-wide strike has not been called pursuant to the Act. It would appear
that the craft employees honouring the picket lines are employed either by
single trade contractors wholly unconnected with the mechanical trades
bargaining except by geography or by multi-trade contractors who do employ
members of Local 663 as well as other trades. We are, however, given to understand
that the single trade contractors constitute the vast majority of the
contractors employing unrelated trades being adversely affected by Local 663
"site-wide" picketing.

locals or affiliated bargaining agents in the Toronto and Hamilton area
who represent about one-half of the employees covered by the province-wide ICI
agreement and who are engaged in the strike, are not picketing at this time. The
understanding in this area is that a project will not be picketed by a striking
trade unless the work previously performed by the striking employees before the

148.- (1) Where
an employee bargaining agency desires to call or authorize a lawful strike, all
of the affiliated bargaining agents it represents shall call or authorize the
strike in respect of all the employees represented by all affiliated bargaining
agents affected thereby in the industrial, commercial and institutional sector
of the construction industry referred to in clause 117(e), and no affiliated
bargaining agent shall call or authorize a strike of such employees except in
accordance with this subsection. 74. No trade union
or council of trade unions shall call or authorize or threaten to call or
authorize an unlawful strike and no officer, official or agent of a trade union
or council of trade unions shall counsel, procure, support or encourage an
unlawful strike or threaten an unlawful strike. 76.- (1) No
person shall do any act if he knows or ought to know that, as a probable and
reasonable consequence of the Act, another person or persons will engage in an
unlawful strike or an unlawful lock-out. (2) Subsection
(1) does not apply to any act done in connection with a lawful strike or lawful
lockout. 5. It is the applicants' submission that the
purpose of section 148 is to provide for uniform industrial conflict when this
proves necessary and that the selective picketing, inflicting greater economic
harm on some mechanical trades employers than on others, constitutes a
violation of the purpose and spirit of the provision. Counsel points out that
certain multi-trade employers such as Comstock International Ltd., Sheafer
Townsend Construction Ltd. and Lummus Canada Inc. employ trades other than the
mechanical trade employees and that, in particular, these employers are being
singled out in the Sarnia area in contrast to similar multi-trade employers in
the Hamilton and Toronto area who have been permitted to carry on construction
with their other trades provided that the work of the mechanical trades
employees is not being performed by anyone else. Alternatively, it is argued
that the picketing constitutes classic secondary pressure causing unlawful
strikes contrary to section 74 and 76 of the statute. Counsel emphasizes that
there is no evidence or allegation that the work of employees participating in
the strike is being performed by anyone else and that therefore the picketing
in question can only have the purpose of causing employees of contractors not
involved in the strike to engage in an unlawful strike activity contrary to
sections 74 and 76. Indeed, counsel accepted that site-wide picketing would be
appropriate if the work in question was being performed.
But such is not the case and it was submitted that section 76(2) is not
intended to shelter such clearly secondary picketing regardless of the
geographical proximity of the employees.

6. On behalf of the respondent, it was submitted
that section 148 did not provide the power to the Board to regulate the
strategies and tactics associated with a province-wide strike after such a
strike had been called and authorized. Counsel stressed that picketing is a
significant labour relations phenomenon that the Legislature would have
specifically mentioned in the context of section 148 if its regulation was
intended. It was submitted that over 1,000 plumbers in the Saria area were on
a lawful strike and that they were entitled to demonstrate this fact. It was further
submitted that the picketing employees had been employed on the various sites
at which they are picketing and that in every sense of the word the picketing
was "primary" and not secondary. Our attention was directed to Canteen
of Canada Limited, [1978] OLRB Rep. Mar. 207 and George Wimpey (Canada)
Limited, [1978] OLRB Rep. Dec. 1096 which were said to stand for the
proposition that as long as a lawful strike was in progress all picketing by
participating employees can be said to arise out of it and is therefore
protected by section 76(2). The same cases were relied on for the submission
that section 74 had to be read in conjunction with the saving section in
section 76. 7. We are of the view that section 148(1) does not
prohibit selective picketing and, indeed, does not purport to regulate
picketing associated with a province-wide strike called pursuant to the section
in any direct sense. Had the Legislature intended the section to be a direct
vehicle for the regulation of picketing it would have been explicit.

8. However, the concept of picketing is in many
ways regulated by the more general provisions contained in sections 74 and 76
of the Labour Relations Act and they must be interpreted with due
sensitivity to the reality of the province-wide single trade bargaining created
by the statute. We also accept that section 74 must be read in light of and
subject to section 76 and the saving provision in that section, i.e. subsection
2. See Canteen of Canada Ltd., supra, paragraph 25. Viewing this
application under section 135 against these sections, we observe that it was
not suggested or argued before us that the application, having been brought
against a trade union and not against particular officers, officials or agents
of the trade union, was technically unfounded. (See the respondent's filing on
the first day this matter came on for hearing.) Rather, the matter was argued
on its merits on the basis that the picketing was either sanctioned by section
76(2) or it was not and not that the applicants had chosen the wrong
respondent(s). On this basis then, we are prepared to accept that by naming
the respondent trade union the applicants were alleging that the officers,
officials and agents of the local trade union in the general sense had
sanctioned the challenged picket line and thereby had procured or encouraged an
unlawful strike within the meaning of section 74 and that the same actions
(i.e. the setting up of the picket lines) by such persons amounted to acts
which they would know or ought to know would cause other persons to engage in
an unlawful strike within the meaning of section 76(1). From this perspective
the conduct of setting up picket lines which cause unlawful strikes contrary to
sections 74 and 76 can be remedied by the Board under section 135 as the
procuring or encouraging of unlawful strikes by officers, officials and agents
of a trade union provided the allegations are made out. At no time was it
suggested that it was necessary for the applicants to name an official or
officer or agent of Local 663 for the matter to be entertained under sections
74 and 76. Had the issue been raised the application might have been amended
at the hearing since an officer of Local 663 had notice of this matter and
attended the hearing.

9. Sections 74 and 76 do
deal with the concept of picketing but do not mention it specifically. See
Laskin, The Labour Relations Amendment Act, 1960, (1961-62), 14 U.T.L.J.
116 at 120. It is well recognized in this province that a picket line can
cause an unlawful strike within the meaning of the Act. See Nelson Crushed
Stone, [1977] OLRB Rep. Nov. 713. See also Local 273, International
Longshoremen's Ass'n v. Maritime Employers' Ass'n, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 120 and
Note, Whether Honouring Picket Lines Constitutes a "Strike" (1979),
11 Ottawa Law Review 771. There
is no argument or evidence before us that the activity of those employees who
recognized the respondent's picket lines was anything other than concerted or
based on a common understanding within the meaning of the legislation. We are
therefore prepared to find that the actions of these craft employees constitute
an unlawful strike within the meaning of the Act in that the procedural
condition precedents to calling a timely and otherwise lawful province‑wide
strike under the statute had not been complied with prior to the work refusals
in question. It goes without saying that this finding is only for the purpose
of this application. The application was not brought against such employees
and there is therefore no need to decide whether our discretion under section
135 ought to be exercised with respect to them having regard to all of the
industrial relations circumstances. See Canadian Elevator Manufacturers, [1975]
OLRB Rep. Nov. 868 at para. 15. This then raises the question of whether the
respondent can rely upon section 76(2) by arguing that the picket lines are in
connection with a lawful strike and therefore protected.

10. We are satisfied that sections 74 and 76 are
designed to deal with, among other things, picketing aimed at employers and
employees wholly unconnected with a lawful strike. On the other hand,
subsection 2 of 76 is aimed at permitting, among other things, picketing
arising out of and related to a lawful strike. Some integrating and melding of
purpose is therefore required in applying these various sections. Industrial
relations experience has proven that neither purpose can be pursued to the
exclusion of the other particularly in light of customs, practices and
psychology surrounding the activity of picketing. Subsection 2 clearly
protects, for example, picketing at a single employer location such as a plant
or manufacturing setting where certain employees of the employer are on strike
and picketing is aimed at fellow employees, suppliers, customers and others
providing services to the struck enterprise. The Board has gone even further
holding that picketing by employees on a lawful strike is permissible at
locations of their employer other than the location at which they are employed. See Canteen of Canada Limited, supra. and George Wimpey (Canada) Limited, supra. Whether or not this approach has been too sweeping in its terms we
do not need to decide on the facts before us. The causes for picketing are
also infinite in variety as is the commercial activity which attracts
picketing. Accordingly, broad general pronouncements are not very appropriate. See, for example, Local 761, I. U.E. v. N.L.R.B. (1961), 48 LRRM 2210; Sailors'
Union of the
Pacific (Moore Drydock Co.) (1950), 27 LRRM 1109;
and Beatty, Secondary Boycotts. A Functional Analysis (1974), 52 Can. Bar Rev. 388. The transfer of struck
work from one location to another may present compelling reasons for expansive
picketing whereas the picketing of another location involved in a totally
different activity might have to stand or fall on the rationale that employees
are entitled to picket an employer's entire economic domain. See Williams
v. Aristocratic Restaurants Ltd., [1951] S.C.R. 762; Brown, Picketing: Canadian
Courts and The Labour Relations Board of British Columbia (1981), 31
U.T.L.J. 153. On the other hand, there can be little
doubt that direct employee picketing of a geographically removed secondary
employer's premises is not protected by section 76(2) subject possibly to considerations
of a roving primary situs or ally considerations. See Wescraft
Manufacturing Ltd., [1975] 2 Can. LRBR 324 and Paterson, Union Secondary
Conduct: A Comparative Study of the American and Ontario Positions,(1973), 8 U.B.C. Law Rev. 77 at 81. While it may be that a clearly
secondary and uninvolved employer can come before this Board for a direction to
require his employees to cross the picket lines, such a remedy is not always
entirely adequate particularly in relation to suppliers and others and we see
little justification for placing the employees of a secondary employer in the
dilemma of choosing between their loyalty to the labour movement and their
legal obligations. Section 76 was designed to remove the source of the
problem, i.e. employee directed secondary picketing. See Arthurs, Labour Law-Secondary
Picketing-Per Se Illegality-Public Policy (1963), 41 Can. Bar Rev. 573 at
584. It is only since the expansion of the Board's remedial authority that the
problem has become one falling within the Board's responsibility. In this
respect, we think the reliance of Canteen of Canada Ltd. in Ford
Motor Co. of Canada Ltd. v. Browning(1978), 86 D.L.R. (3d) 579 at 581 was
understandable but not warranted. Accordingly, Canteen of Canada must
be read in light of the instant decision.

11. Moreover, in the context of province-wide
bargaining in the construction industry we are reluctant to hold that
contractors working on a common construction site but otherwise unrelated to a
dispute involving another trade also located there lose the protection provided
for by sections 74 and 76(1). Nor, with the advent of province-wide
bargaining, do we accept that section 76(2) permits unrestricted picketing
directed at employees of employers unconnected with the labour relations
dispute other than by geography provided that separate entrances can be
established for such employees and provided further that the work of the
striking trade or trades is not being performed. In embarking in this
direction the Board must be sensitive to the custom and practices of trade
unions and to the psychology permeating labour relations conflict. However, we
see little justification for unrestricted common situs picketing in
province-wide bargaining where the work of the striking employees is not being
performed and the employers adversely affected are not connected with the
negotiations. Such employers are not party to the negotiations and can have no
real control on bargaining postures. Picketing directed at such employees and
employers is in every sense secondary and not connected with a lawful strike.
Indeed, we note that Hamilton
and Toronto locals do not see a
need to picket other craft employees even of multi-trade contractors unless
their work is being performed. Thus, in the circumstances of this case, and
where the picketing, either physically or visually, was not limited to single
trade mechanical contractors and the common emloyer multi-trade contractors, we
find and declare that the officers of the respondent trade union intended to
cause an unlawful strike of trades employees employed by employers who are not
part of the mechanical trades negotiations and that, to the extent that the
picketing is directed at and interfering with such employees, the picketing
cannot be said to be in connection with a lawful strike. However, on the very
limited facts before us, we are not prepared to say that the multi-trade
contractors involved in bargaining with the employee bargaining agency of the
respondent local may also seek protection under sections 74 and 76(1). While
there may be additional detail and argument on how the construction industry is
different than a normal industrial setting where various employee groups of a
single employer are employed in proximity to each other and therefore properly
subjected to picketing, we are not prepared to distinguish the construction
industry in this respect at this time. This case should not be taken as a
signal to parties outside the ambit of province-wide construction industry
negotiations to begin establishing reserved gates in an effort to insulate
themselves from primary picketing. This decision is very much centered on the
needs and practices of a particular segment of the construction industry. Finally,
because of the somewhat unprecedented nature of this application, we view our
findings as speaking to the future and no other relief is justified for what
has occurred to date.

12. Having regard to all of the foregoing, the Board
makes the following order: 1. The Board, subject to paragraphs 2,
3 and 4, directs and orders that the officers, officials or agents of the
respondent, the United Association of Journeymen and Apprentices of the
Plumbing and Pipe Fitting Industry of the United States and Canada, Local Union
663, and any other person having notice or knowledge of this direction and
order, cease and desist from establishing or maintaining a picket line,
picketing or doing any other act which they know or ought to know, as a
reasonable consequence of such act, other persons will engage in an unlawful
strike at construction projects in the ICI sector of the construction industry
in the County of Lambton at which employers for whose employees the respondent
holds bargaining rights are working or have worked within the previous six
months, save and except at the entrances to the construction projects for
employees of such employers until a provincial agreement binding upon the
applicant and respondent is entered into or until such further orders or
directions, if any, are made by the Board. 2. Paragraph 1 of this direction and
order shall not apply to a construction project until one entrance to the
project is established for employees of employers whose employees are
represented by the respondent and another entrance to the project is established
for all other employees employed by other contractors.

commenced by issue of a statement of claim in form 2.441(1) All applications both in court and in chambers shall be
by notice of motion except where otherwise specially provided.[18] The applicants rely on Rule 441(2) as authorizing the commencement of
these proceedings by notice of motion. It is contended that insofar as s. 24(1)
of the Charter provides for an application to a court of competent
jurisdiction Rule 441(2) is applicable. In my respectful view, this contention
cannot be sustained.[19] It is unnecessary in this case to determine the precise scope of Rule
441(2). It suffices to say in relation to this case that the expression
“application” in Rule 441(2) does not connote the same thing as the expression
“application” when considered in the context of s. 24(1) of the Charter.
In Rule 441(2), the expression “application” refers to the manner in which
proceedings may be commenced. A statute employing the same expression to
indicate that proceedings may be taken to enforce a claim or right which the
statute has created, comes within the purview of the rule only if it may be
inferred from the context that the expression “application” as used in the
statute is intended to refer to the mode of proceeding and not merely to the
fact that relief is available.

[33] A similar view has been expressed by Eberle, J., in Re Regina and
Brooks et al. (1983), 1 C.C.C.(3d) 506, at page 509 (Ont. H.C.):I do not think that it can be said that, by the use of those
words in s. 24(1), namely, ‘a court of competent jurisdiction,’ Parliament
intended to give all jurisdiction in all matters to all courts. That, it seems
to me, is an interpretation going far beyond the phrase itself and the context
in which it appears. It seems to me that in giving a person a right to apply to
a court of competent jurisdiction, as s. 24 does, the section refers to and
points to the court or courts of competent jurisdiction with respect to the
matter that is sought to be enforced under s. 24.[34] In the formal notice served upon the Attorney General of Canada pursuant
to s. 8 of the Constitutonal Questions Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. C-29, the
applicants advised that the constitutional validity of s. 18 of the Federal
Court Act was being challenged. However, in the original notice of motion
and in the amended notice of motion filed subsequent thereto, there is no
mention of s. 18 of the Federal Court Act as being among the statutory
provisions whose constitutional validity was being impugned in these
proceedings. Therefore, I do not propose to deal with the issue of the
competency of Parliament to enact s. 18, other than to comment on the scope of
the exclusive jurisdiction granted to the Federal Court, Trial Division by s.
18 of that Act.

[35] The scope of s. 18 of the Federal Court Act has recently been
considered by the Supreme Court of Canada in Jabour v. Law Society of British Columbia et oil. and Attorney General of British Columbia et al., [1982] 5
W.W.R. 289; 43 N.R. 451. That case arose, in part, out of the commencement of
an inquiry by the Director of the Restrictive Trade Practises Commission into
“the production, purchase, sale and supply of legal services and related
products in the Province of British Columbia”. The Law Society of British
Columbia commenced an action in the Supreme Court of British Columbia in which
the Society sought declarations that the Act was not applicable to it,
or to the extent to which it purported to be applicable, it was ultra vires
the Parliament of Canada, together with an injunction preventing the Director
from continuing with the inquiry.[36] Counsel for the Attorney General of Canada argued that the Federal
Court, Trial Division had exclusive jurisdiction over declaratory or injunctive
relief against the Attorney-General of Canada and against a federal tribunal
such as the Restrictive Trade Practises Commission. However, the Supreme Court
of Canada held that the exclusive jurisdiction granted to the Federal Court,
Trial Division by s. 17 and s. 18 of the Federal Court Act did not
preclude a Provincial superior court from declaring a statute enacted by
Parliament to be beyond the constitutional authority of Parliament.

[37] The issue of whether a statute or portion thereof, is inconsistent with
the Charter is not a constitutional question in the traditional sense. Before
the enactment of the Constitution Act, 1982, which entrenched the Charter
of Rights and Freedoms as part of the Constitution of Canada,
constitutional issues arose only when legislation was challenged as being
beyond the jurisdictional limits of Parliament of the Legislatures.[38] The role of the judiciary in dealing with these traditional
constitutional issues has been described by Lord Watson, in Union Colliery
Company of British Columbia Limited v. Bryden, [1899] A.C. 580 (P.C.), at
page 585:In assigning legislative power to the one or the other of
these parliaments, it is not made a statutory condition that the exercise of
such power shall be, in the opinion of a court of law, discreet. In so far as
they possess legislative jurisdiction’, the discretion committed to the
parliaments, whether of the Dominion or of the provinces, is unfettered. It is
the proper function of a court of law to determine what are the limits of the
Jurisdiction committed to them; but, when that point has been settled, courts
of law have no right whatever to inquire whether their Jurisdiction has been
exercised wisely or not.[39] However, the enactment of the Constitution Act, 1982, has altered
the role of the judiciary in Canada. The courts are now called on to review the
substance of legislation to determine whether the legislation imposes
unreasonable restrictions on the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the Charter.

of the Constitution Act, 1982, states that “any law that is inconsistent
with the provisions of the Constitution is, to the extent of the inconsistency,
of no force or effect”. Thus, where legislation is challenged as being
inconsistent with the rights and freedoms as guaranteed by the Charter, the
constitutional validity of the legislation is at issue. Therefore, the
reasoning in the Jabour case, supra, applies with equal force to
situations, such as the present situation, in which legislation is challenged
as being inconsistent with the fundamental rights and freedoms guaranteed by
the Charter.[41] For this reason, I conclude that s. 18 of the Federal Court Act does
not confer exclusive jurisdiction on the Federal Court to decide whether
federal legislation is inconsistent with the rights and freedoms guaranteed by
the Charter. This court has jurisdiction to make such a determination.[42] However, it does not follow from this conclusion that s. 24(1)
applications are never within the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal courts.
The nature of the violation must be considered. If the violation is the result
of actions taken by a federal board that are not expressly authorized by
statute, then no issue as to the validity of legislation arises. In my opinion,
s. 24(1) applications for relief in respect to actions of a federal board
remain within the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal courts.

[45] The role that the Commission plays in determining the procedure to be
followed in the examination of witnesses under s. 17(1), has recently been the
subject of an extensive review by the Federal Court of Appeal in Restrictive
Trade Practices Commission et al. v. Irvine et al. (1982), 41 N.R. 375; 65
C.C.C.(2d) 108 (presently on appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada). Chief
Justice Thurlow states at p. 118:As there is no provision prescribing the procedure for the
examination of witnesses under s. 17(1), either at the inquiry stage or at any
other stage, in my opinion, it is for a member of the Commission to determine
what procedure should be followed. What the Commissioner prescribes will, no
doubt, depend on the particular proceeding. . . . [W]hether or not
cross-examination by persons whose conduct is under investigation or by their counsel
is to be permitted in the examination in the course of an inquiry of persons
under oath under s. 17(1) is, in my opinion, a matter for the decision of a
member of the Commission.[46] The Chief Justice went on to rule that it is for the Commission, subject
to the provisions for privacy contained in s. 27(1) of the Act, to determine
what persons will be permitted to attend the examinations of a person under s.
17(1). The only limitation of the Commission’s discretion in this regard is
that he does not have the right to bar counsel who represents the person being
examined, since that right is specifically provided in s. 20(1) of the Act.

respect to the enforcement thereof as any superior court in Canada has for the enforcement of subpoenas to witnesses, including the power to punish for disobedience
thereof. However, insofar as the power sought to be exercised is punitive in
naure, the member must, as a precondition to punishing an offending party,
apply to a court of competent jurisdiction for an order certifying that the
power may be exercised.[55] Also relevant to the issue of the compulsion of evidence is s. 20 of the
Act which provides that:20(1) A member of the Commission may allow any person whose
conduct is being inquired into and shall permit any person who is being himself
examined under oath to be represented by counsel.(2) No person shall be excused from attending and giving
evidence and producing books, papers, records or other documents, in obedience
to the order of a member of the Commission, on the ground that the oral
evidence or documents required of him may tend to criminate him or subject him
to any proceeding or penalty, but no oral evidence so required shall be used or
receivable against such person in any criminal proceedings thereafter
instituted against him, other than a prosecution for perjury in giving such
evidence or a prosecution under section 122 or 124 of the Criminal Code in
respect of such evidence.

[56] Section 20 provides a measure of protection against the abuse of the
broad investigative powers authorized under s. 17. Section 20(1) permits any
person being examined under oath to be represented by counsel. Section 20(2)
extends a limited protection against self-incrimination by providing that no
oral evidence that may tend to criminate a witness shall be used against such
witness in any subsequent criminal proceedings.[57] Briefly stated the applicants contend that s. 7 of the Charter operates
to guarantee the right to life, liberty and security of the person, and that a
necessary concomitant of one or more of these rights is the right not to be
compelled to give self-incriminating evidence. The applicants argue that s. 17,
which compels the giving of evidence, and s. 20, which provides that a person
is not excused from giving evidence on the ground that it may incriminate him,
constitute an interference with their right to life, liberty and security of
the person that is not in accordance with the principles of fundamental
justice.[58] In order to pronounce on the merits of the applicants’ position with
respect to the investigative powers authorized by s. 17 of the Act, it
is necessary to first examine the standard of judicial review authorized by the
phrase “fundamental justice”, and the scope of the phrase “life, liberty and
security of the person” as contained in s. 7 of the Charter.

There is a distinction to be drawn in respect of the privilege
which is commanded by the experience with it in this country and in the United States. The point in the criminal process at which the privilege can be asserted is
one thing; what the privilege embraces at that point is something else. It is
my conclusion that the point of assertion has been fixed in s. 2(d) and I do
not think I can invoke s. l(a) to shift it to a stage which would make it
effective against s. 223.[65] The respondents contend that the reasons of Mr. Justice Laskin apply
with equal force to the present consideration. They suggest that s. 11 (c) of
the Charter sets the point at which the right not to be compelled to give
evidence arises, and s. 7 cannot be invoked to give rise to a similar right at
an earlier stage.[66] While there is some force in this suggestion, I do not believe that it
necessarily follows that since s. 1(a) of the Bill of Rights cannot be
invoked to enlarge upon the rights specifically enumerated elsewhere in that
legislation, that s. 7 of the Charter cannot be invoked to enlarge upon
the rights provided elsewhere in the Charter.[67] It cannot be over-emphasized that the enactment of the Constitution
Act, 1982, and the Charter contained therein, has fundamentally
changed the role the courts play in enforcing rights and freedoms. In my view,
in light of this fundamental change, it is incumbent on the courts to review
the issues that arise under the Charter without being unduly influenced
by pre-Charter decisions.

[68] The usefulness of cases decided under the Bill of Rights, in
determining issues which arise under the Charter, has been considered by
Tallis, J.A., in R. v. Therens (1983), 23 Sask. R. 81; 33 C.R.(3d) 204,
(Sask. C.A.). In that case the meaning of the term “detained” as used in s. 10
of the Charter was in issue. It was argued that the meaning of the word
“detained” should be the same as that attributed to the term in R. v.
Chromiak (1980), 29 N.R. 441; 12 C.R.(3d) 300; 102 D.L.R.(3d) 368,
(S.C.C.). In rejecting this view Tallis, J.A., stated at page 220:I am of the opinion that the principles enunciated in R. v.
Chromiak and R. V. Dedman [(1981), 23 C.R.(3d) 228] are not
determinative of the issues in this case. While cases under statutes such as
the Bill of Rights, R.S.C. 1970, App. III, may be of interpretative
assistance, it must be remembered that the Charter stands on an entirely
different basis. It is not a mere cannon of construction for the interpretation
of federal legislation: vide R. v. Drybones, [1910] S.C.R. 282, 10
C.R.W.S. 334, 71 W.W.R. 161, [1970] 3 C.C.C. 355, 9 D.L.R.(3d) 473.

This court indicated in the Curr case how foreign to
our constitutional traditions, to our constitutional law and to our conceptions
of judicial review was any interference by a court with the substantive content
of legislation. No doubt, substantive content had to be measured on an issue of
ultra vires even prior to the enactment of the Canadian Bill of
Rights, and necessary interpretative considerations also had and have a
bearing on substantive terms. Of course, the Canadian Bill of Rights, introduced
a new dimension in respect of the operation and application of federal law, as
the judgments of this court have attested. Yet it cannot be forgotten that it
is a statutory instrument, illustrative of Parliament’s primacy within the
limits of its assigned legislative authority, and this is a relevant
consideration in determining how far the language of the Canadian Bill of
Rights should be taken in assessing the quality of federal enactments which
are challenged under s. 1(a). There is as much a temptation here as there is on
the question of ultra vires to consider the wisdom of the legislation,
and I think it is our duty to resist it in the former connection as in the
latter.[72] The enactment of the Constitution Act, 1982 has, changed the
fundamental principle underlying the Curr case. The courts now have a
constitutional jurisdiction to review legislation; the Charter is not
merely a statutory instrument. Therefore, in my view, it is incumbent on the
courts to reconsider the reasoning in Curr in light of these fundamental
changes.

reviewed by the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Reference Re Section
94(2) of Motor Vehicle Act R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 288 (1983), 33 C.R.(3d) 22.
That court in dealing with the issue of whether s. 7 of the Charter should
be given substantive effect, chose not to treat the statements made in Curr,
with respect to s. 1(a) of the Bill of Rights, as being determinative of
that issue.[74] For the above reasons, I conclude that the Curr case is not
determinative of the relationship between s. 7 and ss. 8 to 14. The proper
relationship between these provisions should be determined through an
examination of the Charter itself, bearing in mind the purpose and the
constitutional nature of that document.[75] It is suggested that a rule of statutory interpretation, expressed in
the maxim expressio unius est exclusio alterius - the expression of one
thing is the exclusion of another - should apply. As a matter of statutory
interpretation, it is argued, the express right not to be compelled to be a
witness provided in s. 11(c) necessarily precludes the implication of a similar
right in s. 7. It is also argued that the protection against self-incrimination
provided in s. 13 precludes the implication of similar protection in s. 7.
