[76] The problem with this argument is that it assumes that a constitutional
document should be construed according to the ordinary rules of statutory
interpretation. The fallacy of such a view has been pointed out in Minister
of Home Affairs v, Fisher, [1980] A.C. 319; [1979] 3 All E.R. 21. That case
involved the interpretation of the word “child” as used in the Bermuda
Constitution Act, 1967. It was argued that the Constitution should be
interpreted the same as any English statute, thus, a presumption that the word
“child” means ligitimate child should apply. Lord Wilberforce, in giving the
opinion of the Privy Council, dealt with this argument as follows at page 329:. . . [T]he question must inevitably be asked whether the
appellants’ premise, fundamental to their argument, that these provisions are
to be construed in the manner and according to the rules which apply to Acts of
Parliament, is sound. In their Lordships’ view there are two possible answers
to this. The first would be to say that, recognizing the status of the
Constitution as, in effect, an Act of Parliament, there is room for
interpreting it with less rigidity, and greater generosity, than other Acts,
such as those which are concerned with property, or succession, or citizenship.
On the particular question this would require the court to accept as a starting
point the general presumption that ‘child’ means ‘legitimate child’ but to
recognize that this presumption may be more easily displaced. The second would
be more radical: it would be to treat a constitutional instrument such as this
as sui generis, calling for principles of interpretation of its own, suitable
to its character as already described, without necessary acceptance of all the
presumptions that are relevant to legislation of private law.

It is possible that, as regard the question now for decision,
either method would lead to the same result. But their Lordships prefer the
second. This is in no way to say that there are no rules of law which should
apply to the interpretation of a constitution. A constitution is a legal
instrument giving rise, amongst other things, to individual rights capable of
enforcement in a court of law. Respect must be paid to the language which has
been used and to the traditions and usages which have given meaning to that language.
It is quite consistent with this, and with the recognition that rules of
interpretation may apply, to take as a point of departure for the process of
interpretation a recognition of the character and origin of the instrument, and
to be guided by the principle of giving full recognition and effect to those
fundamental rights and freedoms with a statement of which the Constitution
commences. In their Lordships’ opinion this must mean approaching the question
what is meant by ‘child’ with an open mind.[77] Approaching the interpretation of the Charter in this manner,
guided by the principle of giving full recognition and effect to the rights and
freedoms guaranteed therein, and considering the language used in the Charter,
I see no reason to view ss. 8 to 14 as imposing limits on the rights bestowed
by s. 7.

[78] Section 26 of the Charter indicates an intention that the
enunciated rights should not be construed as excluding rights not expressly
mentioned. Section 26 of the Charter provides as follows:26. The guarantee in this Charter of certain rights and
freedoms shall not be construed as denying the existence of any other rights or
freedoms that exist in Canada.[79] In addition, s. 1 provides that the rights guaranteed by the Charter
are subject “only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be
demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society”. In light of this
general limitation it would seem unnecessary and inappropriate to read further
restrictions into s. 7.[80] In my view, the specific rights enumerated in s. 8 to s. 14 are specific
examples or emanations of the general right to life, liberty and security of
the person, and the specific mention of these rights serves to reinforce the
general rights secured by s. 7, rather than to restrict them.[81] Although the specific rights enumerated in s. 8 to s. 14 may come within
the scope of the compendious phrase “life, liberty and security of the person”,
the framers of the Charter in placing certain specific rights outside of
s. 7 afforded them an additional measure of sanctity. Under s. 7 a person may
be deprived of his rights if the deprivation is in accordance with the
principles of fundamental justi’ce. The specific rights in ss. 8 to 14 are not
so limited.

[82] If the relationship between s. 7 and the following sections is viewed in
this way, s. 11(c) does not preclude a right not to be compelled to be a
witness against oneself from arising before a person is charged. Rather, s.
11(c) provides additional protection by setting the point at which the right
not to be compelled to be a witness against oneself is no longer subject to
possible deprivation in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.[83] Similarly, s. 13 guarantees to a witness the specific right not to have
self-incriminating evidence used against him in other proceedings. This is a
separate right which arises regardless of whether the witness testifies
voluntarily or under compulsion. This positive right conferred by s. 13 should
not be taken as a constitutional adoption of the statutory scheme established
by s. 5 of the Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10. There is
nothing in s. 13 that expressly makes a person compellable to give
self-incriminating evidence. Although s. 13 is similar to s. 5(2) of the Canada
Evidence Act, and s. 20(2) of the Combines Investigation Act, there
is no equivalent to s. 5(1) of the Canada Evidence Act, or to s. 17(2)
of the Combines Investigation Act, contained in the Charter. The
restrictive provisions of these latter sections should not be read into the Charter
as necessarily implicit in the positive rights conferred by s. 13.

[84] For these reasons I would hold that the specific rights in s. 11(c) and
s. 13 do not necessarily preclude a more general right against the compelling
of self-incriminating evidence from being within the scope of s. 7. It remains
to be considered whether the compelling of such evidence, as authorized by s.
17 of the Act, is an interference with a person’s right to liberty and
security of the person.[85] I do not propose to attempt any exhaustive definition of the range of
rights encompassed by the phrase “life, liberty and security of the person”.
Indeed, it would be impossible to define the scope of this phrase with any
degree of exactness. The boundaries of this broad right will undoubtedly be
developed by the courts interstitially as different claims arise.[86] In the present case the applicants allege that the phrase includes a
right not to compelled to give self-incriminating evidence. This claim does not
require any judicial exploration of the penumbra of the right to life, liberty
and security of the person. Although the right to life is not in issue here, in
my view, the privilege against self-incrimination is deeply rooted in the right
to liberty and security of the person.[87] The history of the privilege against self-incrimination is well
documented in Levy, Origins of The Fifth Amendment, New York: Oxford
University Press, 1968. Levy points out that the privilege against
self-incrimination was at the root of the historic struggle for individual
liberty.

[88] Furthermore, the phrase “security of the person” includes a right to
personal dignity and a right to an area of privacy or individual sovereignty
into which the state must not make arbitrary or unjustified intrusions. These
considerations also underly the privilege against self-incrimination.[89] In the landmark American case, Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436; 16 L. ed. (2d) 694; 86 S.Ct. 1602, the United States Supreme Court examined the
historical and policy underpinnings of the privilege against
self-incrimination. Chief Justice Warren, in delivering the opinion of the
court, made the following remarks at page 460:Thus we may view the historical development of the privilege
as one which groped for the proper scope of governmental power over the
citizen. . . . All of these policies point to one overriding thought: the
constitutional foundation underlying the privilege is a respect a government -
state or federal - must accord to the dignity and integrity of its citizens.[90] The policy underlying the privilege against self-incrimination is also
examined at length in Wigmore on Evidence, vol. 8 (McNaughton Revision,
1961), s. 2251. Wigmore concludes that there are only two valid purposes to the
privilege. He identifies these purposes at page 318:The first is to remove the right to an answer in the hard
cores of instances where compulsion might lead to inhumanity, the principal
inhumanity being abusive tactics by a zealous questioner. The second is to
comply with the prevailing ethic that the individual is sovereign and that
proper rules of battle between government and individual require that the
individual not to be bothered for less than good reason and not to be
conscripted by his opponent to defeat himself.

[91] Section 7 of the Charter has given constitutional recognition to
the principle that the individual is sovereign, and that there are limits to
the valid exercise of governmental authority over the individual. One such
limit, that is deeply rooted in the individual’s right to “liberty and security
of the person”, is that a person should not be compelled to incriminate
himself.[92] I am mindful that the Ontario Court of Appeal in R. v. Altaeimer (1983),
1 C.C.C.(3d) 7, has held that the Charter does not confer a broad
privilege against self-incrimination. In that case the Ontario Court of Appeal
referred to a brief review of the common law privilege against
self-incrimination made by Dickson, J., in R. v. Marooux and Solomon (1976),
4 N.R. 64; 24 C.C.C.(2d) 1, at page 5 and cited his conclusion as follows:In short, the privilege extends to the accused qua witness
and not qua accused, it is concerned with testimonial compulsion
specifically and not with compulsion generally.. . .[93] The Ontario Court of Appeal in stating that the Charter does not
confer a broad privilege against self-incrimination was merely concluding that
s. 11(c) and s. 13 of the Charter apply only to testimonial compulsion.
However, the court did not consider the nature of the rights secured by s. 7.
In my view the Altseimer case should not be viewed as holding that the
compelling of self-incriminating evidence is not an interference with the
rights secured by s. 7.

[94] The respondents raise an additional issue related to the proper scope of
s. 7. They contend that even if s. 7 does encompass the right not to be
compelled to give self-incriminating evidence, the beneficial provisions of s.
7 do not extend to corporations. They argue that the term “everyone”, as used
in s. 7 does not include corporations. Thus, they argue, the corporate applicants
cannot enjoy rights secured by s. 7.[95] Although this issue of whether or not the beneficial provisions of s. 7
extend to corporations may be critical in certain applications, it is not
necessary to decide this issue in the present case.[96] As I have indicated earlier in these reasons, this court’s jurisdiction
in this matter is limited to a determination of the validity of the impugned
provisions of the Act. If s. 17 is inconsistent with the rights of the
individual applicants, then it is of no force or effect. In my view, the
possibility that the same provision may not be inconsistent with the rights of
the corporate applicants is irrelevant. If the provision is inconsistent with
any rights secured by the Charter, it must be held invalid. It is not
the proper function of this court to rewrite the impugned provision in order to
remedy the inconsistency by making it applicable only to persons whose rights
may not be protected.

[97] However, before leaving this issue, I would like to make some general
comments on the respondents’ submissions.[98] I do not believe that the issue of whether the rights guaranteed by s. 7
extend to corporations can be determined on a narrow and technical
interpretation of the term “everyone”. Regard must be had to the nature of the
rights provided by that section.[99] This approach was adopted in Southern Inc. v. Hunter et al. (1982),
42 A.R. 109; 68 C.C.C.(2d) 356 (Alberta Q.B.), by Mr. Justice Cavanagh in
determining whether the term “everyone” as used in s. 8 of the Charter includes
corporations. He expressed his view as follows at page 364:I would hold that ‘everyone’ as used in section 8 should
include all human beings and all entities that are capable of enjoying the
benefit of security against unreasonable search. This then would include corporations.
That interpretation would not be inconsistent in the other sections where the
word ‘everyone’ is used where only human beings can enjoy the rights given.[100] This statement has been adopted by Scollin, J., in Balderstone v. R.
and Manitoba, Attorney General of (1983), 19 Man. R.(2d) 321; 2 C.C.C. (3d)
37 (Manitoba Q.B.). In that case, Mr. Justice Scollin concluded that a
corporation is entitled to the legal rights guaranteed by the Charter, including
those secured by s. 7.

[101] A similar approach to that adopted by Cavanagh, J., has also been taken
by at least one member of the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Re PPG
Industries Canada Ltd. and Attorney General of Canada (1983), 3 C.C.C.(3d)
97. In that case the court was called upon to determine whether the right to a
jury trial provided in s. 11(f) of the Charter should be extended to
corporations. The issue turned on the meaning to be given to the term “person”.
Nemetz, C.J.B.C., delivering one of the majority judgments stated at page 103:In my view, the context dictates that a restricted meaning be
given to the word ‘person’. In the context of section 11(f), ‘person’ must mean
a natural person, since it is only such natural persons who can be subjected to
imprisonment for five years or more.[102] The approach adopted in these cases seems to me to be a sensible one.
There is no need to ascribe to the term “everyone” a technical meaning, and
then to adopt that meaning wherever that term appears.[103] Since the term “everyone” is capable of including non-natural persons,
in my view, it should be construed as including such where the rights secured
are capable of being enjoyed by non-natural persons. Such an approach is in
accordance with the principle of giving a broad and liberal interpretation to a
constitutional document.

[104] In summary, it is my opinion that s. 7 should be given a broad scope,
that the specific rights enumerated in s. 8 to s. 14 should be viewed as
reinforcing the broad general rights secured by s. 7, and that the right to
“life and liberty of the person” secured by s. 7 encompasses a right not to be
compelled to give self-incriminating evidence.(b) The Standard of Fundamental Justice[105] Having concluded that a right not to be compelled to give
self-incriminating evidence is within the scope of s. 7, it becomes clear that
Part II of the Act constitutes an interference with this right. Section
17 makes a person compellable, and s. 20(2) provides that a person is not
excused from giving evidence on the ground that the evidence may tend to
incriminate him. However, the crucial issue is whether this interference is in
accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.[106] A determination of this issue necessarily involves a consideration of
what standard of judicial review is contemplated by the phrase “principles of
fundamental justice”. Does this phrase contemplate substantive review or merely
procedural review? In either case what yardstick is suggested to measure
whether legislation, which interferes with protected rights, is in accordance
with the principles of fundamental justice?

[107] If the phrase “principles of fundamental justice” merely contemplates
procedural review, then legislation is open to attack only on the ground that
the procedure prescribed or adopted for the achievement of certain policies
falls below a minimum acceptable standard recognized as being indispensable for
the enjoyment of life, liberty and security of the person. On the other hand,
if the phrase contemplates substantive review, then legislation is also open to
attack on the ground that the policies are in themselves incompatible with the
enjoyment of such rights.[108] The Bill of Rights contains a similar provision to s. 7 of the Charter,
except s. 1(a) of the Bill of Rights uses the phrase “due process of
law” instead of “the principles of fundamental justice”. The courts in
interpreting the due process clause in the Bill of Rights have
consistently held that all that is meant by this phrase is that established
legal pro cedure must be followed: see for example, Re State of Wisconsin
and Armstrong (1973), 32 D.L.R.(3d) 265 (F.C.A.).[109] The fact that the framers of the Charter decided not to use the
due process of law clause in the Charter would seem to indicate a desire
that s. 7 be given a broader interpretation than that attributed to s. 1(a) of
the Bill of Rights.

[110] In Curr v. The Queen, supra, Laskin, J. (as he then was),
although he did not expressly rule out the possibility that the due process
clause in s. 1(a) of the Bill of Rights could be used as a means of
challenging the validity of substantive legislation, indicated that he would be
reluctant to employ a statutory jurisdiction to deny effect to substantive
legislation. As I have pointed out earlier, the entrenchment of the Charter
has removed this constraint. The courts now have a constitutional jurisdiction
to deny effect to substantive legislation that is inconsistent with the
provisions of the Charter. Section 52 of the Constitutional Act, 1982
expressly imposes this duty on the courts.[111] The phrase “principles of fundamental justice” is used in s. 2(e) of the
Bill of Rights. This section has received judicial consideration by the
Supreme Court of Canada in Duke v. The Queen (1972), 28 D.L.R.(3d) 129.
In that case Chief Justice Fauteux remarked as follows at page 134:Under s. 2(e) of the Bill of Rights no law of Canada shall be construed or applied so as to deprive him of ‘a fair hearing in accordance
with the principles of fundamental justice’. Without attempting to formulate
any final definition of those words, I would take them to mean, generally, that
the tribunal which adjudicates upon his rights must act fairly, in good faith,
without bias and. in a judicial temper, and must give to him the opportunity
adequately to state his case.

However, the context in which the phrase is used in s. 2(e) must be considered.
It is used in reference to the right to a fair hearing which is a procedural
right. The Chief Justice was not merely defining the phrase “principles of fundamental
justice”, he was considering what is meant by the phrase “a fair hearing in
accordance with the principles of fundamental justice”. In my view, the
statement of Chief Justice Fauteux is not particularly helpful in determining
the meaning of the phrase as it appears in s. 7. In s. 7 the phrase “principles
of fundamental justice” appears in an entirely different context.[113] In this regard, I would refer to a note by John D. Whyte in (1983), 32
C.R.(3d) 107. Professor Whyte states at page 114:Section 2(e) of the Canadian Bill of Rights, R.S.C.
1970, App. III, in a context which is clearly limited to the notion of fair
hearing, uses the phrase ‘fundamental Justice’, and this incident of use may be
what led some to believe that ‘fundamental Justice’ was merely an alternative
to ‘natural justice’. Section 7 of the Charter is, of course, devoid of any
such contextual limitation and, from the point of view of initial impressions,
there is neither any reason to assume that ‘fundamental justice’ must be given
the restricted meaning of ‘natural Justice’ nor any reason not to see
‘principles of fundamental justice’ as encompassing the question of whether
substantive concepts of justice have been complied with. After all, the natural
reading to give to the word ‘justice’ is not a set of procedural standards, but
rather a political virtue applicable to the allocation of benefits and
punishments.

Section 7 of the Charter permits deprivations of
liberty only in accordance with the principles of fundamental Justice.
Considering the disruption of life, the assault upon human dignity and the
degradation associated with being taken into custody by a police agency, a
humanitarian consideration which I conceive to be a principle of fundamental
justice is that law should not jeopardize the right of the liberty of any
person save and except where the weight of compelling factors such as the need
for public protection, or the need to preserve public order, or the need of law
enforcement agencies to investigate crime and preserve evidence, or the
principles of general or individual deterrence - the legitimate interests of
society which justify an -interference with personal liberty - override the
importance of the right to liberty. The absence of such overriding factors in
the promulgation or perpetuation of a law which authorizes arrest ignores that
principle of fundamental justice.[120] Judge Kopstein went on to review the various provincial liquor acts and
concluded that the tendency among the majority of jurisdictions across this
country is to avoid arrest and punitive detentions for intoxication alone. He
went on to hold, at page 370, that under s. 97(b) of the Indian Act:The power to arrest and the loss of liberty which will result
from the exercise of that power does not rest upon any factor which is so
important to the interests of society as to bring it within a principle of
fundamental justice.

In the Canadian legal fabric, offences which carry a minimum
penalty of a term of imprisonment are rare. I have searched in vain for any
such offence which imposes a burden of absolute liability. The fact that s.
94.1(2) and (3) stand alone in that respect is significant. A serious problem
was seen to exist and Draconian measures were thought necessary to deal with
it. However, those measures went far beyond what has, in the past, been seen as
reasonable by any other Legislature.[123] Judge Paradis, at page 246, then referred to the following quote by Mr.
Justice Rand in his article “Except by Due Process of Law” (1961), 2 Osgoode
Hall, L.J. 171:At certain dimensions we can without doubt pronounce
legislation outside of the bounds of traditional process, as where the issue of
river-pilot licenses is limited to persons of blood relation to presently
licensed pilots; or legislation that eliminates most women as barmaids; or
legislation that would take property for an exclusively private purpose, or for
a public purpose without compensation. With such departures from the norm of
living tradition we have no difficulty and they give a clue to the character of
action which due process condemns.[124] Judge Paradis then stated his conclusions as follows at page 247:In my view, to automatically deprive a citizen of his liberty
by a process of absolute liability can only be seen as a ‘departure from the
norm of living tradition’.

[125] In R. v. Carriere, supra, Ontario Provincial Court Judge Belanger
held that the legislation creating writs of assistance constitute a violation
of the right to life, liberty and security of the person that is not in
accordance with the principles of fundamental justice. In holding that s. 7
should be given a substantive effect he stated at page 130:It follows that those legal processes hitherto recognized by
Parliament and the courts are no longer necessarily the standards justifying
deprivation of the right to liberty and security of the person.He went on to state his reasons for finding writs of assistance
to be inconsistent with s. 7 of the Charter as follows at page 131-32:I am of the view that writs of assistance offend the
principles of fundamental justice. The history of the development of our
criminal law is also the history of the development of restrictions and
controls on the actions of individuals charged with the enforcement of that
law. Our democratic society’s will, legislatively expressed, has progressively
become more hesitant to grant wide discretion to the enforcer lest he, quite
apart from wrongful or illegal motives, confuse his duty with his own view of
the law and lend his own colour to events giving rise to collectively defined
rights and wrongs. To this date the only working method devised to adequately
monitor his actions has been the interposition of independent judicial scrutiny
at every significant juncture in the criminal process. It is a method which is
far from perfect, because it is cumbersome and often inexpedient, but it is
difficult to conceive of a better one.

One such juncture - and a most crucial one - arises when
police forces are required to invade a person’s privacy in order to obtain
evidence of crime. There can be no doubt that privacy cannot be held up in all
circumstances as a shield to prevent the detection of crime, but I conceive
that it is so important and fundamental a concept in our society that
interference with it should occur only when it is clear and has been demonstrably
made clear that it cannot stand as an impediment to our collective right to
protection from crime. Convenience and expediency merit consideration only to
the extent that they are reconcilable with that concept.[126] Several themes reoccur in these cases that are possible yardsticks for
reviewing substantive legislation. These are: the historical development of
rights protected by the common law, the legislative tradition in Canada as found in an analogous existing legislation, and community standards or the
“living tradition”. There is also reference to the need for compelling factors
to justify placing the collective interests of society ahead of the rights of
the individual.[127] While I am not suggesting that these concepts make substantive review a
simple matter of application, I do believe that these concepts can provide
useful guidance.[128] With this by way of background, I now turn to examine whether the
interference with the applicants’ right to liberty and security of the person,
as authorized by s. 17 of the Act, is in accordance with the principles
of fundamental justice.

[129] The common law privilege against self-incrimination developed out of
public resentment of the Court of Star Chamber procedure, and in particular the
oath ex officio. (For a complete historical development of the privilege
see: Levy, Origins Of The Fifth Amendment, supra.)[130] Professor Ratushny traces the development of the privilege in his book, Self-incrimination
In The Canadian Criminal Process, Toronto: Carswell, 1979. He points out
that the offensive nature of the Star Chamber procedure was that arbitrary
power was exercised in subjecting persons to inquiries under oath for the
purpose of making out an accusation against them. He states at page 172:The repugnance was found in the procedure whereby a person
would be called before Judges without any specific allegation of wrong-doing on
his part and subjected to a broad range of questions.[131] During the 16th century the common law courts began to restrict the Star
Chamber by granting prohibition against the administering of the oath ex
officio. In so doing, they began to state the general rule, nemo tenetur
prodere seipsum, or no one is bound to betray himself. Professor Ratushny
refers to this development at page 169:Although the Latin phrase has been the subject of considerable
analysis, its precise origins are not clear. However, it is quite possible that
in the 16th century common law courts, it was merely an impressive way of
stating the existing common law rule that no man was bound to produce the
accusation against himself.

[132] A classic statement of the common law privilege against
self-incrimination that evolved from these historic roots is found in Lamb
v. Munster (1882), 10 Q.B. 110. At page 113 Stephen, J., states the rule as
follows:It is not that a man must be guilty of an offence and say
substantially, ‘I am guilty of the offence, but I am not going to furnish
evidence of it.’ I do not think the privilege is so narrow as that, for then it
would be illusory. The extent of the privilege is I think this: the man may
say, ‘if you are going to bring a criminal charge, or if I have reason to think
a criminal charge is going to be brought against me, I will hold my tongue.
Prove what you can, but I am protected from furnishing evidence against myself
out of my own mouth’.[133] Canadian legislative tradition has long since parted company with the
common law privilege. The Canada Evidence Act of 1893 contained a
provision substantially the same as the present s. 5. (For a review of the
history and debate surrounding the original Canada Evidence Act see:
Noble, ‘The Struggle To Make The Accused Competent In England And Canada’
(1970), 8 Osgoode Hall, L.J. 249.)

[134] The original Canada Evidence Act of 1893 made the accused
competent but not compellable, and made other witnesses compellable to answer
questions which may tend to incriminate them, while protecting them from use of
the evidence in subsequent criminal proceedings against themselves.[135] Criminal trials were clearly the focus of concern that lead to the
removal of the common law privilege against self-incrimination, but the
language was not restricted to criminal proceedings. As administrative bodies
began to play an increasing role in the investigation of criminal activities,
s. 5 of the Canada Evidence Act, and its provincial equivalents, were
applied to these forms of inquiry. However, the removal of a witness’s
privilege against self-incrimination in administrative inquiries gives rise to
entirely different considerations.[136] The focus of the criminal proceedings is the conduct of the accused; its
purpose is to determine the guilt or innocence of the accused. In criminal
proceedings the accused’s privilege against self-incrimination is protected, at
trial, by his statutory right of non-compellability, and at the pre-trial
stage, by the exclusionary rules of evidence.[137] A witness in a criminal proceeding is compellable to testify as to the
activities or conduct of the accused. The removal of the witnesses’ privilege
against self-incrimination may result in the witness being compelled to reveal
self-incriminating evidence. But that is not the purpose of the compulsion. The
compelling of self-incriminating evidence is merely incidental to the purpose
of the criminal proceeding.

[138] The removal of the privilege from witnesses in criminal proceedings
reflects a policy that the incidental incrimination of a witness must not be
allowed to thwart the legitimate purpose of the proceedings: the just
determination of the guilt or innocence of the accused.[139] An administrative inquiry, on the other hand, may be directed at
uncovering illegal activity on the part of the witness. The denial of that
witness’s privilege against self-incrimination in this situation may result in

[A]ny system of administration which permits the prosecution
of trust habitually to compulsory self-disclosure as a source of proof must
itself suffer morally thereby. The inclination develops to rely mainly upon
such evidence, and to be satisfied with an incomplete investigation of the
other sources. The exercise of the power to extract answers begets a
forgetfulness of the Just limitations of that power. The simple and peaceful
process of questioning breeds a readiness to resort to bullying and to physical
force and torture. If there is a right to an answer, there soon seems to be a
right to the expected answer, that is, to a confession of guilt. Thus the
legitimate use grows into the unjust abuse; ultimately, the innocent are jeopardized
by the encroachments of a bad system. Such seems to have been the course of
experience in those legal systems where the privilege was not recognized.[151] I am also of the opinion that the protection against subsequent use of
self-incriminating testimony provided in s. 20(2) of the Act and s. 13
of the Charter does not justify the result dictated by s. 17. The
protection against subsequent use of self-incriminating evidence may be
adequate in situations in which the witness is not an accused or a suspect, but
such protection falls short of the standard of fundamental justice in
situations in which the witness is compelled to assist in an investigation of
his own misconduct.

have been infringed or denied” (emphasis added). This would seem to rule out an
application in respect of an impending violation. However, for the several
reasons that follow, it is my view that this section should not be construed so
narrowly.

[160] First, this is not an ordinary statute; it is a constitutional document
which “guarantees the rights and freedoms set out in it”.[161] The famous statement made by Lord Sankey, L.C., in Edwards v.
Attorney General for Canada, [1930] A. C. 124 (P.C.), in reference to the British
North America Act are equally applicable to the Constitution Act, 1982,
and the Charter of Rights contained therein. His Lordship stated at page
136:The British North America Act planted in Canada a living tree capable of growth and expansion within its natural limits. The object of the Act
was to grant a Constitution to Canada. . . .Their Lordships do not conceive it to be the duty of this
Board - it is certainly not their desire - to cut down the provisions of the Act
by a narrow and technical construction, but rather to give it a large and
liberal interpretation. . . .[162] I would also refer to the following statement made by Tallis, J.A., of
the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal in R. V. Therens, supra, at page 221,
which is to the same effect:Our nation’s constitutional ideals have been enshrined in the Charter
and it will not be a ‘living’ charter unless it is interpreted in a meaningful
way from the standpoint of an average citizen who seldom has a brush with the
law, . . . The implementation and application of the Charter should not
be blunted or thwarted by technical or legalistic interpretations of ordinary
words of the English language. Using this approach, our citizens will not be
placed in a position of feeling that the statements in the Charter are
only rights in theory. If these rights are to survive and be available on a
day-to-day basis we must resist the temptation to opt in favour of a
restrictive approach.

[163] If s. 24(1) is interpreted so that persons will be denied access to the
Courts until their rights have actually been violated, persons will be left
without an effective means of enforcing their rights, and the rights will be
rights only in theory.[164] Secondly, a literal reading of s. 24(1) would mean that a person must
establish a violation of his rights before bringing an application for a
remedy. Of course, this is not how the section is being applied. In practice, a
person must establish a violation of his rights as a necessary step in his
application for a remedy. In other words, the establishment of a violation of
rights is pre-requisite to the obtaining of a remedy. It is not a pre-requisite
to the commencing of a s. 24(1) application. There should be no doubt that in
order to bring a s. 24(1) application it is necessary only that the applicant
allege that his rights have been infringed or denied.[165] Thirdly, s. 24(1) refers to rights being “infringed or denied”. If the
term “infringed” is to add anything to the term “denied” it must contemplate a
situation short of an actual denial of rights. In my view, the term “infringed”
should be given an independent meaning; the term is broad enough to encompass
present threats to a person’s rights or freedoms .

[166] It is not difficult to imagine situations in which a present threat of a
violation of a person’s rights may lead to consequences that are as detrimental
as an actual violation. A useful example of such a situation is posited by
Professor Gibson in Tarnopolsky and Beaudoin, Ed., The Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms, Toronto: Carswell, 1982, at 498-99. Professor Gibson
states that where the law empowers authorities to infringe rights or freedoms
in some arbitrary fashion, such as randomly searching homes in the hope of
finding evidence of illegal activity, the threat of an impending violation has
immediate restrictive consequences. He points out that the threat of such
illegal searches may cause persons to take immediate protective steps, such as
the removal or destruction of innocent but suspicious or embarrassing material.
Thus, although the person’s rights have not actually been violated, the threat
of an impending violation constitutes an interference with the person’s
enjoyment of his rights. While such a situation may not constitute a “denial”
of a person’s rights, it can properly be termed an “infringement”.[167] I would conclude that if s.24(1) is given a broad and liberal interpretation, a person
will have standing to bring an application for an alleged impending violation
of his rights, and such an interpretation does not do violence to the words
actually used.

of a person’s rights, it can properly be termed an “infringement”.[167] I would conclude that if <legislation><fragment>s.</fragment></legislation>24(1) is given a broad and liberal interpretation, a person
will have standing to bring an application for an alleged impending violation
of his rights, and such an interpretation does not do violence to the words
actually used.

[168] This conclusion, however, does not mean that all persons alleging an
impending violation will be entitled to a remedy. Section 24(1) leaves the
matter of remedies in the discretion of the court. The imminence of the
impending violation of the applicant’s rights will likely be a factor in
deciding whether to exercise this discretion. (In this regard see: Spry, Equitable
Remedies (2d Ed.), London: Sweet & Maxwell, 1980 at p. 366-69.)[169] I would also note that s. 24 is a remedial section. This fact in itself
imposes some restrictions on who may make application under the section. A
remedy is a means by which a violation, of a right is redressed or prevented. A
declaration that a statute or portion thereof is invalid, will in certain cases
be a remedy. In situations where a person is convicted of an offence by
operation of a statute, and that statute is subsequently declared invalid, the
declaration will result in an acquittal, and is therefore a means of redress.
In other cases where there is a threat that a person will become subject to a
statutory provision that constitutes a violation of the person’s rights, a
declaration of invalidity will be a remedy in the sense that it will prevent an
impending violation of the person’s rights. Thus, in both of these situations a
declaration of invalidity pursuant to s. 52 of the Constitution Act, 1982,
is a remedy available under s. 24(1).

[170] If a person is unable to show that a right personal to him has been
violated or threatened, or he is unable to show that the threat of a violation
is immediate enough to justify the court exercising its discretion in favour of
granting a remedy, it may still be open to that person to challenge the
validity of legislation by means of an action pursuant to s. 52 of the Constitution
Act, 1982. In such a case the common law rules of standing as expounded by
the Supreme Court of Canada in Minister of Justice of Canada et al. v.
Boroweki (1982), 39 N.R. 331; 64 C.C.C.(2d) 97, would presumably apply.[171] Applying the foregoing analysis to the applicants’ motion for a
declaration that s. 45 of the Act is invalid, I would note, that
although the provisions of s. 45 may not be invoked at the present stage, there
is a present threat that the applicants will become subject to the provisions
of that section. Thus, the applicants are alleging an impending infringement of
their rights sufficient to give them standing to apply under s. 24(1) for the
declaration sought.[172] I now turn to the merits of the applicants’ position with respect to s.

[173] As I have indicated, the applicants allege that s. 45 of the Act is
inconsistent with their rights under s. 7 and s. 11(d) of the Charter. While
s. 45 can apply to prosecutions under the Act - that is to situations in
which a person is charged - it also can apply to proceedings before the
Commission in which no formal charges have been layed. In light of my earlier
conclusions with respect to the proper relationship between s. 7 and the other
legal rights contained in ss. 8 to 14 of the Charter, it should be obvious
that I would not preclude an argument being raised under s. 7 in situations in
which the person has not been charged. However, on this branch of the
applicants’ challenge to the Act, I believe that I can deal with the
arguments raised under s. 7 rather briefly.[174] The applicants’ position with respect to s. 7 seems to be based on an
assumption that any legislation that abrogates the common law principles of
evidence is not in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice. They
argue that at common law the mere production of documentary evidence was not
sufficient to make the documents admissible. In the case of private documents,
it was required that the court be satisfied that the document was duly executed
or that the origin and authorship the document was established before the
document could be introduced as evidence: see, Sopinka and Lederman, The Law
of Evidence In Civil Cases, Toronto: Butterworths, 1974, at page 429.

[175] The applicants cite R. v. Anthes Business Forms Ltd. et al. (1976),
10 O.R.(2d) 153, as authority for the proposition that s. 45 of the Act has
abrogated these common law principles and rules of evidence. However, authority
for that proposition is hardly needed. It is clear that s. 45 has changed the
common law rules of evidence, but that fact alone does not mean that it is
inconsistent with the applicants’ right to life, liberty and security of the
person. The applicants do not allege any specific interest, other than their
right to be presumed innocent, which is interfered with. For my part I find it
difficult to conceive what other fundamental right is abrogated by this change
in evidentiary rules. In this regard I wish to adopt a statement made by
Cartright, J., in Howard Smith Paper Mills Limited et al. v. The Queen, [1957]
S.C.R. 403 at 420:While s. 41 (now s. 45) [of the Act] makes a
revolutionary change in the law of evidence, it creates no offence, it takes
away no defence, it does not render criminal any course of conduct which was
not already so declared before its enactment, it does not alter the character
or legal effect of any transaction already entered into; it deals with a matter
of evidence only. . . .

[176] With respect to the applicants’ submission that s. 45 constitutes a
violation of the presumption of innocence, I consider it unnecessary to deal
with s. 7. Presumably s. 7 would only be resorted to where a person has not
been formally charged, that is at an investigatory stage. If the person
alleging the infringement of his right to be presumed innocent has been charged,
his interest will be squarely within the protection of s. 11(d).[177] I propose to examine whether s. 45 is inconsistent with a person’s
rights under s. 11(d). If s. 45 is not inconsistent with the presumption of
innocence in a situation in which a person has been charged, then it is
difficult to see how it could be offensive in situations where a person has not
been charged.[178] Section 11(d) has received extensive judicial consideration at appellate
court level. At least four appellate courts have dealt with s. 11(d): see, R.
v. Oakes (1983), 2 C.C.C.(3d) 339 (Ont. Ct. A.); R. V. Carroll (1983),
40 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 147; 115 A.P.R. 147 (P.E.I.C.A.); R. V. Cook (1983),
56 N.S.R. (2d) 449; 117 A.P.R. 449 (C.A.); R. v. Stanger; R. v. Bramwell
(1983), 46 A.R. 241 (Alta. C.A.). All of these cases involves successful
challenges to s. 8 of the Narcotics Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1.

A rebuttable presumption of law is a conclusion that a fact
(‘the presumed fact’) exists which must be drawn, in the absence of further
evidence, if another fact (‘the basic fact’) is proved ‘or admitted.[184] A permissive presumption is an inference that may, not must, be drawn
when a basic fact is proved.[185] Mr. Justice Martin then deals specifically with the term “prima facie
evidence” that is used in some statutes. He indicates that this term is capable
of contemplating either a permissive or a mandatory inference. At page 727 he
states as follows:Wigmore points out that the term ‘prima facie evidence’
is used in two senses. It is sometimes used as equivalent to the notion of a
presumption, even in the strict sense of a ruling of the judge putting upon the
opponent the duty of producing evidence. When the term prima facie is so used,
it is applied to the stage of the proceedings where the party having the legal
burden of proving the issue or the burden of persuasion, has not only removed
by producing sufficient evidence the duty of producing evidence to get past the
judge to the jury, but has gone further and, either by means of a presumption
or by a general mass of strong evidence, has entitled himself to a ruling that
the opponent should fail if he does nothing more in the way of producing
evidence. The second and more usual sense in which the term ‘prima facie
evidence’ is used is where the proponent having the first duty of producing
some evidence in order to pass the judge to the jury, has fulfilled that duty,
satisfied the Judge, and may properly claim the jury be allowed to consider his
case: see Wigmore on Evidence, 3rd ed. (1940), volume IX, pps. 293-94.

[186] Mr. Justice Martin finally defines a permissive presumption in these
terms at page 730:If the Crown establishes a prima facie case, in the
sense that it has produced evidence which requires the case to be submitted to
the Jury, the accused risks conviction if he fails to satisfy the
evidential burden of adducing evidence by way of explanation or denial, but he
will not necessarily be convicted. The Jury may not be satisfied beyond
a reasonable doubt of the accused’s guilt, even though there is evidence upon
which they could be so satisfied. Discharge of the evidential burden by
the accused is not a prerequisite to an acquittal: see Phipson on Evidence,
13th ed. (1982), at pp. 48-49.And at page 732 His Lordship defines a mandatory presumption as
follows:. .. [Upon] proof of the basic facts giving rise to the
presumption, the accused is not required to disprove an essential ingredient of
the offence on a balance of probabilities, it is sufficient for him to adduce
evidence which raises a reasonable doubt . . . . However, when the presumption
arises, if he fails to . adduce evidence (through the Crown witnesses or
defence witnesses) which raises a reasonable doubt with respect to those
elements, conviction will ensue.[187] After establishing these two types of statutory presumptions, his
Lordship held that a mandatory presumption should be treated the same as a
reverse onus provision for the purposes of s. 11(d). His conclusion in this
regard is stated as follows at page 733:

A mandatory presumption and a ‘reverse onus’ provision with
respect to an essential element of an offence have in common that when the
presumption arises and it is not displaced, the trier of fact is required to
find that the presumed fact has been proved. The essential difference between
the two is that in the case of a mandatory presumption (rebuttable presumption
of law) the presumption is displaced by evidence which is not rejected and
which raises a reasonable doubt as to the existence of the presumed fact. In
the case of a ‘reverse onus’ provision, the presumption is only displaced by
proof to the contrary on a balance of probability.In my view, it is their common feature, that is, the mandatory
nature of the conclusion required to be drawn when they arise, which requires
that they be treated alike for the purpose of determining their constitutional
validity.[188] Mr. Justice Martin concludes that reverse onus clauses and mandatory
presumptions will be held inconsistent with s. 11(d) of the Charter, unless
they satisfy the rational nexus test expounded in Oakee. It is implicit
in his reasons that a permissive presumption does not offend s. 11(d).[189] I am of the opinion that the prima facie presumptions arising
under s. 45 of the Act are of the permissive type.[190] I am reinforced in this conclusion by the Supreme Court of Canada
decision in Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen, [1969] 2
C.C.C. 189, reversing a judgment of the Appeal Court of Ontario, [1967] 3 CC.C.
149.

[191] In the Supreme Court of Canada, Ritchie, J., held at page 195 as
follows:Section 41(2)(c) [now s. 45] simply provides that documents,
such as these letters, which were in the possession of the accused ‘shall be
admitted in evidence without further proof thereof and shall be prima facie
evidence’ that the accused had knowledge of the documents and their contents
and that anything recorded in them as having been done, said or agreed upon by
the accused or its agent, was done, said or agreed upon. This does not mean
that the trial Judge, having accepted the letters as prima facie evidence
of their contents, is precluded from assessing the weight to be attached to
that evidence in considering the issue of the accused’s guilt or innocence.[192] Since the presumptions arising by virtue of s. 45 of the Act are
permissive presumptions, I hold that they are not inconsistent with the Charter.[193] The result is that the applicants are entitled to a declaration that s.
17 of the Combines Investigation Act is inconsistent with s. 7 of the Charter
and is therefore of no force or effect. The other relief sought by the
applicants is denied for the reasons given.[194] I make no order as to costs.Application allowed in part.

17</fragment> of the <title>Combines Investigation Act</title></legislation> is inconsistent with <legislation><fragment>s. 7</fragment> of the <title>Charter</title></legislation>

FACTS:2 Burlington leased to Baseline a dock in
Vancouver. The respondent Cerescorp Incorporated has operated the dock and
terminal facilities on the premises pursuant to an exclusive licence granted by
Baseline on April 14, 1988. Cerescorp was added as a party to these
proceedings by the Order of the Court of Appeal, on review. 3 Under the lease, Baseline was to pay
$600,000 to Burlington in the first five years of the lease. This amount was
payable in 60 monthly instalments of $10,000 commencing on March 1, 1988. 4 In May 1989, Baseline was in arrears and
on May 24, 1989 Burlington made a demand for payment of arrears which
stipulated that Baseline had 30 business days to pay or "Burlington
Northern shall re-enter the premises and declare the lease forfeited". 5 Baseline did not make payment of the
arrears until sometime in August of 1989 but apparently Burlington took no
steps to forfeit the lease. Baseline ceased making lease payments on August
31, 1989. 6 Clause 14(a) of the lease reads as
follows:14.(a) If
and whenever the rent hereby reserved or any part thereof shall not be paid on
the day specified for payment thereof, whether demanded or not or in case of
breach, non-performance or non-observance by the Lessee of any of the
covenants, agreements, or provisos on the part of the Lessee to be kept,
performed or observed herein or in case the Premises shall be vacated or remain
unoccupied for 15 days, then and in every case, it shall be lawful for the
Lessor to give notice that the term hereof shall be forfeited and void and
thereupon all of the right, title and interest of the Lessee hereunder shall
expire and cease absolutely and the Lessee shall thereupon quit and surrender
the Premises to the Lessor.

forfeited. The critical issue is whether the lease was terminated prior to the
appointment of the Trustee in Bankruptcy. 13 In his reasons for judgment the learned
judge below said, at p.154: In
the present case, Baseline failed to pay its rent within 7 days of the time
agreed upon under the lease and thus s.28(1)(a), rather than s.28(1(b), of the Commercial

input:
"Moore
v. Ullcoats Mining Co.
[1908] 1 Ch. 575, 77 L.J. Ch. 282, is authority for the proposition that a writ
claiming possession simpliciter and any further relief which is incidental
to a claim for possession is equivalent to re-entry. The claim for double
yearly value can only be valid if the lease is at an end. The language of sec.
14 [16?] of the Landlord and Tenant Act, R.S.B.C., 1911, ch. 126, is
explicit on this point in my opinion. If so, the claim is one incident to a
claim for possession." In
Standard Trusts, unlike in the case at bar, the claim for rent due was
incidental to a claim for pos­session. In
the present case, no covenant in the lease was breached nor was the lease
automatically terminated upon the bankruptcy of Baseline. Moreover, the demand
made by Burlington on August 15, 1991 could not be said to be equivalent in law
to re-entry. The demand was made in apparent anticipation of Baseline making
payment of arrears, as it had done before, and did not amount to an unequivocal
election to treat the lease as terminated. As
the lease was not forfeited prior to the appoint­ment of the Trustee in
Bankruptcy, the Trustee has the right to possess the leased land and premises
under s.30(1)(k) of the Bankruptcy Act, and s.32(2) of the Commercial
Tenancy Act.

that the learned judge below erred:A. in finding that the lease was not
forfeited and void prior to the appointment of the Trustee in Bankruptcy, and B. in finding that the appellants
were applying under s.28(1)(a) of the Commercial Tenancy Act and that
Baseline could have remained in possession by paying the rent in arrears (and
costs). DISCUSSION:15 With respect to ground A. the appellants
submit that the chambers judge erred in finding that the lease was not
forfeited and void prior to the appointment of the Trustee in Bankruptcy by the

to Baseline by the appellants on August 15, 1991 and Baseline's subsequent
inaction during the period of the notice. They submitted, alternatively, that
the lease came to an end when Burlington issued its petition pursuant to s.28
of the Commercial Tenancy Act which, Mr. Harney argued, constituted in

between Burlington and Baseline. Mr. Harney argued that the lease was
terminated on the giving of the notice of August 15, 1991 or, at the latest, 31
business days thereafter, the arrears of rent not having been paid in the
interval.

18 The first part of Clause 14(a) appears to
support the appellants' submission that the lease would be forfeited and void
upon the giving of the notice. However, the latter portion of clause 14(a)
provides that if the lessor intends to re-enter and forfeit the lease by reason
of the lessee's default, it must give the lessee at least 30 business days'
notice of its intention to re-enter and forfeit the lease and set out the
default complained of. The lessee would then have 30 business days to remedy
the default, after which time the lessor would be entitled to proceed to
re-enter the premises and forfeit the lease. Clause 14(a), read in its
entirety, clearly indicates that the lessor must do something beyond merely
giving the notice it gave in order to re-enter and forfeit the lease. 19 If clause 14(a) of the lease ended before
the term "PROVIDED THAT" and did not contain the words which follow,
it might have been open to Burlington, Mr. Edgson argued, simply to give notice
that the term shall be forfeited and thereupon the interest of the lessee would
be at an end and it would be obliged to deliver up the premises. But, he
submitted, the saving provision, on its true construction, clearly contemplated
and required a two step process calling for two notices. The first would
declare the term forfeit and the second, not to be acted upon by re-entering
for 30 business days, would give notice "of its intention to do so",
and during that period the lessee would have the right and opportunity to
remedy the default. No such second notice was given.

20 With respect to the notice itself, Mr.
Edgson submitted that, as the lease cannot be forfeited twice, that notice, without
more, cannot operate to forfeit the lease. It is in essence a demand for the
arrears of rent and, in the event of non-compliance, notice that the lease
shall, in the future, be forfeited and that Burlington then intends to
re-enter. However, it could not do so without giving the second notice
required by clause 14(a). 21 I think these submissions are sound. 22 In May of 1989 Burlington gave notice to
Baseline pursuant to paragraph 14(a) of the lease that Baseline was in default
of the payment of rent. The letter of May 24, 1989, after alleging the
default, stated: You
have thirty (30) business days to pay Burlington Northern $80,753.31 thereby
curing the default or Burlington Northern shall re-enter the premises and
declare the Lease forfeited. (emphasis added) Notwithstanding the giving of this
notice, Burlington took no steps to re-enter and forfeit the lease and in
August of 1989 the arrears were paid. 23 For convenience I will set out here again
the critical wording of the notice Burlington gave Baseline on August 15, 1991,

Summary
dispositions of conflicting claims between landlord and tenant are provided by
two separate pro­cedures outlined in ss.18 and 28 of the Commercial Tenancy
Act. Both sections are to be construed strictly: see Gulf Oil Can. Ltd. v.
Persall (1977), 75 D.L.R. (3d) 471 (B.C. Co. Ct.), and cases cited therein
at p.473. In addition, forfeitures are regarded with disfavour by the courts
and their upholding will be avoided even for trifling reasons: Big Valley
Collieries v. MacKinnon (1915), 9 W.W.R. 4, 23 D.L.R. 62 (Alta. T.D.). If
a landlord complains of a breach of covenant and seeks an order for possession,
he must elect from the start whether he is going to proceed under s.18 or s.28.
The crucial difference between the two sections is that s.18 requires a
determination or end to the lease on the part of the landlord by notice, before
he can move under s.18; but no such step to end the lease is required before
the landlord can proceed under s.28: Misarol Farms Ltd. v. Lemer (Prelutsky)
(1978), 6 B.C.L.R. 170 at 173, 5 R.P.R. 178 (Co. Ct.).

Since
it is a condition precedent to the jurisdic­tion of this court under s.18 of
the Commercial Tenancy Act that the lease must first be terminated and then
followed with a demand for possession, do the letters of 8th and 29th March and
20th April 1983 from the land­lord's solicitors to the tenant constitute
determination? It
is clear that the letter of 8th March 1983 is merely an indicated intention on
the part of the landlord to forfeit the lease if conformed use of the premises
by the tenant is not forthcoming. In
Re Simpson and Young & Biggin Ltd. (1971), 22 D.L.R. (3d) 291 (Ont.
C.A.), it was held that a notice by a landlord terminating a lease for
non-payment of taxes and demanding possession on a fixed date about a month
ahead was not sufficient to forfeit the lease since the notice itself contemplated
continued occupancy by the tenant. Such also is the situation here with the
letter of 29th March 1983 granting continued possession until 13th April 1983. The
letter of 20th April 1983 is nothing more than a demand for possession.
Although the demand for pos­session is also a condition precedent to the right
to invoke s.18, it cannot be served until after the lease has been
terminated: Re Anderson (1966), 56 W.W.R. 30, 57 D.L.R. (2d) 561 (B.C.
Co. Ct.).

Therefore,
at law, I must conclude that the pur­ported determination is not valid and a
necessary step to invoke s.18 has not been taken. Accordingly, on this
application under s.18, the court is without jurisdic­tion. 28 Mr. Harney stated in the course of his
argument that Burlington elected to proceed under s.28 rather than s.18
because, by doing so, it would not have the burden of proving that the lease
had been terminated by the notice of August 15, 1991. For the reasons which I
have given, that notice did not terminate the lease, nor did it demand
possession; it was nothing more than a demand for rent and a statement of
intention to forfeit the lease and re-enter. 29 It is incongruous for the appellants to
suggest that the lease was terminated and then bring its action pursuant to
s.28 of the Commercial Tenancy Act. An application under s.28 of the Commer­cial
Tenancy Act presupposes that the tenancy has not been determined. In the
result, until an order for possession is made, Baseline was still a tenant and,
at the time of the application before the learned chambers judge, the Trustee
in Bankruptcy had been appointed and s.32 of the Commercial Tenancy Act
and s.30(1)(k) of the Bankruptcy Act applied.

30 Mr. Harney then argued, in the
alternative, that by institut­ing proceedings under s.28 the appellants had in
law effected a re-entry and thereby brought the lease to an end. He referred
to Robinson, Little & Co. (Trustees of) v. Marlowe Yeoman
Ltd. (1986), 5
B.C.L.R. (2d) 67 (B.C.C.A.) where Craig J.A. said, at 71: Paragraph
7(a) of the lease provides that the landlord may determine the lease by
re-entry if the lessee breaches any of the conditions specified in the
paragraph. Mr. Mass, the associate counsel for the appellant on the appeal and
solicitor for the appellant, forwarded a notice to quit to the trustee on 20th
June stating that because of the breach, the lease was "terminated
immediately". The following day he forwarded a demand for possession. At
first blush, one might reasonably think that this would be tantamount to
re-entry, but English and Canadian text writers on the law of landlord and
tenant, citing cases, state that a notice to quit and demand for possession is not
tantamount to re-entry; Moore v. Ullcoats Mining Co., [1908] 1 Ch. 575; Prudential
Ins. Co. of Amer. v. McLean, [1943] O.R. 377, [1943] 3 D.L.R. 307 (C.A.); Chernec
v. Smith, [1946] 3 D.L.R. 765, [1946] O.W.N. 513 (C.A.); Winbaum v.
Ginou, [1947] O.R. 242, [1947] 2 D.L.R. 619. In Prudential Ins. Co. v.
McLean, the Ontario Court of Appeal pointed out that if a lease provides
for forfeiture by re-entry, the landlord's right to re-enter can be exercised
"... only by an actual re-entry, or by the issue of a writ ..." or
by taking some proceeding under a statutory authority to recover possession.

The
right that the landlord has under s.17 of The Landlord and Tenant Act is a
right to re-enter. This right can be exercised only by an actual re-entry, or
by the issue of a writ, or taking such a proceeding as the present to recover
possession. Notice of his intention to re-enter for non-payment of rent need
not be given by the landlord (s.18, subs.2), and where given it is not
effective to put an end to the lease when a re-entry is prescribed: Moore v.
Ullcoats Mining Company, Limited, [1908] 1 Ch. 575 at 588. When the
landlord has in fact re-entered, or has done the equivalent by taking proceed­ings
to eject the tenant, his determination to exercise his right of forfeiture so
evidenced is irrevocable. There is no equivalent to s.17 in the Commercial
Tenancy Act. 32 Further, the
Prudential case
is distinguishable because the lease there in question did not contain any
provision equivalent to clause 14(a) of the lease before us. Had it done so
s.17 of the Ontario Act would not have applied. 33 I am unable to accept Mr. Harney's
alternative submission. In Moore v. Ullcoats Mining
Co., supra,
Warrington J. at 587 stated the applicable principle thus:

landlord proceeds under sec.29 (a) then his demand must be one "to
pay the rent." If the landlord proceeds under sec. 29(b) then his

Quite
conceivably there could be no rent in arrears, or rent in arrears for a period
of less than seven days; while at the same time the tenant has made default in
observing a "covenant, term or condition of his tenancy * * * of such a
character as to entitle the landlord to re-enter or to determine the
tenancy." Obviously in such a "case" the landlord could not
proceed under sec. 29 (a) but could proceed under sec. 29 (b). Moreover,
if the landlord proceeds under sec. 29 (a), all the tenant need do to
retain or remain in possession is "to pay the rent" (and costs);
while if the landlord proceeds under sec. 29 (b) and is successful, mere

following the notice of August 15, 1991 and the passage of 30 business days

in bankruptcy. The Appellants petitioned for occupation of the Premises, not
for payment of the rent in arrears. 39 In view of the conclusion I have reached
with respect to the effect of the notice of August 15, 1991, I must reject this
ground of appeal. 40 In any event, since the only alleged

thereby be permitted to continue in its former tenancy. Therefore, the
proceeding by the appellants pursuant to s.28 of the Commercial Tenancy Act
based upon an alleged breach of non-payment of rent cannot be said to be an
unequivocal election by the appellants to treat the lease as terminated and an
action for possession simpliciter. As such, the lease would not be terminated
by the commencement of the action. 41 In my opinion the learned chambers judge
did not err.

Supreme Court of Prince Edward Island - Appeal
DivisionReference re
Remuneration of Judges of the Provincial Court of Prince Edward IslandDate: 1994-12-16G.L. Campbell and E.P. Rossiter, Q.C.,
for Attorney-General of Prince Edward Island.D. Sanderson, for accused persons
generally.P. Ghiz, for Omar Pineau, Robert Christie
and Merlin MacDonald.Court File No. AD-0570The judgment of the court was delivered by[1] Mitchell J.A.:—The Lieutenant-Governor in Council, pursuant to s. 18 of the Supreme
Court Act, R.S.P.E.I. 1988, c. S-10, referred the following questions to
this court for hearing and consideration:1. Can the Legislature of the Province of Prince Edward Island make
laws such that the remuneration of Judges of the Provincial Court may be
decreased, increased, or otherwise adjusted, either:(a) as part of
an overall public economic measure, or(b) in certain
circumstances established by law?2. If the answer to 1(a) or (b) is yes, then do the Judges of the
Provincial Court of Prince Edward Island currently enjoy a basic or sufficient
degree of financial security or remuneration such that they constitute an
independent and impartial tribunal within the meaning of Section 11(d) of the Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms and such other sections as may be
applicable?[2] The hearing took place from November 29 to
December 2, 1994, and during that time, the court heard submissions on behalf
of the Attorney-General of Prince Edward Island as well as from counsel
representing accused persons generally, who argued the opposing point of view,
and from counsel representing three specific accused persons who had challenged
the independence of the Provincial Court in other proceedings. As well, Chief
Judge Plamondon (as he then was), of the Prince Edward Island Provincial Court,
and the Canadian Association of Provincial Court Judges were given an
opportunity to make submissions but declined to do so. The Attorney-General of
Canada was also given notice, but he too declined the opportunity to make
submissions.

[3] The reference has come about because, following
the coming into force of the Public Sector Pay Reduction Act, S.P.E.I.
1994, c. 51, numerous accused persons challenged the competence of the
Provincial Court to exercise jurisdiction over them. These accused persons
contend the court has lost its status as an independent tribunal within the
meaning of s. 11(d) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms due to the fact the aforesaid legislation reduced the salaries of
the Provincial Court judges (along with those of many others paid from the
public purse) by 7.5%. These challenges have caused considerable controversy,
uncertainty, and delay in and about the Provincial Court, and in the
administration of justice in the province generally.[4] The Government of Prince Edward Island in 1994,
like most others in Canada at the time, was faced with a severe deficit problem
and saw an urgency to cutting its spending so as to get the province’s finances
into acceptable order. Accordingly, as a deficit reduction measure, the
government introduced, and the legislature passed, the Public Sector Pay
Reduction Act. According to s. 2, the specific purpose of this legislation
is: (a) as a deficit reduction measure, to reduce the pay rates of all those
persons, except independent contractors, who on behalf of a public sector
employer, perform duties and functions that entitle that person to pay, and (b)
to implement certain other cost reductions in the public sector. The term “public
sector employer” is very broadly defined in s. 1(d) of the Act. Section
2(2) declares that these reductions would be without compensation or any other
offsetting considerations. Section 3 provides that, where there is a conflict
with other legislation; the provisions of the Public Sector Pay Reduction
Act prevail.

[5] The Public Sector Pay Reduction Act is
divided into five parts. Part I deals with interpretation. The heading of Part
II is “Public Sector Employees”. This
part includes ss. 5 to 8 of the Act and deals with reductions to employees of
public sector employers, including those covered by collective agreements.
Under s. 6, the pay of those public sector employees earning $28,000 or less is
reduced by 3.5% and the pay of those earning more than that is reduced by 7.5% so
long as they do not go below $26, 950. Part III is headed “Persons Paid From Public Funds”, and
provides for reductions in the amounts paid to persons appointed as members of
provincial tribunals, commissions, agencies, and to Provincial Court judges and
medical doctors. Section 10 under this part contains the one and only specific
reference in the entire Public Sector Pay Reduction Act to the
Provincial Court. It simply purports to amend the existing salary-fixing
formula (for those presently sitting, 100% of the average salary paid to
Provincial Court judges in the other provinces) provided for in s. 3(3) of the Provincial
Court Act, R.S.P.E.I. 1988, c. P-25, so that the salaries of the judges
will be 7.5% less than they would otherwise have been had the formula remained
unchanged. The effect of the amendment is to reduce the salary of each of the
three currently sitting Provincial Court judges in Prince Edward Island from
100% to 92.5% of the average of that paid to the Provincial Court judges in the
other provinces of Canada.

[6] Similar deficit reduction measures have been
introduced in other provinces. Recently, McDonald J. of the Alberta Court of
Queen’s Bench in R. v. Campbell, November 15, 1994 (unreported)
[summarized 25 W.C.B. (2d) 397], and Scollin J. of the Manitoba Court of Queen’s
Bench in Manitoba Provincial Judges Assn. v. Manitoba (Minister of Justice),
November 25, 1994 (unreported) [now reported 30 C.P.C. (3d) 1, 51 A.C.W.S.
(3d) 1047], have held that public sector pay cuts affecting Provincial Court
judges in those provinces violated the financial security of the judges and
thus conflict with s. 11(d) of the Charter. However, while
McDonald J. ruled the Alberta reductions to judges’ salaries were invalid,
Scollin J. decided instead to uphold the constitutionality of the Manitoba
legislation by reading it down so, he says at p. 5 of his judgment [p. 38
C.P.C.]:… as to provide only for a temporary
suspension of the actual payment of full compensation, subject, on the expiry
of the legislation, to full retroactive reinstatement of all compensation that
was suspended.[7] In this province, K.R. MacDonald C.J.T.D. in Lowther
v. Prince Edward Island, September 21, 1994 (unreported) [now reported 118
D.L.R. (4th) 665, 24 C.R.R. (2d) 145 sub nom. R. v. Lowther, 122 Nfld.
& P.E.I.R. 221], held that it was not the reduction itself but the fact
that the Public Sector Pay Reduction Act allowed for judges of the
Provincial Court to negotiate with government the manner in which the reduction
would be implemented that created a perception they lacked judicial
independence. Subsequent to this decision, the Lieutenant-Governor in Council,
on September 29, 1994, approved a regulation purportedly made pursuant to s. 13
of the Public Sector Pay Reduction Act which, among other things, renders
the provisions for negotiation in the Act inapplicable to Provincial Court
judges.

[8] The issues raised in the aforementioned cases
are not so novel as they may seem to some. Peter Hogg in vol. 1, 3rd ed., of
his Constitutional Law of Canada (Scarborough, Ont.: Carswell, 1992)
[updated to 1994], says at p. 7-6:… during the depression of the 1930s, there
was much controversy in Canada (and England) as to whether it was proper to
reduce judicial salaries by ten percent (20 percent in England) by a statute
which applied to the entire federal civil service as well. The argument that
such a nondiscriminatory reduction would threaten judicial independence seems
fantastic, but it was seriously advanced by constitutional lawyers, judges,
government ministers and members of parliament.More recently, these issues were raised in
the Supreme Court of Canada in R. v. Valente (1985), 23 C.C.C. (3d) 193,
24 D.L.R. (4th) 161, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 673, and in Canada v. Beauregard (1986),
30 D.L.R. (4th) 481, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 56, 26 C.R.R. 59. In Valente, the
Supreme Court held that the judges of the Ontario Provincial Court were
independent within the meaning of s. 11(d), even though one of the
grounds of objection (see No. (14), p. 198 C.C.C., p. 166 D.L.R.) was that the
judges had the same sick leave terms as civil servants and their salary would,
therefore, be reduced in the same manner as a civil servant when sick. And in Beauregard,
the Supreme Court of Canada held that an amendment to the federal Judges
Act requiring judges to contribute to the cost of their pensions (which
effectively reduced their salaries) was not prohibited.

[9] With all the foregoing said as background, I
will now restate and answer the questions posed in the reference for the
opinion of this court.Question No. 1Can the Legislature of the Province of
Prince Edward Island make laws such that the remuneration of Judges of the
Provincial Court may be decreased, increased, or otherwise adjusted, either:(a) as part of an overall public economic
measure, or(b) in certain circumstances established by
law?Answer[10] There is no law which explicitly prohibits the
legislature of Prince Edward Island from reducing or otherwise altering the
salaries and benefits of Provincial Court judges once they have been
established, but that does not mean that it has unlimited power to do so. The
supremacy of the legislature and its power to make laws affecting Provincial
Court judges is subject to s. 11(d) of the Charter, which provides:11. Any person charged with an offence has
the right. . . . .(d) to be presumed innocent until proven guilty
according to law in a fair and public hearing by an independent and
impartial tribunal;(Emphasis added.) Section 11(d) is
part of the Constitution of Canada, and therefore, according to s. 52 of the Constitution
Act, 1982, is the supreme law of Canada, and any law that is inconsistent
with its provisions is to that extent of no force or effect. In Valente,
supra (a case in which the Supreme Court of Canada dealt with the specific
issue of whether a Provincial Court judge sitting as the Provincial Court
(Criminal Division) in Ontario in December, 1982, was an independent tribunal
within the meaning of s. 11(d) of the Charter), Le Dain J.,
writing for a unanimous seven-member panel, says at pp. 201-2 C.C.C., pp.
169-70 D.L.R.:

The word “independent” in s. 11(d)
reflects or embodies the traditional constitutional value of judicial
independence. As such, it connotes … a status or relationship to others,
particularly to the Executive Branch of government, that rests on objective
conditions or guarantees.Then, at p. 204 C.C.C., p. 172 D.L.R., Le
Dain J. says that the test for independence for purposes of s. 11(d) is
an objective one whether the tribunal can reasonably be perceived as
independent. At pp. 204-5 C.C.C., pp. 172-3 D.L.R., he says:The perception must … be a perception of
whether the tribunal enjoys the essential objective conditions or guarantees
of judicial independence, and not a perception of how it will in fact act,
regardless of whether it enjoys such conditions or guarantees.(Emphasis added.) Le Dain J. then went on,
at p. 216 C.C.C., p. 184 D.L.R., to identify “financial security” as one of the
essential conditions of judicial independence for the purposes of s. 11(d).
He says:That means security of salary or other
remuneration, and where appropriate, security of pension. The essence of such
security is that the right to salary and pension should be established by law
and not be subject to arbitrary interference by the executive in a manner that
could affect judicial independence.

whether the tribunal enjoys the essential objective conditions or guarantees
of judicial independence, and not a perception of how it will in fact act,
regardless of whether it enjoys such conditions or guarantees.(Emphasis added.) Le Dain J. then went on,
at <decision><fragment>p. 216</fragment> <citation>C.C.C.</citation>, <fragment>p. 184</fragment> <citation>D.L.R.</citation></decision>, to identify “financial security” as one of the
essential conditions of judicial independence for the purposes of <legislation><fragment>s. 11(d)</fragment></legislation>.
He says:That means security of salary or other
remuneration, and where appropriate, security of pension. The essence of such
security is that the right to salary and pension should be established by law
and not be subject to arbitrary interference by the executive in a manner that
could affect judicial independence.

[11] Currently, the salaries for Provincial Court
judges in Prince Edward Island are established according to a formula adopted
by the legislature. They are not left to be determined by the executive branch
as they were in Ontario at the time of Valente, supra. Nevertheless,
what the Supreme Court of Canada said about the essential conditions for
judicial independence within the meaning of s. 11(d) also applies as a
limitation on the power of the legislative branch: see Beauregard, supra, and
R. v. Lippé (1991), 64 C.C.C. (3d) 513, [1991] 2 S.C.R. 114, 128 N.R. 1.
Therefore, the legislature of Prince Edward Island does not have an unfettered
right to deal with the salary and other benefits of Provincial Court judges. It
does, however, have a limited constitutional authority to alter the salary and
benefits of the judges of the Provincial Court and could reduce them as part of
an overall public economic measure so long as in so doing: (1) it does not
remove the basic degree of financial security which is an essential condition
for their independence within the meaning of s. 11(d) of the Charter,
and (2) there is no indication that the legislation amounts to arbitrary
interference with the judiciary in the sense that it is being enacted for an
improper or colourable purpose, or that it discriminates against judges vis-à-vis
other citizens: see Valente, supra; Beauregard, supra, at p. 497, and R.
v. Généreux (1992), 70 C.C.C. (3d) 1 at pp. 19-20, 88 D.L.R. (4th) 110 at
pp. 128-30, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 259.
