[12] The essence of financial security for Provincial
Court judges is the right to have salary and pension established by law and not
subject to discretionary or arbitrary interference by the government in a
manner that could affect judicial independence. As Le Dain J. says, at p. 218
C.C.C., p. 186 D.L.R. of Valente, supra:The essential point … is that the right to
salary of a provincial court judge is established by law, and there is no way
in which the executive could interfere with that right in a manner to affect
the independence of the individual judge.[13] A general pay reduction for all who hold public
office, including judges, which is enacted by the provincial legislature as
part of a broad public economic measure, and which does not discriminate
against judges, would not in itself violate the degree of financial security
essential for judicial independence within the meaning of s. 11(d). So
long as the salaries of the judges, even though reduced as aforesaid, remain
established by law and beyond arbitrary interference by the government in a
manner that could affect the judicial independence of the individual judge, the
reasonable and informed person, viewing the matter from an objective
standpoint, should still perceive the court as enjoying the essential condition
of judicial independence. That, the authorities say, is the test that must be
applied to determine whether a tribunal is independent within the meaning of s.
11(d) of the Charter: see Valente, supra, at p. 204 C.C.C., p.
172 D.L.R.; Lippé, supra, at pp. 533-4, and Généreux, supra, at
pp. 20-1 C.C.C., pp. 129-31 D.L.R. Accordingly, my answer to Q. 1 would be a “qualified
yes”.

[2] It raises issues concerning the standards expected of a lawyer in
the conduct of litigation and the nature of the relationship between that
lawyer and his client as it impacts on decisions made with respect to the
manner in which the litigation is carried on.[3] Although advanced on a number of different bases, the main thrust
of CSE's claim to special costs is that, on the facts, it was
"impossible" for CSE to have been found liable to any of the
plaintiffs and that the plaintiffs knew this or at the least could have
satisfied themselves that such was the case if they had taken the opportunities
presented to examine the information available. By not doing so, it was
submitted, the plaintiffs improperly dragged CSE through an unnecessary and
extremely expensive trial. CSE's position was vindicated, it is said, by the
fact that the plaintiffs were ultimately non-suited.Background(a) The Non-suit[4] On May 18, 1995, I granted a non-suit motion in favour of CSE
following the conclusion of the plaintiffs' case after over 90 days of trial.
At the request of the parties, I reserved on the issue of costs flowing from
the non-suit pending further application and argument. The decision on the
merits of the non-suit motion has been reported at (1995), 131 Nfld. &
P.E.I.R. 351. The interrelationship of the parties and the factual background
of the case, as well as an outline of the pleadings, is set out in another
previous decision of mine reported at (1994), 120 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 313 as
well as in the final judgment on the merits of the claim filed on July 31,
1998, [[1999] Nfld. & P.E.I.R. TBEd. JN.001], with addendum dealing with
costs on September 2, 1998 (as yet unreported).

[5] The trial of the claims against the other defendants proceeded
after some delay due, amongst other things, to the withdrawal of plaintiffs'
counsel and an appeal against the non-suit decision which did not proceed
because of the plaintiffs' failure or inability to put up security for costs
which had been ordered by the appeal court. As indicated, the trial has now
been concluded and judgment rendered.[6] In order to appreciate the basis of the current application, it
is necessary to review parts of the convoluted history of the conduct of the
case from the time of its inception, which was long before I became involved as
the trial judge. A number of pretrial applications had been made, some of which
have a bearing on the current application, particularly as they relate to
alleged representations that were made by counsel in the course of argument. I
have reviewed the court files with respect to these matters. In some cases, I
have been provided with transcripts of what was said.(b) The Claims[7] The present proceeding, as ultimately tried, resulted from the
consolidation of four separate actions that had been commenced between 1989 and
1991. The first action, commenced by Harold Efford on May 16, 1989, ([1989] St.
J. No. 1515; hereinafter, the "Delay Claim") claimed damages flowing
from an alleged delay in the delivery by Eastern Shipbuilders Limited (ESB) of
the M.V. Shelby Ann, a 64' 11" fishing vessel which ESB had agreed to
construct for Efford. The second action, also commenced by Efford, this time on
August 23, 1989, ([1989] St. J. No. 2516; hereinafter the "Unseaworthiness
Claim") claimed damages from ESB resulting from alleged improper
construction of the vessel. In relation to that claim, Efford had commissioned
a marine architect, Clarence Carroll, to inquire into and prepare a report
concerning what were perceived by Efford to be potential seaworthiness and
stability problems with the vessel.

[8] The third action was commenced on November 16, 1990 by Arthur
Petten and Joyce Petten personally ([1990 B. No. 290; hereinafter the
"Business Loss Claim") claiming financial loss suffered by the
Pettens, directly and through their company ESB, allegedly resulting from the
negligent preparation and dissemination of the Carroll Report. At the time of
the preparation of the report, Carroll had been working with Evans, Yeatman
& Endall (Associates) Ltd. and its subsidiary, Evans, Yeatman & Endall
(Newfoundland) Ltd. At the time of the commencement of the action, however
Carroll was working with CSE, which had bought out the assets of the Evans
companies on May 31, 1989. While employed by CSE, Carroll had continued to
undertake some follow-up work in connection with the report which had been
previously prepared by him.[9] The Pettens alleged that a number of statements and recommendations
contained in Carroll's report were inaccurate and based on wrong information
and that certain governmental agencies, including the Canadian Coast Guard and
the Fisheries Loan Board, acted on the report and took steps that effectively
resulted in the plaintiffs' shipbuilding enterprise being shut down and the
plaintiffs' bank calling their loans, including the Pettens' personal
guarantees. It was also alleged that Efford took steps to publish the report
and other false and misleading statements about the Pettens and their business
that compounded the problem. Carroll and Efford were named as defendants, as
was CSE, Carroll's then current employer. The Evans companies, as the former
employers of Carroll, were not named as parties. Indeed, it is not clear that
the Pettens would have known at that time sufficient of the details of the
corporate arrangements which had taken place between the Evans companies and
CSE to have appreciated the significance of the changeover. With Carroll as the
named defendant, however, the details were not important because they had
before the court the person who had been involved throughout, in whatever
different employment guise.

[26] The language used by counsel for CSE, as quoted above, is,
perhaps, unfortunate. Viewed in isolation it could be said to give the
impression that CSE was giving a blanket indemnity for any liability for which
Carroll might be ultimately held responsible. One must, however, view those
comments in context. The Yeatman affidavit makes it clear that liability for
Carroll's actions was being acknowledged "by the appropriate company ...
depending on the timing of the event involved". Furthermore, the
application itself states the position of CSE that Carroll was acting as an
employee, at different times, of CSE "and its predecessor company"
and that CSE's representation of acceptance of liability was intended to be in
respect of the actions of Carroll while he acted as an employee of CSE.
Finally, at other places in the transcript counsel for CSE does in fact refer
to the role of the Evans' companies as the employer of Carroll at an earlier
point in time. For example, he is also reported as stating:"... prior to June of 1989 he [Yeatman] was an officer of
Evans, Yeatman and Endal Associates Limited who is not a party to this action
which employed the second defendant Clarence Carroll up until the company sold
its goodwill and physical assets to CSE Marine. Now, very early in this matter
when the defendants were served, our law firm contacted the plaintiffs' lawyers
and indicated to them that they should amend their statement of claim. We
recommended they should amend their statement of claim because, in fact, the
third defendant [sic; should read 'second defendant' was involved not with the
present first defendant [CSE], he was involved initially with the company
called Evans, Yeatman and Endal Associates Limited, and in June of 1989 Evans,
Yeatman and Endal Associates Limited became dissolved and transferred its
assets to EYE Marine Consultants. So, for the purpose of clarifying the record,
we were just recommending to the plaintiff that they - the cause of action
should really be against the present first defendant and as well including this
prior company, Evans, Yeatman and Endal and Associates Limited ... So to
eliminate all doubt, my lord, Clarence Carroll carried on his operations as an
employee of both of those companies throughout his time involved in this report
which is the subject of this cause of action."

[27] After some discussion in the courtroom, counsel for the
plaintiffs, in response to questions from the judge, agreed with the
application to strike Carroll as a party and stated:"With Mr. Templeton's comments and with the affidavits as
filed, we really have no difficulty with his application."[28] It is clear from this exchange that in conceding the matter,
counsel for the plaintiffs was not relying solely upon the alleged blanket indemnity
on behalf of CSE but upon the whole of the comments made by counsel for CSE and
the affidavit material which was filed. Indeed, shortly following the
application, and the removal of Carroll as a party, the plaintiffs amended
their statement of claim so as to name the Evans companies as well as CSE as
defendants, thereby inferentially recognizing the potential of liability by the
Evans' companies, and not CSE, for the acts of Carroll undertaken while their
employee. Furthermore, if the plaintiffs were relying on the indemnity argued
for, one would have expected that it would have been put forward as any
absolute bar to CSE's subsequent non- suit motion and in affidavits filed in
opposition to other applications by CSE, as hereinafter described, to be removed
as a party. The plaintiffs did not do so.[29] Accordingly, I do not regard the statements of counsel for CSE as
amounting to a blanket indemnity, as alleged, for any liability for which
Carroll might ultimately be held responsible and as a justification, in itself,
for the refusal of the plaintiffs or their counsel to countenance the possible
subsequent removal of CSE as a party.

[30] Having said that, however, it can be said that what was
represented to the court and to the plaintiffs was that there was no need for
Carroll, the employee, to remain as a defendant because: (i) CSE would be
responsible for any negligence which occurred while Carroll was CSE's employee;
and (ii) the Evans companies would be responsible for any negligence which
occurred while he was their employee. Yeatman was in a peculiarly appropriate
position to give these assurances because he was a former owner of the Evans
companies and was a current manager of CSE.[31] There can be no doubt that the existence of these representations
(although in a more attenuated form than argued for by counsel for the
intervenors) had an effect on the positions taken by the plaintiffs in response
to the subsequent efforts by CSE to extricate itself from the litigation.[32] What I find disturbing about this situation is that at the time
of the application before Bartlett, J., the Evans companies were no longer
operating entities with any assets and were acknowledged by Brian Waring as
being "judgment proof." That would have made the representation that the
Evans companies would be responsible for Carroll's negligence while he was
their employee virtually meaningless.[33] I am not satisfied that this point was sufficiently made to
Bartlett, J., or was sufficiently appreciated by the plaintiffs at that time.
Yet, counsel for CSE (who was also counsel for the Evans companies and Carroll)
was suggesting that the claim would have to be amended to reference the Evans
companies as Carroll's employer for the period prior to the purchase by CSE
and, indeed as noted, the plaintiffs did subsequently add the Evans companies
as defendants. The reality was that as a result of the order, the plaintiffs
lost the actual author of the alleged negligence as a party and gained a shell
company as a defendant instead. In terms of having anyone of substance to
answer for the negligence of Carroll, therefore, it is easy to see how the
plaintiffs, upon becoming aware of the status of the Evans companies, would
have regarded the continued presence of CSE in the litigation as important.

(ii) Subsequent Pre-trial Applications to Strike[34] Following the filing and service of the plaintiffs' amended
statement of claim naming the Evans companies, as well as CSE, as defendants, a
joint defence was filed by solicitor Kenneth Templeton on behalf of both Evans companies
and CSE. In it, the defendants alleged that the plaintiffs' claims were
frivolous and vexatious. In particular, it alleged that CSE could not be held
liable for the preparation and dissemination of the Carroll report because the
report had been prepared before CSE's involvement by acquisition of the assets
of the Evans companies. As well, Evans, Yeatman and Endal (Associates) Ltd.
claimed that it could not be liable because it was not carrying on business in
Newfoundland at the time of the preparation of the report. The defence
concluded that both CSE and Evans (Associates) would apply, prior to trial, to
be removed as parties to the action.[35] These were not insignificant statements. Shortly before,
representations had been made that Carroll was not necessary as a party because
the "appropriate company" would acknowledge responsibility for
Carroll's liability "depending on the timing of the event involved."
Now, the position was advanced that CSE and one of the Evans companies should
also be removed, leaving no real defendant to answer for Carroll. Mr. Petten
testified that he became very concerned that CSE was now trying to avoid any
involvement. He became suspicious of CSE's motives. Of course, no plaintiff is
entitled to have a particular defendant before the court simply because that
defendant is one of substance. Nevertheless had the full implications of
removing Carroll as a party been appreciated, it may well be that Bartlett, J.,
would not have been as disposed to granting the application and the plaintiffs
may well have not ultimately acceded to the request.

[36] As the subsequent discussion at para. indicates, it is not an
immutable legal principle that an employee who acts negligently, in the course
of his employment, performing the very essence of his employer's contractual
obligations, is necessarily able to avoid personal liability. As the matter had
developed, therefore, one can appreciate why the plaintiffs would be reluctant
to concede the removal of any of the corporate defendants, including CSE,
unless there was no possibility of any of them being found liable.[37] Of course, that is the very position CSE was taking. It was
arguing that it came on the scene after the negligent act of preparing the
report had been completed and that if any corporate defendant was to be held
vicariously liable for any negligence of Carroll, it could only be one of the
Evans companies no matter how insolvent they might be. The success of that
argument depended on there being no connection between CSE and the preparation
of the report and no evidence of any other actions by Carroll, after he became
an employee of CSE, that could be characterized as negligent. It is clear that
CSE and its counsel firmly believed this to be the case; however, it is not
CSE's belief that is important, nor is it significant that CSE was ultimately
successful in its non-suit motion. What is important for this application is
whether the plaintiffs acted appropriately in pursuing the claim and resisting
attempts by CSE to remove itself given the plaintiff's knowledge base and their
opportunities to satisfy themselves as to the role, if any, which CSE played.
Clearly, if the plaintiffs knew or ought reasonably to have concluded that
their claim against CSE was baseless, then the inference can be drawn that they
must have acted for improper motives or that their behaviour in improperly
invoking the judicial system against CSE, is of the type that warrants an order
for special costs.

attempts by CSE to remove itself given the plaintiff's knowledge base and their
opportunities to satisfy themselves as to the role, if any, which CSE played.
Clearly, if the plaintiffs knew or ought reasonably to have concluded that
their claim against CSE was baseless, then the inference can be drawn that they
must have acted for improper motives or that their behaviour in improperly
invoking the judicial system against CSE, is of the type that warrants an order
for special costs.

[38] Mr. Petten had in his possession a document which, he felt, showed
a potential involvement of CSE prior to the purchase of the Evans assets. It
consisted of a letter dated November 23, 1989, on CSE letterhead, addressed to
the Canadian Coast Guard and signed by Carroll, in which Carroll (who at that
time was an employee of CSE) stated that "initially our company became
involved with the M/V Shelby Ann December 1988 - January 1989. ..." Mr.
Petten believed that this indicated that CSE was involved before the report was
written.[39] In addition, there were other documents indicating that after the
purchase of the Evans assets, Carroll continued to do work for Mr. Efford
respecting the Shelby Ann, including correspondence with the Coast Guard
respecting some of the positions taken by the Coast Guard in response to that
report. His view of this material, as ultimately explained in argument, was
that these actions by Carroll, now on behalf of CSE, involved a republication
and reaffirmation of the negligent misstatements in the original report or a
negligent failure to correct those statements. Could these peripheral
indications of possible CSE involvement withstand scrutiny in light of the
detailed information being supplied by CSE indicating that it had in fact
purchased the Evans assets on May 31, 1989 and had not been involved previously?[40] In response to the plaintiffs' filing of a request for trial on
December 3, 1991, CSE and Associates applied to the court on December 10, 1991
to be removed as parties. A subsequent application made on October 16, 1992 by
CSE alone also sought the same relief. The applications were accompanied by
affidavits from Martin Yeatman and Brian Waring of CSE in which they asserted
that CSE had no involvement prior to its take over of the Evans companies as of
the end of May, 1989, when those companies "ceased to exist." Waring
deposed that CSE had "absolutely nothing to do" with the preparation
of the Carroll report. Attached to the affidavit material were extracts from
the Agreement of Purchase and Sale and other related documents designed to
verify the assertions that were made.

[41] Waring asserted that it was "totally inappropriate" to
require CSE to participate in the proceeding since "it was not
possible" for Harold Efford to have engaged CSE to prepare the report.[42] Arthur Petten filed an affidavit in response to the application
in which he referred to the Carroll letter of November 23, 1989 which implied
that CSE had in fact been involved in the preparation of the report prior to
its take over of the Evans companies. As well, he highlighted the contrast, as
noted above, between the assertions given before Bartlett, J., that
responsibility for Carroll's actions would be assumed by the "appropriate
company" and the position, now being taken, that CSE should not have to be
further involved.[43] An affidavit in response to Petten was filed by Yeatman. In it he
asserted that "the impression" left by the November 23 letter that
CSE was involved in the preparation of the report was "not accurate"
because, as asserted previously, CSE only came on the scene with the asset
purchase of May 31, 1989.[44] These applications to strike were dismissed, without written
reasons, with costs to the plaintiffs.(iii) Withdrawal of Counsel[45] On December 3, 1992 Mr. Templeton withdrew as counsel for the
Evans companies and was given leave to file a separate defence on behalf of
CSE. Shortly thereafter, an application by CSE against the plaintiffs for
security for costs of the trial was made but denied. In the course of giving
his oral reasons, the Chief Justice of the Trial Division is reported as
observing that if the evidence submitted at trial confirmed the submissions of
counsel for CSE relative to CSE's non-involvement in the matter, there was a
risk that the plaintiffs would be exposed to considerable costs.

[46] With a scheduled trial date looming on January 16, 1993, CSE
applied, on January 7, 1993, for, and obtained, an order that the plaintiffs
answer certain interrogatories which had previously been delivered and that
documentary disclosure be made within ten days. At that time the commencement
of trial was rescheduled for March 23, 1993.[47] Shortly after the making of the production order, Mr. Moores,
plaintiffs' counsel, applied on January 27, 1993, for and obtained an order
entitling him to withdraw as counsel. The intervenor Owen Myers deposed that he
had been retained by the plaintiffs as their solicitor on January 16, 1993, and
that at that point he knew there was an outstanding order requiring the
plaintiffs to make document production. He said that he worked for the next six
weeks "almost exclusively" in reviewing the mass of documents and
exhibits with a view to filing a list of documents in compliance with the
previous court order. He succeeded in filing a list of documents on March 4,
1993, the day another application by CSE to have the proceeding dismissed for
non-compliance with the production order was to be heard. Myers deposed that in
his opinion, "it was not possible to comply with the order of the Chief
Justice more expeditiously ... given the condition in which the file documents
were received" from previous counsel and the fact that he had become
involved in the matter at a late date.

[48] As a result of the plaintiffs' change of solicitors and the late
document production, as well as other matters, the trial date was again pushed
back to September 13, 1993. The trial did in fact start on that date.(d) Applications During Trial[49] Following Mr. Myers' retention as solicitor for the plaintiffs
but before the trial actually started, counsel for CSE repeated his request
that the involvement of CSE in the matter be reviewed and that the plaintiffs
voluntarily agree to allow CSE to be removed as a party. The plaintiffs would
not agree.[50] Subsequently, during trial, the question of CSE's further
involvement was dealt with on a number of occasions by way of application or
was commented on in the course of other applications.(i) Application to Strike[51] Twenty-seven days into the trial, the plaintiffs made application
to, amongst other things, amend their pleadings to add ESB and ESEL as
plaintiffs and to allege additional causes of action, including defamation,
injurious falsehood, conspiracy, intimidation, inducement of breach of
contract, interference with economic relations and breach of fiduciary duty.
CSE took issue with the way in which this application was made, in particular,
with the fact that no draft of the proposed amended statement of claim
accompanied the application and that the matter had to be delayed to enable the
plaintiffs to provide such a draft.[52] CSE responded to the application with a further application to be
removed as a party to the proceedings or, in the alternative, for an order for
security for costs. These applications were supported by an affidavit from
Brian Waring which set out in considerable detail the relationship between the
Evans' companies and CSE and the nature of the transaction that involved the
transfer of assets to CSE. No cross-examination on this affidavit was made.

liability of each is alleged to be founded." Although an amended statement
of claim was filed, the plaintiffs did not, as required, segregate the causes
of action and their factual bases as they applied to each separate defendant.
Instead, composite pleas were maintained against CSE and both Evans companies

Carroll report, were equally attributed to CSE.[54] With respect to CSE's claim to be removed as a defendant, I

spend some time on follow-up on the report and other related matters after the

"... while the claim against CSE appears to be very
tenuous, it cannot be said that it is without hope of success. Accordingly, I
conclude that CSE has failed to satisfy me that it should be removed as a party
at this stage."It may be felt that, because of the very limited (if
any) potential connection of CSE to the matters in issue it would be unfair to
force CSE to continue to participate in the trial, especially where its
prospect of recovery of costs against the plaintiffs, if it were successful,
would be minimal. Nevertheless, the plaintiffs are entitled to make claims
against any person they choose provided they comply with the rules of pleading
and allege a cause of action known to the law. In the circumstances of this
case, a balancing of these two competing interests can best be achieved by
application of the rules respecting security for costs."[55] Because I felt that "the plaintiffs' claims against CSE as
they presently appear seem tenuous at best" I made an order for security
for costs in favour of CSE. I observed:"CSE's position had been made known to the plaintiffs at
an early date; yet, as was pointed out by CSE, no effort was made by the plaintiffs
to pursue either oral or documentary discovery of CSE to determine whether
CSE's position is well founded. The plaintiffs therefore are assuming a
significant risk that they will be unsuccessful at the end of trial against
CSE. It is, of course, their choice to take such risk. However, it is manifest
that the costs of this trial will not be insignificant. It would be not
consonant with justice, given the apparent weakness in the plaintiffs' case in
this regard to place CSE in the position of having to continue to participate
in the trial in these circumstances without some assurance that they will be
able to recover at least some of their costs at the end if their predictions of
success on this issue are well founded.

"This is especially so where, because of the apparent
weakness of the claims, CSE might well be able, if it is successful at the end
of trial, to claim extra costs against the plaintiffs pursuant to Rule 14.20 on
the basis that the plaintiffs, having been presented with information as to CSE's
position at an early date, ought to have admitted those facts and not forced
CSE to litigate those issues."[56] The foregoing observations were intended by me as a "wake-up
call" to the plaintiffs, with a view to indicating that while they escaped
having CSE removed as a party at that stage, the court was certainly going to
be looking with care at the evidence to determine whether the plaintiffs could
make out a case against CSE at the end of the day. It has been said that an
application for security for costs "acts as a deterrent to frivolous
litigation and reminds the plaintiff that a lawsuit is not to be undertaken
lightly". (See Rochon, Terry & Gray, Interlocutory Proceedings,
Strategy and Practice (Toronto: Butterworths, 1996) p. 121) The order for
security was in effect a test of the plaintiffs' resolve to proceed against CSE
as well as a reminder that lack of success usually attracts costs. It further
encouraged them to analyse carefully the case they had specifically against
CSE. It also effectively invited the plaintiffs to address the adduction of
further evidence tying CSE to the role of Carroll in preparation and
dissemination of the report.

(ii) Delays in Provision of Security for Costs[57] Counsel for the plaintiffs and CSE engaged in some discussions as
to the possible variation of the form which the security of costs which I
ordered could be made. Because the deadline for provision of the security
passed, an additional application was made to deal with the question of the
form of security and whether an extension of time ought to be granted for its
provision. I ruled, in a decision reported at (1994), 121 Nfld. & P.E.I.R.
338 that it would be fair to extend the time for provision of security because
of the discussions which had been ongoing relative to the possibility of
providing alternative forms of security due to the apparent difficulty which
the plaintiffs were having in arranging security in the form originally
envisaged. On the issue of what was an appropriate form of security, the
plaintiffs ultimately provided a cash deposit with the court even though it was
they who had initiated the discussions respecting the provision of alternative
security. CSE was awarded costs with respect to these matters.(iii) Application for Further Security[58] Following the failure of the plaintiffs to satisfy the order for
payment of costs, CSE made a further application later in the trial for
additional security. A hearing was held with respect to this matter in which
the financial and other information provided by the plaintiffs and the manner
in which they dealt with the application was far from satisfactory.
Negotiations had also been undertaken between the parties with respect to the
provision of additional security by consent but ultimately those negotiations failed
because Mrs. Petten disagreed. In yet another decision, reported at (1995), 130
Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 205, I issued a restraining order preventing the
disposition by the Pettens of certain property owned by them pending resolution
of trial issues involving CSE.

(iv) The Allegation of an Undertaking to Call Witnesses[59] At the conclusion of the plaintiffs' case, CSE made its non-suit
motion. In response, Mr. Myers asserted, amongst other things, that a non-suit
motion was inappropriate because counsel for CSE had undertaken to call Brian
Waring as a witness at the trial so that the plaintiffs would have an
opportunity to cross- examine him.[60] Counsel for CSE took strong exception to this suggestion,
regarding it as an unfounded imputation on his professional character. After
some discussion, during which it became clear that the plaintiffs may have made
certain assumptions based on earlier discussions between counsel respecting the
availability of witnesses for certain purposes relating to earlier
applications, and statements made early in the trial about contemplated
witnesses, Mr. Myers, quite properly and professionally, withdrew the
suggestion that an undertaking had been given.[61] Although the suggestion of an undertaking was withdrawn and the
plaintiff proceeded to deal with the non-suit motion without the benefit of Mr.
Waring's evidence, the occurrence of this incident has another dimension. It
demonstrates that the plaintiffs were interested in exploring with Mr. Waring,
by way of examination in court, the involvement of CSE in the preparation and
dissemination of the Carroll report both before and after the acquisition of
the Evans assets. I am satisfied that, though the existence of an undertaking
was not established, the plaintiffs honestly, though mistakenly, believed that
they would, at some point have an opportunity to question Mr. Waring during the
trial process.

[62] As matters turned out their assumption in that regard was
mistaken, and, inasmuch as they had not called Mr. Waring as their own witness
they were, as a matter of tactics, deprived of that evidence. Of course, Mr.
Waring's evidence may or may not ultimately have been of assistance but one
cannot speculate on what impression may have been presented following
cross-examination and the possible eliciting of new information. Nevertheless,
a belief in the need to cross- examine Mr. Waring suggests a bona fide
intention to attempt to build on the information that the plaintiffs had by
further linking CSE, through a cross- examination of Mr. Waring, to the case.(v) The Non-Suit Application[63] The non-suit application proceeded and, as I have already

evidence" from the plaintiffs' witnesses and the consent exhibits was that

(a) Costs against the Plaintiffs[71] As a general rule, costs follow the event. See Rule 55.03(1) and Sooley
v. Canadian Home Insurance Co. (1994), 115 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 47; 360
A.P.R. 47 (Nfld. C.A.), per Morgan, J.A., at paragraph 13.[72] Accordingly, CSE should be entitled, at the very least, to costs
on a party and party basis for the whole of that portion of the trial in which
they participated and in respect of all pre-trial applications in which CSE
participated and in which costs were ordered in the cause.[73] The question is whether, in the circumstances of this case,
something further should be ordered.[74] The underlying rationale for awarding costs in the ordinary
course of things is one of indemnification. The awarding of party and party
costs, of course, represents only a partial indemnity. Nevertheless, such an
award is generally regarded as striking the proper balance between the burden
of costs which must be borne by a potentially successful litigant and the risk
of putting litigation beyond the financial reach of a potential loser. In other
words, party and party costs represent the balance that is generally struck
between the cost of justice and access to justice. For complete indemnity to be
justified, therefore, it must appear that justice (taking into account the
balancing of cost versus access) demands that result. In our system of justice,
that would be the exceptional case.

[75] The starting point for consideration of this issue is the
decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Young v. Young et al., [1993]
4 S.C.R. 3; 160 N.R. 1; 34 B.C.A.C. 161; 56 W.A.C. 161; [1993] 8 W.W.R. 513;
108 D.L.R.(4th) 193; 84 B.C.L.R.(2d) 1; 18 C.R.R.(2d) 41; 49 R.F.L.(3d) 117, in
which McLachlin, J., speaking for the majority, described the circumstances
under which solicitor and client costs should be awarded against a party to
litigation, in the following terms at p. 283:"Solicitor-client costs are generally awarded only where
there has been reprehensible, scandalous or outrageous conduct on the part of
one of the parties. Accordingly, the fact that an application has little merit
is no basis for awarding solicitorclient costs ...The court affirmed the British Columbia Court of Appeal's ruling
that the trial judge was in error in awarding solicitor-client costs except for
four days of trial and four days of interlocutory proceedings concerning
financial issues on the basis of the husband's nondisclosure of financial information.
The court specifically rejected the notion that solicitorclient costs should be
awarded solely on the basis of the fact that a claim had "little
merit".

input:
"It can include conduct which is scandalous, outrageous
or constitutes misbehaviour, but it also included milder forms of misconduct.
It means simply 'deserving of reproof or rebuke.'"Cameron, J.A., also referred with approval, however, to the
comments of Marshall, J.A., in House of Haynes to the effect that awards
of solicitor and client costs are generally reserved "to sanction
misconduct by a party" and represent an expression of censure or
chastisement and "will engender a certain amount of opprobrium".
Reservation of awards of solicitor-client costs for such cases promotes the
policy of not unduly discouraging access to the courts by allowing allegations
to be made by way of pleading or argument so long as they are not clearly
frivolous, scandalous or an abuse of process.[80] Thus, while the effect of an award of solicitor-client costs is
to provide a greater degree of indemnification than that provided by party and
party costs (thereby serving a compensatory function), the justification for
affording that greater degree of cost protection is the misconduct of the other
party which is deserving of reproof or rebuke. The awarding of solicitor-client
costs may therefore be justified where there is a causal relationship between
the misconduct deserving reproof or rebuke and the special costs incurred for
which additional indemnification is sought. For example, in Young the
actions of the litigant against whom costs were awarded only attracted
solicitor-client costs related to the four-day period by which the litigant's
obstructive behaviour extended the proceedings and thereby exposed the other
party to increased cost. There will also be cases, however, where
solicitor-client costs may be awarded, based on conduct deserving reproof or
rebuke, which nevertheless cannot be linked directly to any increase in cost or
other harm suffered by another party. The court always retains an inherent
jurisdiction to express its disapproval of the conduct of a party in litigation
by the awarding or withholding of costs. The awarding of solicitor- client costs
thus serves both a compensatory and a punitive function.

setting down of a case for trial where the plaintiff had "a legitimate
reason" for its delay: Charcoal Pit- delay by an
administrative agency in issuing an unconditional licence necessitating
litigation to require its issuance, where the delay in the circumstances could
not be characterized as an abuse of process or scandalous or vexatious conduct
constituting harassment: Wishingwell Early Childhood Centre Ltd. v. Daycare
and Homemakers Service Licening Board (Nfld.) (1992), 99 Nfld. &
P.E.I.R. 336; 315 A.P.R. 336 (Nfld. T.D.) - "vigorously" defending
and resisting a claim up to the date of trial and then choosing not to
participate in the trial itself, and withdrawing one's defence, where there was
no evidence to suggest that the actions were designed to obstruct or injure the
claimant: Rose (T.) Construction- pursuing a
claim to which the plaintiff had no entitlement in law in the face of a defence
which clearly identified the basis of the plaintiff's lack of entitlement but
where the lack of entitlement "was not immediately apparent from the
pleadings until demonstrated at trial" and where the claimant was acting
for himself: Janes[84] A comparison between cases which have awarded solicitor-client
costs and those which have declined to do so reveals that not all types of
behaviour constituting misconduct will necessarily attract such a costs award.
The misconduct must be such that it is serious enough to injuriously affect the
other party or is so flagrant that it merits the court's censure for that
reason alone.

[85] In many cases, the claim for an award of solicitor-client costs
arises where it is subsequently determined that a claim or defence in fact had
no merit. The winning party then claims either that a more careful reading of
the situation by the loser would not have provided a justification for forcing
the other person to incur the expense of a full trial, or that the loser knew
that his case had no merit but was nevertheless standing firm for some ulterior
or improper motive. There are elements of those sorts of allegations in this
case.[86] No doubt, as Marshall, J. A., observed in Janes at p. 212,
the jurisdiction to award solicitor-client costs may be invoked "to
dissuade harassment of a party by the pursuit of fruitless actions". Such
a policy also extends to a defendant who baselessly defends a legitimate claim.
See Charcoal Pit, per Gushue, J.A., at p. 258 where he equated
"misconduct" by a party, for the purposes of the rule to a situation
"where a party has ... defended an action on an obviously frivolous or
groundless basis or has acted on improper motives". Balanced against these
statements, however, is the statement by McLachlin, J., in Young,
previously quoted, that the fact that an application "has little
merit" is no basis for awarding solicitor-client costs.

[87] The analysis of this issue must be undertaken from the point of
view, reasonably assessed, of the party who is potentially subject to the
award, and not from the judge's point of view with the benefit of hindsight
after having heard the case. To do otherwise would expose potential litigants
to a significant risk of costs, dissuade the development of the law by the
submission of novel claims and discourage or impede litigants' access to the
courts. The deliberate, or even possibly the reckless, pursuit of a claim known
or believed to be unfounded will often be good evidence of having taken the
action out of malice or for other improper motive and thereby constitute an
abuse of process which would fall within the notion of reprehensible,
scandalous or outrageous conduct. The importance of examining whether a claim
is in fact unfounded is with respect to the inferences which may be drawn
concerning the motivation of the claimant. It is for this reason that when
examining the question of whether a claim is unfounded the focus must be on the
knowledge base of the claimant and his solicitor rather than on the basis of
hindsight. The correct approach is exemplified by the following comment of
Hardinge, J., in Shedwill v. Wilson (1991), 48 C.P.C.(2d) 70 (B.C.S.C.)
at p. 73:"With the benefit of hindsight I have decided the
allegation was unfounded. However, looking at the matter from the point of view
of the plaintiffs when they commenced their action and even at trial, I am not
prepared to go so far as to say the allegation was obviously unfounded, made
recklessly or out of malice."

[88] The distinction must be drawn, when viewing cases from the point
of view of the claimant, between those which have "little merit"
which Young tells us does not form a basis for awarding solicitor-client
costs, and those which have obviously no merit. This distinction explains
comments in some of the Newfoundland Court of Appeal cases which assert that
solicitor-client costs are appropriate where a party has commenced or defended
an action "on an obviously frivolous or groundless basis" (per
Gushue, J., A. in Charcoal Pit at p. 258) and where there is a
"deliberate advancing of a frivolous claim" which would normally
require, additionally, "fraud or other malicious, wanton or scandalous
conduct" (per Marshall, J.A., in Janes at p. 212). The advancing of
a weak case or one which becomes clear, only with the benefit of hindsight,
that it was groundless, will not be sufficient. Sooley is an example of
a case of that type. There, the taking of proceedings which might ultimately be
determined to be groundless against an insurance company even though it was not
a party to the particular insurance contract in question was held not to
justify an award of solicitor-client costs because the action was taken out of
an understandable abundance of caution.[89] I will now turn to the consideration of the specific examples of
alleged improper conduct (itemized in paragraph [67]) advanced by CSE in
support of its claim for solicitor-client costs.

- Pursuing an alleged non-meritorious claim against
Clarence Carroll[90] The suggestion put forward by CSE's counsel is that it was wholly
inappropriate for the plaintiffs to have sued Mr. Carroll in his personal
capacity where there was no suggestion that his work with respect to the
preparation of the report was done otherwise than in the course of his
employment with either the Evans companies or CSE.[91] Reliance on this circumstance as a basis for a claim by CSE for
solicitor- client costs is not supportable. An application was made on behalf
of Carroll by counsel, who at the time was also counsel for CSE, to have
Carroll removed as a party. That order was granted and Carroll was awarded his
costs. It is Carroll, if anyone, who could have made a claim, at the time of
his removal as a party, for solicitor-client costs. Except insofar as the
naming of Carroll as a party can be said in a general sense to be indicative of
a "mind set" or improper approach by the plaintiffs to the litigation
generally, including the claims against CSE, the fact that Carroll was
ultimately removed as a party is not in itself a ground for an award of
solicitorclient costs in favour of CSE.[92] In any event, the making of a claim against Carroll did not, in
the circumstances, amount to the assertion of a claim that was, to the
knowledge of the plaintiffs or their counsel, wholly unsupportable. Until the inter-relationship
between the two Evans companies and CSE became better known, it would not have
been inappropriate to name Carroll as a party as being the person who actually
allegedly negligently prepared and disseminated the report. Furthermore, as the
discussion of this issue in London Drugs Ltd. v. Brassart and Vanwinkel,
[1992] 3 S.C.R. 299; 143 N.R. 1; 18 B.C.A.C. 1; 31 W.A.C. 1; 97 D.L.R.(4th) 261
and Edgeworth Construction Ltd. v. Lea (N.D.) and Associates Ltd. et al.,
[1993] 3 S.C.R. 206; 157 N.R. 241; 32 B.C.A.C. 221; 53 W.A.C. 221, makes clear,
it does not necessarily follow that an employee acting negligently but in the
course of his employment and performing the "very essence" of his or
her employer's contractual obligations to a customer, is always immune from
personal liability. The particular facts of each case are relevant to that
determination.

[93] It cannot be said in this case that, even if the pursuit of the
claim against Carroll was relevant to the entitlement of CSE to
solicitor-client costs, it was so plain and obvious that the claim being
pressed was a frivolous one and was being advanced for a malicious or other
improper motive so as to count as reprehensible, scandalous or outrageous
conduct.- Pursuing an alleged non-meritorious claim against CSE[94] The success of CSE's non-suit motion in a sense vindicated its
claim that it was not liable to the plaintiffs. My decision confirmed that CSE
could not, as a matter of law, be held liable on the basis of assumption of
liabilities previously incurred by the Evans companies and also confirmed that
there was no evidence meeting the test of probative sufficiency that could link
CSE to the negligence of Carroll in the preparation and distribution of his
report. However, it does not follow from these findings that an award for
solicitor-client costs is appropriate. The fact that the claim was ultimately
found to have had no merit (in the sense of not meeting the test of probative
sufficiency) does not mean that its pursuit necessarily amounts to reprehensible,
scandalous or outrageous conduct. At the time of the issuance of the relevant
statement of claim, the plaintiffs could not necessarily be expected to have
known of the precise interrelationship of the proposed corporate defendants or
of the essentially private commercial transaction whereby the Evans' assets
were transferred to CSE or of the specific date and effect of such transfer.
The initial suit against CSE could not therefore be faulted.

[95] CSE argues, however, that subsequent events should clearly have
brought home to the plaintiffs or their counsel the fact that CSE could not be
found liable or, if they could not be said to have known of that circumstance,
their failure to examine the information provided by CSE amounted to a reckless
closing of one's eyes to the reality of the situation, thereby leading to the
inference that they must have been motivated by improper purposes to press on
against CSE. There can be no doubt that from an early date counsel for CSE
brought to the attention of the plaintiffs, through their then counsel,
information concerning the nature of the relationship between the Evans
companies and CSE and disclosed circumstances concerning the transfers between
those corporate bodies. This disclosure of information was accompanied by
requests to reconsider the necessity of keeping CSE as a party. CSE's position
was reiterated in its defence. Applications were made to have CSE removed. At
that time, further information and explanation were provided.[96] There is no evidence to suggest that this information was
considered, analysed and investigated in any concerted way. At most, it can be
said that Mr. Petten remained steadfast in his belief, based upon certain
incidental references in letters and upon Carroll's continuing involvement in
subsequent discussions of the report while an employee of CSE.[97] As noted, CSE made pre-trial applications to be struck as a
party, as well as a pre-trial application for security for costs. In that
latter context, the presiding applications judge, while denying the
application, made some incidental comments suggesting weaknesses in the
evidentiary base for the claim against CSE. It is argued that the actions of
CSE in seeking to be struck and in its openness with respect to disclosure of
the circumstances surrounding the take over of the Evans' assets by CSE, as
well as the obiter judicial comments in court, should have signalled to the
plaintiffs that the involvement of CSE in this matter was going to continue to
be a serious issue and that, accordingly, the plaintiffs came under a duty to
investigate the matter with care to satisfy themselves that they were not
mistaken about the involvement of CSE and were not in fact pursuing a claim
which in fact had no merit.

[98] Against this, however, one must consider the fact that in
opposing CSE's applications to strike, Mr. Petten recited, in his affidavit
material, some of the documentary evidence which he said supported his belief
that CSE was in fact involved and, indeed, the court after hearing submissions,
did not accede to CSE's request to strike. Furthermore, even though the judge
reportedly made comments reflecting on the lack of strength of that evidence,
he was not prepared to make an order for security for costs which, as noted
previously, can sometimes be used as a signpost to a plaintiff that the law
suit should not be undertaken lightly and that it is in danger of being
considered to be frivolous. The success of the plaintiffs in these matters
would no doubt have bolstered their belief that it was appropriate to continue
to proceed against CSE.[99] When the matter was once again raised before me during the course
of the plaintiffs' case at trial, I again refused to strike out CSE as a
defendant. Nevertheless, my comments at that time, to the effect that on the information
then existing the claims against CSE were "tenuous at best" and that
the plaintiffs were "assuming a significant risk that they will be
unsuccessful at the end of trial against CSE", could not be taken other
than as a blunt reminder that something further would likely have to be
presented to the court for the plaintiffs to have a realistic chance of success
against CSE. When those comments are coupled with the order which I made that
the plaintiffs should particularize in their pleadings the factual bases upon
which the liability of CSE, as separate from that of the Evans companies, was
alleged to be founded, and the fact that I ordered security for costs
specifically on the basis of the apparent weakness of the plaintiffs' case
against CSE, the argument of CSE that the plaintiffs must have realized that
their position against CSE had to be addressed becomes more compelling.

[100] Furthermore, the amendment which I allowed the plaintiffs to make
to their pleading, to allege that CSE assumed the liabilities of the Evans
companies, would also have brought home to the plaintiffs that they would have
to provide to the court some basis in the evidence or at law for concluding
that that alleged assumption took place.[101] Notwithstanding these matters, it can be said that for the
remainder of the plaintiffs' case, there was virtually no evidence presented
which could be said to impact further on the issues between the plaintiff and
CSE. Indeed, Carroll's evidence effectively eliminated potential reliance by
the plaintiffs on the November 23 letter as a realistic basis for tying CSE
into the original preparation of the report.[102] Can the failure on the part of the plaintiffs to present any
further evidence, in the face of the previous comments on the apparent
weaknesses in the existing evidence, while at the same time requiring CSE to
remain as a defendant until the end of the plaintiffs' case, be said to amount
to reprehensible, scandalous or outrageous conduct justifying solicitor-client
costs?[103] As noted previously, the fact that I concluded that the
plaintiffs should be nonsuited against CSE does not, in itself, equate to a
conclusion that the plaintiffs should have been expected to cease proceeding
against CSE at an earlier stage. One must approach the matter from the point of
view of the reasonableness of the beliefs of the plaintiffs, given their
knowledge base. Though a slender connecting thread, the plaintiffs had the
statements in the November 23 letter to rely on. Ought they to have been
expected to give up reliance on that in the light of the information provided
by CSE as to the date when CSE in fact took over the Evans companies? It must
be remembered that the statements in the letter were authored by Carroll at a
time when he was an employee of CSE. They were, therefore, CSE's statements. In
contentious litigation where tactics are important, it is not unreasonable for
parties to be cautious before giving up a claim where there is a possibility
that an opposing position - especially one stated by the other side - exists.
This is especially so where the consequences might be significant. Having had
the author of the report removed as a potential defendant and having been
presented with the knowledge that the Evans companies were judgment proof, the
consequence of CSE being removed as a defendant meant that the plaintiffs might
face the prospect of a finding of negligence with no person to answer for it.

plaintiffs should be nonsuited against CSE does not, in itself, equate to a
conclusion that the plaintiffs should have been expected to cease proceeding
against CSE at an earlier stage. One must approach the matter from the point of
view of the reasonableness of the beliefs of the plaintiffs, given their
knowledge base. Though a slender connecting thread, the plaintiffs had the
statements in the November 23 letter to rely on. Ought they to have been
expected to give up reliance on that in the light of the information provided
by CSE as to the date when CSE in fact took over the Evans companies? It must
be remembered that the statements in the letter were authored by Carroll at a
time when he was an employee of CSE. They were, therefore, CSE's statements. In
contentious litigation where tactics are important, it is not unreasonable for
parties to be cautious before giving up a claim where there is a possibility
that an opposing position - especially one stated by the other side - exists.
This is especially so where the consequences might be significant. Having had
the author of the report removed as a potential defendant and having been
presented with the knowledge that the Evans companies were judgment proof, the
consequence of CSE being removed as a defendant meant that the plaintiffs might
face the prospect of a finding of negligence with no person to answer for it.

[104] From the perspective of the plaintiffs, one can understand that,
given the events that occurred pre-trial, they might be cautious and even
mistrustful of CSE's motives in fighting so hard to be removed, given: (i) the
previous undertaking given to Bartlett, J., that CSE would accept
responsibility for Carroll's actions while an employee of CSE, ie. after June
1, 1989. (It is not without significance that the plaintiffs were also arguing
that the actions of Carroll after June 1, 1989 reaffirmed his previous
negligent misstatements and involved CSE in liability of that score as well);
and (ii) the representations made to Bartlett, J., by Yeatman and counsel for
CSE that the Evans companies would stand behind Carroll's actions prior to June
1,1989. The result of CSE's subsequent procedural manoeuvres was that CSE
effectively sought, knowingly, to have only an insolvent company stand behind
Carroll. The reaction of the plaintiffs was a reaction to positions taken by
CSE.[105] Furthermore, the evidence of Carroll's involvement in discussions
and investigations flowing from his report, after he became a CSE employee,
must also be considered. The plaintiffs argued that this amounted to either
separate acts of negligence or a reaffirmation of the previous negligence for
which CSE could be vicariously liable. As indicated, I did not accept that
characterization of that evidence; however, I cannot say that the plaintiffs'
view was not a reasonably-held possible alternative interpretation to be placed
on Carroll's actions. The fact that the evidence, given my characterization of
its significance, did not meet the test of probative sufficiency in the
non-suit motion does not mean that the plaintiffs were not justified in relying
on it for the purpose of pressing on with their claim without having the
inference drawn that they were abusing the process of the court, acting for
improper motives or otherwise engaging in reprehensible, scandalous or
outrageous conduct.

[106] I do not accept, as suggested by Mr. Waring that the plaintiffs
were "mean-spirited ... who were only interested in making life miserable
for anyone who had been involved with the F.V. Shelby Ann whether or not a
cause of action existed."; rather, they were acting out of an abundance of
caution in complicated litigation that involved a complex web of
interrelationships and evidence which, depending on how they or it were viewed
by the trier of fact, might or might not have involved CSE in liability. It was
not a case, as argued by CSE, of it being "impossible" for CSE to be
held liable. The actions of Carroll in continuing to deal with the report after
joining CSE opened the theoretical possibility (ultimately determined by me on
the non-suit motion to be groundless) that CSE could be held liable on the
basis of those actions. In stressing the "impossibility" of CSE being
held liable because of its non-involvement prior to the take-over of the Evans
companies, CSE appears to overlook, or at least unnecessarily downplay, the
role of Carroll as an employee of CSE after June 1, 1989.[107] To require the plaintiffs to have taken a leap of faith and
concluded, in advance of a ruling by the court, that there was no possibility
of success against CSE would in the circumstances of this case be to place the
threshold for awarding solicitor-client costs too low. It would require the
plaintiffs to judge the evidence. True, the plaintiffs took a big risk of
proceeding with a weak case against CSE, and lost. For that, they should pay,
just as any losing litigant should, but that in itself does not justify an
order for payment on the basis of solicitor-client costs. Even if the evidence
of Carroll eliminated the possibility of the November 23 letter being relied on
to connect CSE with the original preparation of the report, the subsequent
actions of Carroll also provided a possible basis for the plaintiffs to argue
for liability to be imposed on CSE. In light of that, no matter what degree of
analysis (and acceptance) by the plaintiffs of the information provided by CSE
as to the date and circumstances surrounding the take over, one could not
necessarily expect that reasonable persons in the position of the plaintiffs
would or should withdraw their claim entire-

[108] In all the circumstances, even if it could be said that the
plaintiff did not seriously consider the material submitted by CSE and that
that failure constituted misconduct, it could not be said to amount to
reprehensible, scandalous or outrageous conduct, nor is it the type of
behaviour deserving of such reproof or rebuke as to attract an award of
solicitor-client costs.- Failing, prior to commencement of litigation. to
provide relevant information to Carroll that could have affected the
preparation of his report.[109] This submission is based upon evidence at trial that Mr. Petten
contacted Mr. Carroll and told him that he did not have accurate plans of the
vessel but nevertheless refused to provide those plans to him. In my decision
on liability, I described these events as follows:"[160] Mr. Petten became aware that Mr. Carroll was
carrying out some sort of study of the vessel and contacted him to advise him
that he did not have the most up-to-date sets of plans and that any work that
Mr. Carroll did would therefore be inaccurate. Mr. Efford had previously
instructed Mr. Carroll not to communicate with Mr. Petten. By this time Mr.
Petten was also very defensive. Mr. Carroll said he asked Mr. Petten for the
drawings and was told they were ESB's property and he would see them in court.
As a result, all of the information from the builder's perspective including
the 'hands on' knowledge of what was done during construction of the Shelby
Ann, was not made available to Mr. Carroll."

[110] While it is true that, as Heywood demonstrates, the
pre-litigation activities of a party may form the basis of an award of
solicitor-client costs, the circumstances of the present case do not provide
that justification.[111] It is too simplisticto argue in effect, that in the circumstances
of this case, Mr. Petten was the author of his own misfortune and that if he
had disclosed to Mr. Carroll the most recent plans for the vessel the
litigation would not have been necessary. My findings with respect to the
deficiencies in the Carroll report were based not only on the absence of
accurate plans but on other factors as well. Furthermore, I also noted that
Carroll could have, but did not, properly qualify his opinions based upon the
gaps in his knowledge base.[112] In any event, by the time Carroll was commissioned to prepare his
report, there was very definitely an adversarial atmosphere existing. As I
noted in my decision with respect to liability of the other parties, it was
understandable for Mr. and Mrs. Petten to be suspicious and defensive given
their exclusion from some of the previous discussions and investigations
concerning the "problem" with the Shelby Ann. I agree with the
argument of Mr. Myers' counsel that the fact that plaintiffs do not cooperate
with a party adverse in interest relating to pending litigation should not
generally attract solicitor-client costs. Furthermore, Mr. Carroll had been
instructed by Harold Efford not to talk to Mr. Petten. Certainly, in the
circumstances of this case one can understand the reluctance of Mr. Petten to
cooperate where, if he did provide information to Carroll, the conversation
would be only one-way and where his experience to date had been one of having
to face accusation after accusation by others and having other information used
against him. While Mr. Petten's actions could, in hindsight, perhaps be
described as ill-advised, I cannot agree with CSE's counsel's characterization
of these actions as "reprehensible" or "scandalous".

- Making an improper allegation against counsel for CSE
respecting an undertaking that had not been given.[113] Counsel for CSE characterizes as "embarrassing disrespectful
tactics" the assertion made by counsel for the plaintiffs at the close of
the plaintiffs' case that counsel for CSE had given an undertaking to have
Brian Waring testify at the trial when, in fact, no such undertaking had been
given.[114] While on the face of it this incident should perhaps be more
properly dealt with in connection with the claim for costs against counsel, it
is clear that the Pettens also believed that this undertaking was given and Mr.
Myers was certainly authorized to raise the issue.[115] I am satisfied that the assertion by counsel for the plaintiffs
was made hastily under a misunderstanding arising out of previous discussions
with counsel for CSE.[116] When faced with the denial by counsel for CSE that any such
undertaking was given in respect of trial evidence, Mr. Myers, quite properly
and professionally, withdrew his assertion and apologized. Under these
circumstances, the hasty and mistaken action taken by Mr. Myers, which was
subsequently withdrawn with an apology, does not merit censure in the form of
an order for solicitorclient costs. There is no indication that the making of
the allegation occasioned any additional expense to CSE and, given Mr. Myers'
proper and professional response, I do not believe that an award to support the
integrity of the judicial system is necessary.

- Repetitious non-compliance with court orders.[117] There is no doubt that the plaintiffs did not comply with the
time limits imposed in respect of certain pre-trial court orders as well as
orders during trial; however, the costs consequences of such non-compliance
should have been, and in some cases were, dealt with at the time of subsequent
applications seeking enforcement.[118] Some of the non-compliance is explicable. For example, the
failure to comply with an order for production of documents finds at least a
partial explanation in the fact that new counsel took over the file and faced a
massive task of familiarizing himself with the material before preparing and
filing an organized book of documents. Again, with respect to the failure to
file security within the time limited by my first order for security for costs,
the matter was complicated by the discussions which were ongoing between
counsel with respect to the possibility of substituting other forms of
security. Subsequently, I was persuaded, following argument, that an extension
of the time should be granted. In so doing, I awarded CSE a portion of their
costs on a solicitorclient basis.[119] This is not a case of a simple ignoring of court process
indicating a flagrant disrespect for the court system. These events do not
constitute reprehensible, scandalous or outrageous conduct meriting an award of
solicitor-client costs on this basis.- Failing to carry out trial procedures in an
"effective" manner.

[120] CSE's argument with respect to this allegation is essentially
that the trial was unnecessarily prolonged because of the manner in which it
was conducted. It was suggested that the manner of questioning witnesses
indicated that counsel often had no idea as to what the witnesses were likely
to say and was effectively using the trial process as a form of discovery. It
was also suggested that the unfocused nature of the examination of the
witnesses was what led to the application during trial, previously referred to,
for substantial amendments to the pleadings calling for the addition of further
causes of action.[121] There is nothing to suggest that the conduct of the trial was not
done with the approbation of Mr. & Mrs. Petten. In fact, if anything the
Pettens believed that more, not fewer, questions should have been asked and
evidence presented.[122] I have to say that there were points during the trial where I
experienced feelings of frustration over the manner in which the case was
developing and I began to question the direction it was taking. That led me to
suggest, after twenty- seven days of trial, that all counsel participate in a
discussion on the record as to how the case could be more focused and
organized. I do not place complete blame for this, however, at the feet of the
plaintiffs or their counsel. It must be remembered that Mr. Myers assumed
carriage of the file, following the withdrawal of Mr. Moores as counsel, after
pleadings had closed and discoveries had concluded. The withdrawal of Mr.
Moores as counsel was, in practical terms, beyond the control of the Pettens.
The involvement of new counsel inevitably engages the possibility of a
different approach to the conduct of the trial based upon differing perceptions
of the strengths and weaknesses of various aspects of the case. In response to
my request for a discussion as to the future direction of the case, counsel
sought amendments to the pleadings. That was perhaps understandable under the
circumstances. It is also not without significance that many of the witnesses
called by the plaintiff were employees, or former employees of, or were
otherwise associated with, persons adverse in interest to the plaintiff. In
some cases, it could be said that they were not wholly cooperative and the
plaintiff had to seek leave to cross-examine as hostile witnesses which, in
some cases, was granted. This reality inevitably extended the examination process.
No doubt, as well, some of the examination was in the nature of discovery but,
again, counsel did not have the benefit of having conducted the original
discoveries.

[125] The authority of the court to award costs against a solicitor
personally flows from the inherent jurisdiction of the court to control its own
process and the conduct of persons coming before it (Young per
McLachlin, J., at p. 284) and from Rule 55.14(2) which provides in pertinent
part:"(2) Where in a proceeding, costs are incurred
improperly, or without reasonable cause, or arise because of delay, neglect or
other default, the court may, when the solicitor whom it considers to be
responsible, whether personally or through a servant or agent, is before the
court or has notice, make an order. . . .
.(c) directing the solicitor personally to indemnify any other
party against costs payable by the party; ..."[126] The basis of the jurisdiction is founded on the notion of control
and discipline of the courts' officers. Members of the Law Society of
Newfoundland, with the designation of both barristers and solicitors, are
officers of the Supreme Court: Law Society Act, R.S.N. 1990, c. L-9,
s.79. The power to award costs against a lawyer personally is one which should
be used with caution. Although emphasising that costs are generally awarded as
compensation for the successful party, McLachlin, J., in Young described
the dangers of too liberal an exercise of this jurisdiction as follows at p.
284:

."Moreover, courts must be extremely cautious in awarding
costs personally against a lawyer, given the duties upon a lawyer to guard
confidentiality of instructions and to bring forward with courage even
unpopular causes. A lawyer should not be placed in a situation where his or her
fear of an adverse order of costs may conflict with these fundamental duties of
his or her calling."[127] The majority of the Supreme Court generally approved the more
detailed discussion of the costs issues engaged in by Cumming, J.A., in the
British Columbia Court of Appeal in Young v. Young (1990), 75 D.L.R.(4th)
46 (B.C.C.A.). At p. 111, Cumming, J.A., stated:"An award of costs should not be made against a solicitor
personally on the ground that proceedings brought on behalf of a client lacked
merit unless it is beyond doubt, not only that the proceedings are devoid of
merit and that the solicitor knew or ought to have known them to be so, but
also that the responsibility for continuing with the proceedings despite their
lack of merit lies with the solicitor, rather than the client. Firstly, a
solicitor should not usurp the function of the court by pre-judging a client's
case. Secondly, it will generally be impossible for a solicitor to defend a
charge that he or she is responsible for proceeding with a meritless claim, by
showing that the client has been advised of the improbability of success and
has nevertheless insisted on proceeding, without a violation or waiver of
solicitor-client privilege."

I agree with these comments.[128] The comments of Cumming, J.A., emphasize the dilemma in which a
solicitor may find himself or herself when dealing with an application for
costs against him or her personally where it is conduct by the solicitor,
acting on behalf of a client in the conduct of a case, which forms the basis of
the claim: the difficulty of differentiating between actions of the solicitor
undertaken with the approbation or under the instructions or implied authority
of the client (which should generally be attributed to the client) and those
for which, in the words of Cumming, J.A., "the responsibility ... lies with
the solicitor, rather than the client". The disentanglement of these
differing situations is complicated by the role of solicitor-client privilege
or the potential occurrence, even if solicitor-client privilege is waived, of
an unseemly exchange between the lawyer attempting to avoid personal
responsibility and the client trying to distance himself or herself, after the
fact, from the actions of the lawyer.[129] In this case, Mr. Myers sought a waiver of solicitor-client
privilege from the plaintiffs but they failed to give it. He deposed generally,
however, that at the outset of the trial he believed that if the witnesses
called by the plaintiff testified as he was instructed they would, the
plaintiffs had a prima facie case against CSE, but that many witnesses did not
testify as he expected. He further deposed that "the plaintiffs attended
every day of trial and sat directly behind me and gave me instructions both
orally and in the form of notes which they passed to me during the trial"
and that "I sought to follow my clients' instructions and act in their
interests and in discharge of my obligation to the court at all times, to the
best of my abilities". Mr. Myers was not cross-examined with respect to
these assertions. The inference which I draw from this is that in pursuing the
claim against CSE and in otherwise acting as he did in the course of the trial,
Mr. Myers was acting within the scope of his instructions from his clients.

[130] Of course, the blind following of clients' instructions, whatever
they may be, does not absolve a lawyer from personal responsibility. As an
officer of the court, he also owes duties to the court, to his fellow lawyers
and the legal profession, and to the preservation of the system of
administration of justice by ensuring that it is not abused or subverted for
improper purposes or by false or misleading assertions. As stated by Professor
Gold in "The Court's Authority to Award Costs Against Lawyers" in
Gertner (ed.), Studies in Civil Procedure (Toronto: Butterworths, 1979)
at p. 63, the obligation to act on a client's instructions is "limited to
the employment of tactics, procedures and behaviour consistent with the goals
of the judicial system." Thus, it is said that a lawyer has a duty not to
pursue a claim which he knows to be false or without merit and if a client
nevertheless insists upon going forward, the lawyer should withdraw from the
case. Unfortunately, such a rule, which can be simply stated, has difficulty in
application in a case such as this. Even if Mr. Myers believed that there was
no basis for a claim against CSE (which, according to his uncontradicted
assertion was not the case) and even if he unequivocally informed the
plaintiffs of the lack of merit but they nevertheless insisted that he proceed,
the fact is that he had taken over a case involving many issues and a number of
defendants and the trial was well underway by the time I commented on the
tenuousness of the claim and awarded security for costs in April of 1994. It is
unrealistic to have expected in these circumstances for Mr. Myers, assuming
there was a conflict between his view and his clients' instructions with
respect to the claim against CSE, to seek to withdraw from the whole case,
thereby placing the whole litigation in limbo. Indeed, in these circumstances
it would not be automatic for the court to allow Mr. Myers to withdraw. In such
a scenario, one must be extremely cautious in attributing responsibility to a
lawyer personally for proceeding with a claim that is ultimately determined to
have had no merit.

[131] What, then, is the standard below which a lawyer must fall in
order to be subject to an order for costs against him or her personally? As the
discussion above indicates, the standard should not be set so high as to make
the lawyer the judge of his or her own clients' case. On the other hand, a
lawyer may not hide behind a client's instructions in order to do things that
involve a breach of his or her duties as an officer of the court or his or her
obligations to opposing counsel. He or she is expected generally to follow both
the spirit and letter of the rules of battle.[132] There are no reported Newfoundland Court of Appeal decisions
addressing this issue directly. However, in two decisions where the question
was whether the alleged inappropriate actions of counsel should be attributed
to a party for the purposes of awarding solicitor-client costs against that
party, there were comments made which may be of assistance. In House of
Haynes, Marshall, J.A., commented at p. 37:"The grounds for such awards ought not be extended to
mere negligence of the type attributed to counsel by the appeal court judge in
the case at bar that is not accompanied by recklessness or misconduct."There are important policy reasons supporting such a
stance. If the liability were extended to mere negligence, effective operation
of legal proceedings would be impaired. A bar which was conscious that counsel
could be sanctioned for misapprehensions, oversights or like errors by
imposition of penal costs might well be inhibited in pursuing its advocacy with
the force and rigour that the occasion demands. This would have an obviously
undesirable and detrimental effect upon the justice system."

In Canadian Paraplegic Association, an order for
solicitor-client costs was upheld on the basis of the failure of a solicitor to
make material disclosure to the court since it amounted to a failure to observe
a "fundamental obligation imposed on an officer of the court" to
follow not only the words but the spirit of the rules of procedure, which justified
indemnifying the other party against unnecessary costs associated with such
behaviour.[133] These cases suggest that something more than mistake, error of
judgment or mere negligence would be necessary to justify an order against a
solicitor. Serious misconduct or disregard of duty will generally have to be
shown. While the Supreme Court of Canada in Young does not expressly
affirm that negligence alone will be insufficient, that is a fair inference to
be drawn from the cautionary words used by McLachlin, J., which were previously
quoted. That is certainly the approach taken in decisions in a number of lower
courts. In Perley v. Sypher et al. (1990), 109 N.B.R.(2d) 427; 273
A.P.R. 427 (C.A.) the New Brunswick Court of Appeal held that in order to fix
costs against a solicitor the solicitor's actions must amount to "a
serious breach of duty", more than mistake, error of judgment or mere
negligence. The Court approved the statement that "there must be a serious
dereliction of the solicitor's duty to the court, something which justifies the
use of the word "gross"". In Cini v. Micallef et al.
