"The question is not whether the solicitor was negligent
but whether there was gross negligence or a failure on the part of the
solicitor to carry out his professional duty to the court."[134] Notwithstanding such statements, counsel for CSE asserts,
nevertheless, that "the established law allows mere negligence to
be sufficient for an award of costs against a solicitor". He bases this
argument on two things. First, he points to the general statement made by
McLachlin, J., in Young that the basis of a cost award is
"compensation ..., not in order to punish a barrister" as implying
that because compensation is the purpose, one need not show misconduct
exceeding negligence before an award is made. Secondly, he relies upon the
decision of the House of Lords in Myers v. Elman, [1940] A.C. 282 (H.L.)
and in particular the statement of Viscount Maugham therein at p. 208:"In my opinion the jurisdiction as to costs is quite
different [from the jurisdiction to strike a solicitor off the rolls for
professional misconduct]. Misconduct or default or negligence in the course of
the proceedings is in some cases sufficient to justify an order. The primary
object of the court is not to punish the solicitor, but to protect the client
who has suffered and to indemnify the party who has been injured."Counsel stresses the distinction drawn in Myers between the
disciplining, for punitive purposes, of lawyers on grounds of professional
misconduct which, in England, the court may also engage in, and the exercise of
a compensatory jurisdiction by the awarding of costs. The argument presented
was that once it is recognized that the punitive jurisdiction of the court is
related to discipline for professional misconduct (a matter in which in this
jurisdiction is assigned to the Law Society and not the court) it becomes clear
that the fulfilling of a compensatory purpose need not be tied to the finding
of serious misconduct on the part of the lawyer concerned.

[135] These arguments cannot be sustained. When the judgments in Myers
are read as a whole, a much more narrow test emerges. Other Law Lords in Myers
asserted that the jurisdiction to award costs against a solicitor also
fulfilled a punitive function. See Lord Atkin at pp. 302-304; Lord Wright at
pp. 318-319; Lord Porter at pp. 333-335. Lord Russell of Killowen on the other
hand, agreed generally with Viscount Maugham.[136] In any event, regardless of whether the jurisdiction fulfills
punitive and/or compensatory purposes, that still begs the question as to what
is the standard expected of a solicitor below which he or she must fall in
order to trigger the right to compensation by an award of costs. Even Lord
Maugham at other points in his judgment appears to set a higher standard than
that of mere negligence. At p. 292 he observed that although it is not
necessary to show that the lawyer has been guilty of conduct which would
justify punishment by striking him off the rolls or suspending him from
practice, he nevertheless asserted that the jurisdiction to award costs ought
to be exercised "only when there has been established a serious
dereliction of duty". Indeed, the facts of the case disclosed much more
than negligence in any event. It involved conduct of the solicitor in
permitting the swearing of an untrue affidavit of documents which Viscount
Maugham described as "dishonourable conduct in the course of the
proceedings". Lord Atkins spoke of the standard in terms of "gross
negligence", as did Lord Porter. Lord Wright referred to it as "gross
neglect or inaccuracy" including "a failure on the part of a
solicitor ... to realize his duty to aid in promoting, in his own sphere, the
cause of justice". He further stated, "a mere mistake or error of
judgment is generally not sufficient".

[137] Although Myers was referred to with apparent approval by
the Supreme Court of Canada in Pacific Mobile Corp. v. Hunter Douglas Canada
Ltd. and Robitaille, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 842; 26 N.R. 453, a case decided
before Young, the court did not indicate which of the speeches, or which
parts of the speeches, in Myers were specifically agreed with.[138] Read as a whole, the decision in Myers is not inconsistent
with the approach taken in Canada, as disclosed in the cases cited above.
Indeed, in subsequent cases in England, Myers has not been interpreted
in the manner argued for by counsel for CSE. Even though the jurisdiction to
award costs has a compensatory thrust, there is still a disciplinary element
involved. In R & T Thew Ltd. v. Reeves (No. 2), [1982] 3 All E.R.
1086 (C.A.), Denning, M.R., stated at p. 1089:"This compensatory jurisdiction still retains, however, a
disciplinary slant ... The cases show that it is not available in cases of
mistake, error of judgement or mere negligence. It is only available where the
conduct of the solicitor is inexcusable and such as to merit reproof."Denning, M.R. cited the decision of Myers v. Elman as his
authority. Again, in Edwards v. Edwards [1958] 2 All E.R. 197 (P.D.)
Sach, J., referred with approval to the portion of Viscount Maugham's judgment
in Myers where he emphasized the necessity for a serious dereliction of
duty, "something which justifies ... the use of the word gross". See
also Holden & Co. v. Crown Prosecution Service, [1990] 1 All E.R.
368 (C.A.).

[139] It is also not without significance that even if counsel for
CSE's wider interpretation of Myers is correct, that case concerned an
order that the solicitor pay one-third of the other side's party and party
costs. The court did not have to consider what level of misconduct by a
solicitor would attract liability for solicitor-client costs, which is what is
sought here. I conclude from this analysis that although the basic purpose
behind the award of costs may be the compensation of the party affected by the
solicitor's conduct of the litigation, there are punitive elements still
involved. Although the effect of an award may be to compensate the other side,
the triggering event for recognizing such entitlement to compensation must
involve serious misconduct on the part of the solicitor for which he or she,
rather than the client, can be said to be responsible. By making such an award,
the court indirectly expresses its disapproval of the conduct of the solicitor.
In that sense, the exercise of the jurisdiction has punitive features. I do not
regard the reference to compensation in Young as being inconsistent with
this analysis. The expressions of caution about placing a lawyer in a situation
where fear of an adverse order of costs may conflict with his or her duties,
and by stressing matters of "bad faith" and "encouraging ...
abuse and delay" and tying the court's inherent jurisdiction to
"abuse of process" and "contempt", McLachlin, J., is
implicitly setting the standard for an award of costs against the solicitor
higher than that of mere mistake, error of judgment or negligence. That is the
law in Canada regardless of whether or not counsel for CSE's interpretation of Myers
v. Elman is correct.

and by stressing matters of "bad faith" and "encouraging ...
abuse and delay" and tying the court's inherent jurisdiction to
"abuse of process" and "contempt", McLachlin, J., is
implicitly setting the standard for an award of costs against the solicitor
higher than that of mere mistake, error of judgment or negligence. That is the
law in Canada regardless of whether or not counsel for CSE's interpretation of <decision><title>Myers
v. Elman</title></decision> is correct.

[140] Is CSE's position advanced by the application of Rule 55.14(2)
instead of reliance on the inherent jurisdiction of the court to award costs
against a solicitor? That rule allows such an award where costs are incurred
(i) improperly; or (ii) without reasonable cause; or where they arise because
of: (iii) delay; (iv) neglect; or (v) other default. It has generally
equivalent counterparts in England and other Canadian jurisdictions. Does the
fact that the rule refers to "neglect" and "other default"
expand the circumstances where costs may be awarded against a solicitor
personally? I do not believe so. In the Court of Appeal in Young, where
the similar British Columbia rule (57(30)) was considered, the comments of
Cumming, J.A., previously referenced, were nevertheless made; indeed, the views
of McLachlin, J., in the Supreme Court, which acknowledged that the court's
authority in this regard came not only from its inherent jurisdiction but also
from statute, must be taken to have been intended to apply to the scope of the
applicable British Columbia rule as well.[141] The view that the applicable rule does not alter the scope of the
inherent jurisdiction of the court also exists in England. In Holden,
Lord Lane, C.J. noted that in Myers v. Elman Viscount Maugham referred
to the equivalent English rule but nevertheless stated that "the
jurisdiction ought to be exercised only when there has been established a
serious dereliction of duty ...". Lord Lane concluded that the current
rules of court (which had since been amended to include a reference to
"failure to conduct proceedings with reasonable competence and
expedition") nevertheless did not alter the common law rules as to the
jurisdiction of the court to award costs against a solicitor personally.
Approving the comments of Denning, M.R. in Thew, he continued to
formulate the test as one of "serious dereliction on the part of the
solicitor of his duty to the court."

[142] While I would not pretend that all cases interpreting similar
rules in Canadian jurisdictions are uniform in their approach, it is apparent
from the way in which some have applied the rule, that there is a concern not
to apply it with too broad a brush. See, Kern v. Kern and Wylie (1986),
50 R.F.L.(2d) 77 (Ont. H.C.); Weldo Plastics Ltd. v. Communication Press Ltd.
(1987), 19 C.P.C.(2d) 36 (Ont. Dist. Ct.); and Real Securities of Canada
Ltd. v. Beland et al. (1987), 16 C.P.C.(2d) 230 (Ont. Dist. Ct.).[143] While it is true that the British Columbia and English rules
refer to "misconduct" instead of "neglect" as in the
Newfoundland rule, I do not believe that this necessarily signals a broader
jurisdiction in this province. I do not regard the reference to
"neglect" as being equivalent to negligence; rather, I would equate
it more to the notion of dereliction of duty that appears in the cases dealing
with the court's inherent jurisdiction. That would be consistent with the
cautionary approach to the exercise of the power evident not only in Young
but also in Holden.[144] Counsel for CSE relies on the factual situation in Edwards
as indicating the appropriateness of awarding costs in this case. In Edwards,
a matrimonial dispute, the wife's solicitors were ordered to pay costs
personally (on a party and party basis) "where the solicitor throughout
was bent on pressing on with litigation regardless of all other factors"
even though as a result of discovery of the husband's financial information
provided by the husband's solicitors, it was apparent that no challenge to the
husband's financial circumstances could be successful. CSE analogizes that
situation to the refusal to discontinue against CSE in this case
notwithstanding the disclosure to the plaintiffs of information verifying that
CSE could not have been involved before June 1, 1989.

[145] I have concluded, however, that the two situations can, and
should be, distinguished. As noted in the previous discussion relating to the
liability of the plaintiffs to pay costs, there were acts of Carroll after June
1, 1989, which could reasonably have been viewed by the plaintiffs and relied on
to form the basis for an argument that the negligent statements in the Carroll
report were reasserted again by Carroll while an employee of CSE. While,
obviously, I was ultimately of the view that that was not the correct
interpretation, I cannot say that the contrary view was so fanciful that the
plaintiffs' holding that view was unreasonable and without any realistic
foundation. Thus, unlike Edwards, where the disclosure of information,
if properly considered and analysed, provided a complete answer to the claim,
CSE's simple emphasis on the timing of its acquisition of the Evans assets did
not provide such a complete answer in this case.[146] In this case, there is nothing to suggest that Myers did not have
an honest belief in a realistic possibility of success against CSE or to
suggest that, in the circumstances, he was acting otherwise than pursuant to
instructions to continue to pursue the claim against CSE. In the convoluted
circumstances of this case, including the stage at which Myers became involved and
his duty to act for his client with respect to the other issues and against the
other defendants, it was not realistic, even if he himself could not have
honestly believed in the possibility of success against CSE, for him to have
sought to withdraw totally from the case. I draw the inference that the
plaintiffs were determined to proceed against CSE based on the information they
had and that, in the circumstances, Myers had no choice but to continue to seek
to maintain a claim against CSE. At most, failure to present other evidence to
support the claim against CSE (assuming, but without deciding, that such
evidence existed) might constitute negligence for which Myers might be
answerable to his own client but such negligence (if that is what it was) would
not justify an order for costs in favour of CSE against Myers. In any event, it
cannot be said on the information available that the actions of Myers amounted
to negligence as opposed to compliance with instructions by the plaintiffs to
continue to press the claim even though there was no other evidence available
and to rely solely on the slender uncontextualized threads of connection that
had previously been identified. The actions of proceeding against CSE in these
circumstances must in the circumstances be regarded as the actions of the
plaintiff and not those for which individual responsibility on the part of the
solicitor must be attributed. There is, therefore, no basis for a claim for
costs against Mr. Myers on the basis of the pursuit of an unmeritorious claim
against CSE.

"The fact that Myers was hired 'at the eleventh hour'
after pleadings closed and discoveries had concluded and accordingly that the
trial was used to discover the evidence of witnesses is entirely beyond his
control. The Pettens may bear the risk of extra costs thereby attracted; Myers
does not. The fact that applications for amendments were therefore necessary
stands on the same footing. If counsel hired on the eve of trial becomes
personally liable for solicitor-client costs if he finds it necessary to seek
amendments to pleadings and to obtain evidence which has not already been
obtained at discovery, no party could ever change counsel."[150] Viewing the actions of Myers as a whole in the context of how
this case developed, it cannot be said that the conduct for which he is
responsible exhibited "bad faith" or "serious dereliction of
duty" or "gross neglect" or "serious misconduct".
There is therefore no basis for holding Mr. Myers liable personally for costs.General Observations[151] In summary, it should be observed that the definition and scope
of solicitor- client costs awards against opposing parties and/or their counsel
engages broad issues respecting the role of the court in the administration of
justice in the community.[152] No doubt, improper conduct of counsel in the representation of a
client's claim as well as abuse of the court process for improper purposes by
litigants have the potential of reflecting adversely on the reputation and
effectiveness of the courts as the proper dispensers of justice to citizens.
The court should be alert to these concerns and should, in appropriate cases,
take steps to counteract and discourage such actions.

[153] Counsel for CSE submits that such considerations are central to
this case and justify the court awarding solicitor-client costs. In his words:
"it is time for this court (meaning the collective not just the presiding
judge) to act." In support of a pro active role for the court in this
regard, he made reference to the Gold article previously cited where the
following occurs at pp. 83 and 86:"Courts, it is suggested, have done little to impose
sanctions in cases of misconduct by lawyers. The tendency has been to focus
only upon blatant misconduct or petty errors. There is no identifiable trend on
the part of our courts to enforce the lawyer's duty to act honestly, fairly and
competently in the conduct of litigation. While it may be that the profession
itself should be more vigilant of its members' activities and more demanding of
their performance, courts ought not to deny their responsibility to reprove
misconduct and error."To succeed in creating the judicial process discussed
earlier, it is necessary to promote activity which will result in its practical
achievement. In other words, lawyers must be called upon to account for their
actions. The lawyer's accountability for behaviour which constitutes a breach
of duty is the basis of the jurisdiction to award costs against a solicitor.. . . .
."A fearless and independent bar must be faced squarely by
a fearless and independent judiciary, one that is prepared to exercise its
authority to sanction misconduct and negligence."

[154] While these comments were made in the context of a discussion of
awarding costs against lawyers personally, the tenor of counsel for CSE's
submissions respecting the claim for solicitor-client costs against the
plaintiff equally involved exhortations to the court to be pro-active to
control, by the use of special costs awards, the assertion of claims which do
not have merit.[155] As important as the control of improper conduct of counsel and
litigant is in the effective administration of justice, other fundamental
values are equally important. Central among these is the need to ensure easy
access to the courts. It is imperative that no undue tariff be placed on people
for seeking resolution of their claims by invoking the help of the courts.
Freedom of access to the court is one of the bases of social stability, so that
disputes may be resolved by application of law rather than by force or other
types of self-help by frustrated or disgruntled individuals who feel their
views are not being heard and have nowhere else to turn.[156] The control of the improper use of the court for the presentation
of meritless claims can be effected by resort to other mechanisms besides the
imposition of solicitor-client costs. Rule 14.24 enables frivolous and
vexatious claims or ones that are an abuse of the process of the court to be
dismissed or stayed on application by the affected party. The very fact that
the courts are reluctant to invoke that power unless the circumstances are
"plain and obvious" (per Wilson, J., in Hunt v. T & N pic et
al., [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959; 117 N.R. 321; 4 C.C.L.T.(2d) 1; 43 C.P.C.(2d)
105; 49 B.C.L.R.(2d) 273; 74 D.L.R.(4th) 321; [1990] 6 W.W.R. 385, at p. 980
[S.C.R.]) that the claim is certain to fail, is reflective of the policy of not
denying a litigant access to the court to have his or her claim dealt with on
the merits. Again, even where the untenability of a claim is not apparent from
the pleadings, but a party nevertheless believes that on the available evidence
it is impossible for liability to be imposed on a given issue or against a particular
defendant, mechanisms such as applications for trial of a preliminary question
of law or fact under Rule 38 or for summary trial of an issue under Rule 17A
can be availed of to derail the proceeding and save the expense of a full
trial.

[157] Placed in perspective, therefore, using solicitor-client costs as
a means of controlling meritless claims is not necessarily the preferred
mechanism to be employed to accomplish this objective. Other mechanisms might
well be able to be invoked in appropriate cases without the risk of
discouraging access to the courts.[158] Such considerations must be balanced against the understandable
desire not to let the system be subverted for improper purposes. Litigants
already operate with the Damoclean sword of a potential adverse award of party
and party costs hanging over their heads. The threat of an additional award of
special costs, unless judiciously applied, may well have the effect of driving
litigants from the courtroom or dampening the efforts of counsel in the
fearless pursuit of the client's interests. This is the theme underlying Young,
where McLachlin, J., spoke against such costs awards against parties even where
the claims had "little merit" and warned against placing the lawyer
in a situation "where his or her fear of an adverse order of costs may
conflict with ... fundamental duties of his or her calling." That is why
it is not inappropriate to set the threshold high and generally to limit awards
of solicitor-client costs to events which can attract the types of descriptions
discussed earlier in this decision: scandalous, outrageous, reprehensible,
deserving of reproof or rebuke, bad faith, serious misconduct, flagrant acts
meriting censure, acting on improper motives, serious dereliction of duty and
gross neglect - conduct bordering on abuse of the court and its process, not
merely negligence or mistake in bona fide assuming a case has some merit when
in fact it does not. It is at that point where the scales tip in favour of
using costs more aggressively because, then, it can fairly be said that the
other side has abused the privilege of easy access to the system and should no
longer be entitled to that privilege without having to compensate fully the
other party affected, or without having to risk the censure of the court.

Judgment Interest on Costs[159] With respect to entitlement to prejudgment interest, s. 3(2) of
the Judgment Interest Act, R.S.N. 1990, c. J-2 provides:"(2) The court shall not award interest. . . .
.(d) on an award of costs in the action;"[160] In the context of ordinary court proceedings, where the awarding
of costs is made as part of or shortly after the judgment dealing with the
substantive issues in dispute, the intent of this provision is clear: unlike
monetary awards arising out of the substantive judgment, entitlement to costs
will not, for the purpose of calculation of pre-judgment interest, be treated
as arising at the time of the accrual of the cause of action on which they are
based, but will be calculated at the earliest, from the date of judgment. Only
post-judgment interest is therefore payable on costs.[161] Where the awarding of costs occurs as part of the judgment on the
merits the party entitled to costs can, in short order, proceed to have them
taxed and seek payment from the other side. But, what of the situation where
the determination of costs is, at the request of the parties, reserved and a
long delay occurs before the costs disposition is made? Does interest run from
the date of the costs award or from the date of the judgment on the merits on
which the later costs award is based? Put another way, is post-judgment
interest payable only post-(cost) judgment, or is it payable post-(merits)
judgment by notionally back-dating the costs disposition to the date of the
decision on the merits which after all is the decision on which any claim to
costs depends?

[162] The resolution of this question is of some significance in this
case. Here, CSE was successful on a non-suit motion halfway through the trial.
In theory, it was entitled to ask the court to proceed to make a costs
disposition arising from that decision. Indeed, counsel for CSE did make such
an application before the trial of the other issues concluded; however, in the
exercise of my discretion I declined to hear the application until the full trial
was completed so that all findings of fact were known and all issues of costs
involving the other parties could also be dealt with. I remain of the view that
that was the right course of action in the circumstances. Indeed, as this
judgment indicates, I have referred to certain findings in my decision on the
merits in the course of making my costs disposition in this case.[163] The consequence of that decision, however, is that CSE was
delayed in recovering its costs for the remainder of a very long trial and for
a considerable period after its conclusion. If it is entitled to its costs
without any interest prior to the date of this decision, the value of the award
in its hands today is less than if it had been able to have a decision for the
same amount at the conclusion of the non- suit motion, which, as I have said,
it was in theory entitled to have.

[164] It is true that success on the merits of a case does not
guarantee an award of costs, because costs are always in the discretion of the
court; yet as Sooley v. Canadian House Insurance Co. reiterates, a
successful party, in the absence of special circumstances, has a
"reasonable expectation" of obtaining an order for payment of at
least party and party costs. Thus, while, technically, a party has no legal
entitlement to costs until they are awarded, success on the merits for
practical purposes will, except in special cases, amount to a signpost of
entitlement.[165] In principle, where the delay has not been caused by CSE, it
should not be placed in any worse position as a result of the events that
transpired. The plaintiffs are not really in a position to complain since, at
least in theory, they have had the use of the money in the interim or at the
least have been spared having to face paying the costs at an earlier date.[166] Section 5 of the Judgment Interest Act, which deals with
post-judgment interest, provides that "every judgment debt" bears
interest from the day on which it is payable "under the judgment".
Section 2(d) defines "judgment debt" to include "a sum of money
or costs ... made payable under a judgment ...". The Act appears to
operate on the assumption (correct in most cases) that a costs award will form
part of the judgment on the merits. It does not expressly address the situation
where there is a bifurcation in the overall dispository decision.

[167] The Act must be given a purposive interpretation to enable
its objectives to be accomplished. Its application should not depend on the
happenstance of two decisions temporally separated, instead of one composite
disposition, being made. Section 5 mandates the payment of interest
post-judgment. A costs award, whether made at the same time as the decision on
the merits or subsequently, is still part of the overall disposition in the
case. The judgment is not over and the court not "functus officio"
until all required dispositions have been made.[168] The costs award is parasitic upon the disposition on the merits.
It is that decision which triggers the "reasonable expectation" of a
costs award. A costs decision is therefore part of the original judgment in the
sense of arising out of or, to use the words of the Act,
"under" that judgment.[169] Accordingly, there is no compelling reason why the notion of
"judgment" in the Act should be dissected into constituent
dispositions for the purpose of awards of post-judgment interest on costs, as
opposed to treating it as the decision from which the reasonable expectation of
costs flows.[170] This interpretation does not contravene the prohibition in s.
3(2) (d) against awarding pre-judgment interest on costs because once the
judgment "under" which the costs are payable is treated as the
judgment on the merits which triggers the right to claim costs, the issue is
one of post-judgment interest rather than pre-judgment interest. The notion of
denying interest on costs prior to judgment is still respected.

of Ontario and licensed and registered to carry on business in the Province of
Manitoba"; and b) English Electric Company Limited (English Electric),

owner of English Electric Company of Canada, Limited, now known as GEC Alsthom

[4] In 1963, Hydro contracted with the appellant
John Inglis to design and manufacture three turbines for the generating plant
it was proposing to construct at Grand Rapids. The turbines were designed and developed
essentially by English Electric, and manufactured by John Inglis.[5] Hydro issued a completion certificate on July 1,
1967, triggering the guarantee period under the contract of one year for all
components other than the stay vanes and the runner blades. Significant
problems had developed with respect to the stay vanes and runner blades that
had been the subject of ongoing discussion and review among the parties. By
supplementary agreement dated July 14, 1967, between Hydro and John Inglis, it
was agreed that a 36-month guarantee period would apply with respect to the
stay vanes and the runner blades.[6] On the same day, English Electric guaranteed to
Hydro the performance by John Inglis,… of the extended guarantee granted by the
Supplementary Agreement dated as of July 14, 1967 between The Manitoba Hydro
Electric Board and John Inglis Co. Limited.[7] On March 10, 1992, an explosion occurred which
seriously damaged the outer head cover on one of the turbines. This allowed
water and oil to escape into the powerhouse. Hydro claims that it suffered a
loss by reason of this occurrence, including loss of profits, totalling
approximately $30,000,000.[8] It is Hydro's position that the limitation
period in tort could not have expired before the incident occurred since it
could not have been discovered until the time of the failure. For the same
reason, Hydro claims the limitation period in contract also had not yet
expired. Hydro, on March 9, 1993, filed an application seeking an order that
the limitation period did not commence to run until March 10, 1992, or in the
alternative that it be granted an extension of time in which to commence an
action against the respondents for damages allegedly suffered as a result of
the failure. The application was supported by affidavit evidence.

[9] As a result of an earlier decision of this Court
and with the consent of all parties, Hydro's application was converted into a
trial of the issue and the matter proceeded to hearing. Eventually, leave was
granted to commence an action in tort and contract against John Inglis and
English Electric and a declaration issued that the action was not
statute-barred by the Act.[10] The facts on which Hydro based its application
are set out in paras. 30 and 31 of the reasons of the motions court judge
MacInnes J. [reported 128 Man. R. (2d) 199]:The evidence adduced on behalf of Hydro was
to the effect that there were substantial vibrations in unit 1 which occurred
shortly after the installation and commencement of operation of that unit and
that these vibrations caused cracks to occur in the studs which secured the
outer head cover of unit 1. Over time, Hydro asserts that these cracks
propagated ultimately resulting in a sufficient decrease of strength so that
they were no longer capable of holding the outer head cover in place. In the
result, the outer head cover on unit 1 was blown off damaging equipment and
permitting water and oil to flood the powerhouse and the generating station.Hydro's evidence was that it did not
perform any inspection of the outer head cover studs from the time of
installation until the explosion because it expected the studs to last as long
as or longer than the effective working life of the unit and they received
nothing from the manufacturer suggesting otherwise, or recommending periodic
inspection. Having said that, Hydro acknowledged that it could have inspected
the outer head cover studs had it seen fit to do so and, that had it inspected
and discovered cracked studs, it would in all probability simply have replaced
the studs and by reason of the relatively insignificant cost of so doing,
likely would not have advanced any claim against the manufacturer in that
regard. Unfortunately, however, the cracked studs were not discovered before
the March 10, 1992 explosion and the damage resulting was, of course,
substantial and substantially more than replacing some head cover studs.

[11] John Inglis and English Electric sought to call
evidence to rebut Hydro's allegations. MacInnes J. heard evidence from John
Inglis and English Electric on the understanding that he would rule at the
conclusion of the hearing whether such evidence could properly be received in
an application of this nature. The evidence as set out in para. 32 of the
reasons provided the following:They assert firstly, that there is no
evidence, or no reliable evidence of excessive vibration which would have
caused cracking of the head cover studs. As well, they dispute the suggestion
of small cracks initiating many years ago and propagating over time, leading to
the explosion on March 10, 1992. They also assert that Hydro, as part of its
normal maintenance program, and/or in the course of the substantial maintenance
that was performed by Hydro upon unit 1, on at least two occasions during the
lifetime of the unit, ought to have inspected and if necessary replaced the
outer head cover studs. In short, the respondents assert that you could not
have a situation whereby small cracks would begin many years ago and propagate
over time to failure, but rather that the cracking would have begun only within
a short time before failure, and further that if the studs had cracked years
ago and the cracks had propagated over time, these should have become known to
Hydro well before the explosion on March 10, 1992 had a reasonable inspection
and maintenance program been followed.

[12] Eventually, MacInnes J. refused to receive the
evidence.[13] MacInnes J. then went on to make the following
findings with respect to the issues that were still before him:(a) He found that Hydro's application was
wide enough to include a claim in tort at paras. 27 and 28:The point, however, is that I am satisfied
that the allegations contained in paragraph 13 and 14 of the Law affidavit do
constitute claims in tort, paragraph 13 being allegations that apply to both
Inglis and E.E. England [English Electric], and paragraph 14, to the latter
only.I conclude, as well, that the additional
allegations of faulty design and manufacture of the studs constitute further
particulars of the causes of action raised in the application and do not raise
a new cause of action.(b) That Hydro satisfied the requirements
of s. 14(1) of the Act at para. 34:… it is my view based upon the evidence
available to me for consideration on this application, that it was the
explosion of March 10, 1992 that gave rise to Hydro's learning of the various
facts relating to their proposed cause of action, which facts were material
within the meaning of s. 20(2) of the Act. Hydro's discovery of these
material facts of a decisive character clearly occurred within twelve months
prior to March 9, 1993, the date of its application. Further, in my view, it
was only the incident of March 10, 1992 that could reasonably have given rise
to Hydro's discovering the alleged deficiencies of which it now complains and
the nature and extent of the damages for which it now seeks to sue. I conclude,
therefore, that Hydro has complied with s. 14(1) of the Act.

In my view, the language of s. 15(2) is
clear. Its intent is to ensure that if the court is going to grant leave to
extend the limitation period and permit suit, such suit should not be on its
face of dubious merit but rather prima facie should be a suit which has a
reasonable prospect of success. But to allow the respondent to call evidence
could, and in many instances would likely, result in the full blown
introduction of evidence on this preliminary application, resulting in substantially
increased costs while the parties effectively go through two trials rather than
one, the first one simply being for the purpose of deciding whether leave will
be granted. In addition this might also lead to the rather unseemly result of
the motions judge deciding that there was a reasonable prospect of success and
therefore granting leave, whereas the trial judge, on essentially the same
evidence, might conclude that there was no merit and dismiss the claim.[16] English Electric did not proffer any evidence
and took no position with respect to this issue.[17] In argument, John Inglis forcefully asserted
that, despite the words "in the absence of any evidence to the
contrary" in s. 15(2), MacInnes J. could not reasonably consider the
evidence submitted on behalf of Hydro — consisting exclusively of expert
evidence — or determine its sufficiency under s. 15(2) in the absence of the
contradictory expert evidence adduced by John Inglis. Having accepted the
expert testimony of Hydro's experts, Dr. Tennesey and Mr. Pawlikewich, the
motions court judge, according to John Inglis, was left in a position where he
could not realistically assess the weight and credit to be attached to their
testimony in the absence of viva voce evidence from the respondents.
Cross-examination, it was urged, is not enough. Otherwise, as dramatically put
in the factum of John Inglis, "Rather than being a guardian of the gate on
leave applications, the Court is reduced to the function of doorman".

[18] Mr. Baigrie, who presented this portion of the
argument on behalf of John Inglis, also emphasized the use of the word
"may" in s. 14(1) of the Act. Section 14 is the key provision
that, as we shall shortly see, creates the statutory right to an extension of
the limitation period under the defined circumstances contained in the Act.
He argued that the court has an inherent discretion which should have been
exercised in favour of hearing all of the evidence on the critical issue of the
likely success of Hydro's action if allowed to proceed.[19] Finally, the motions court judge himself in his
reasons was of the view that in certain "rare cases" a respondent
could call evidence if of a critical and decisive nature. Where, Mr. Baigrie
asks, should one draw the line?[20] To all of this Hydro simply responds that the
wording of s. 15(2) — with its clearly stated prohibition against consideration
of "evidence to the contrary" to that called in support of the
application — is determinative of the issue. Hydro notes that there are two
different tests provided by Part II of the Act (set out in ss. 14(1) and
15(2)). With respect to the latter, the section mandates that the court is not
to look at evidence tendered by or on behalf of the respondents in determining
if there is a prima facie case. Once it is determined on evidence
presented by the applicant that the threshold of a reasonably arguable case
has been met, only then is the motions court judge in a position, pursuant to
the broad discretion given by s. 14(1), to permit evidence to be tendered to
assist in the exercise of the discretion given only by that provision.

authority to support it. See: Rebizant v. Greenwood (1998), 127 Man. R.

decisive character upon which the action is based; and(b) the date on which the application was made to the court
for leave.

[23] John Inglis and English Electric argue that the
motions court judge erred in concluding that the proposed claim against John
Inglis in contract and tort, and against English Electric in tort, had a
reasonable prospect of success.[24] Strong reliance is placed by John Inglis on the
requirements of s. 20(3) of the Act which provides as follows:20(3) For the purposes of this Part, any of
the material facts relating to a cause of action shall be taken, at any
particular time, to have been facts of a decisive character if they were facts
which a person of his intelligence, education and experience, knowing those facts
and having obtained appropriate advice in respect of them, would have regarded
at that time as determining, in relation to that cause of action, that, apart
from any defence based on a provision of this Act or any other Act of the
Legislature limiting the time for bringing an action, an action would have a
reasonable prospect of succeeding and resulting in an award of damages or
remedy sufficient to justify the bringing of the actions.[25] In order to satisfy s. 14(1) of the Act,
the applicant must show three things: that it learned of facts that are
"material" within the sense of s. 22, and of a "decisive"
character within the meaning of s. 20(3); and that this knowledge was acquired
during the twelve months immediately preceding the date of the application. Einarsson
v. Adi's Video Shop (1992), 76 Man. R. (2d) 218 (C.A.) at para. 13.

[26] Lack of awareness of the "nature or extent
of the injuries or damages" suffered is one of the grounds for granting an
extension of time pursuant to the Act. See Heaman v. Isaac
(1993), 89 Man.R. (2d) 63 (Q.B.) at para. 9.[27] John Inglis argues that the motions court judge
erred in precluding it from tendering viva voce evidence with respect to
whether Hydro knew or ought to have known of the alleged fatigue problem in the
studs more than twelve months prior to March 10, 1993 (the date of the
application). But the only evidence tendered by John Inglis was that of Dr.
Cahoon who opined that the studs fractured at the same time and in series and
that there was no prior warning. This hardly comports with the theory now
advanced by the respondents that Hydro should have known of the fatigue problem
well before the incident of March 10, 1992. In our opinion, the motions court
judge was entirely correct when he held at para. 33:… having ruled the evidence of Dr. Cahoon
inadmissible, there is no evidence for my consideration on the application
which supports the respondents' position.[28] Realistically, this is the end of the matter,
but we pass on to consider the remainder of John Inglis's submission, given the
importance of the issue and the time devoted in argument to it.

[29] Simply stated, John Inglis's argument is that
Hydro, as a sophisticated and expert client, has the "intelligence,
education and experience" referred to in s. 20(3) and either did inspect
or ought to have inspected the 120 studs in question in light of their
essential and critical function of maintaining the outer head cover in
position. Such a procedure could readily have been undertaken. Indeed, John
Inglis says the studs are in close proximity to other areas subject to
vibration concerns and could have and should have been inspected by
non-destructive testing.[30] Even more aggressively, John Inglis asserts that
it is open for this Court to conclude that Hydro, during the 1980 and 1986
overhaul of Turbine No. 1, in fact removed the outer head cover and/or the
outer head cover studs. It was suggested that Mr. Pawlikewich, Hydro's witness,
had changed his testimony with respect to whether the outer head cover had been
removed. As well, there was evidence that the O-ring, acting as a watertight
seal, had been removed and replaced. This suggests that the outer head cover
had also been removed (which would require removal of the studs). Thus, the
respondents say, there is evidence that the motions court judge could have
accepted demonstrating "intervention and removal" of the outer head
cover.[31] English Electric joined in the argument
presented by John Inglis, and submitted that Hydro's maintenance records and
testimony show that Hydro made a number of judgment calls with respect to
maintenance of the turbines and, having elected not to do its own inspections
of the outer head cover studs, must now bear the consequences. This is
especially significant since it was well known that the joint between the outer
head cover and the stay ring is the weakest connection with respect to the head
cover components.

[32] As previously stated in para. 13(b) of these
reasons, MacInnes J., after reviewing the evidence, concluded that it was the
explosion of March 10, 1992 which permitted Hydro to learn of the various facts
relating to the proposed cause of action and that Hydro had satisfied the
requirements of s. 14(1) of the Act.[33] Having considered the strong representations
made by the respondents that there was evidence that the motions court judge
could have accepted to conclude that Hydro knew or ought to have known of the
fatigue problem with the studs long before March 10, 1992, we respond in two
different ways. Firstly, this is not our sense of the weight of the evidence.
Secondly, and more importantly, while there may well be evidence that the
motions court judge could have accepted to support the inferences and
conclusions urged by the respondents, there was ample evidence to the contrary
that he did accept, and properly so. There is ample evidence to support
this finding, particularly given the limited scope of the motions court judge's
function. That is the end of the matter.The Contract Documents[34] As might be expected in a matter involving the

documents are numerous and complex. In this case, they consist of
specifications prepared by Hydro's consulting engineer (H. G. Acres &
Company Limited), the successful tender of John Inglis and the Hydro
acceptance, together with numerous appendices. Along the way, numerous
discussions, on-site meetings and negotiations took place between John Inglis,
the contractor, and Hydro during the course of the design and construction of
the project, including the turbines. There can be no doubt that Hydro, John
Inglis and English Electric were experienced and sophisticated parties
possessing or having access to the very best expertise in engineering, legal
and contractual matters.

the Purchaser's Completion Certificate, any part of the work becomes broken or

. .The Contractor's liability under this
Section shall be in lieu of any warranty or condition implied by law as to the
quality, design or fitness of the work for any particular purpose, and save as

or damage resulting from any such defects.Provided the Contractor is not otherwise in

satisfactory periodic inspections of the turbine blades on Units 1, 2, and 3
and stay vanes for Units 1, 2, 3 and 4 the latest of which was carried out this
spring with yourself in attendance, your firm is now relieved of their
obligations in connection with warranties on the units.[41] Clearly, the outer head cover and studs were not
part of the three-year "extended warranty".[42] In a nutshell, John Inglis argues that it is
entitled on and after twelve months had expired from June 30, 1967 to the
protection afforded by the guarantee. It was "not otherwise in
default" of the contract, and indeed had never been formally notified of a

limitation period under Part II of the Act. The clause only makes sense,
it is argued, if it means that any defect had to be brought to John Inglis's
attention in writing within the first twelve months after the completion
certificate was issued.[43] John Inglis says Hydro wanted

introduction of English Electric's individual guarantee. The sophisticated
parties allocated the risk between themselves and the court should not disturb

[44] Therefore, says John Inglis, there is no
realistic prospect that the action will succeed, since whatever may be the
provisions of Part II of the Act, the completion certificate issued by
Manitoba Hydro on June 30, 1970 is a complete bar to the success of Hydro's
action. Part II of the Act can apply only to the statutory limitation
period and cannot affect a separate and independent contract between John
Inglis and Hydro which resulted in a complete release and satisfaction of John
Inglis's contractual obligations.[45] Hydro's response to the question of the meaning
of the guarantee (and release), contained in para. 21 of the general
conditions, is to assert an interpretation that it says flows from the plain
wording of the general conditions and other relevant documents when considered
in the context of the purpose and object of the contract as a whole. Simply
stated, Hydro says that so long as it can be demonstrated that the studs
cracked or began to crack within the first year of operation (or presumably
prior thereto), the guarantee applies. The twelve-month "limitation"
in the guarantee applies, Hydro argues, only to the defect or failure itself
and not to the notification requirement, for which no specific time is
provided. Assuming in such circumstances that the requirement is that notice be
given within a reasonable time, how then, Hydro submits, could notice possibly
have been given prior to the explosion in March 1992 which was the first
occasion on which Hydro knew, or could reasonably have known, of the defect? It
is an unambiguous, straightforward provision which should be given its plain
meaning, namely, that the guarantee applies if "any part of the work
becomes defective … within twelve months". At a minimum, Hydro asserts the
issue is one that is reasonably arguable, and may well be eventually dependent
on the findings of fact at trial with respect to the origin and timing of the
fatigue cracks in the studs.

It is a cardinal rule of the construction
of contracts that the various parts of the contract are to be interpreted in
the context of the intentions of the parties as evident from the contract as a
whole: K. Lewison, The Interpretation of Contracts (1989), at p. 124; Chitty
on Contracts (26th ed. 1989), vol. I, at p. 520.See as well Bow Valley Husky (Bermuda)
Ltd. v. Saint John Shipbuilding Ltd., [1997] 3 S.C.R. 1210, 153 D.L.R.
(4th) 385, at para. 28 per McLachlin J., and at para. 118 per Iacobucci
J.; Hillis Oil & Sales Ltd. v. Wynn's Canada Ltd., [1986] 1 S.C.R.
57 at p. 66, 25 D.L.R. (4th) 649; and Consolidated-Bathurst Export Ltd. v.
Mutual Boiler & Machinery Ins. Co., [1980] 1 S.C.R. 888 at p. 901, 112
D.L.R. (3d) 49, per Estey J.[50] To this end, a court should endeavour to read
the clauses of a contract in such a way that they can be reconciled with each
other. Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. v. Canadian Commercial Bank (1991),
79 Alta.L.R. (2d) 294 (C.A.), appeal dismissed [1992] 2 S.C.R. 3.

subsequent conduct can be admissible (at least in Canada) as a guide to the
interpretation of a written contract. See Ottawa (City) v. Canadian National
Railways, [1925] S.C.R. 494, [1925] 3 D.L.R. 762; Firestone Tire and
Rubber Co. of Canada v. Canada (Commissioner of Income Tax), [1942] S.C.R.
476, [1942] 4 D.L.R. 433; Turvey & Mercer v. Lauder (1956), 4 D.L.R.
(2d) 225 (S.C.C.); and Hayduk v. Waterton; Flechuk v. Waterton, [1968]
S.C.R. 871, 68 D.L.R. (2d) 562; and G.H.L. Fridman, Q.C., The Law of
Contract in Canada, 3rd ed. (Scarborough, Ont.: Carswell, 1994) at 464.[52] In this instance, the plain wording of the
guarantee in the context of the contract as a whole certainly suggests that it
applies to defects which occur within one year as opposed to defects
which appear within one year. (An interesting comparison can be made to
the facts in Hunter Engineering Co. v. Syncrude Canada Ltd., [1989] 1 S.C.R.
426, 57 D.L.R. (4th) 321 which led the Supreme Court to the opposite
conclusion.) However, it can also be argued that the plain meaning
interpretation of the guarantee has an effect contrary to the intentions of the
parties given the subsequent conduct of the parties and the terms of the June
1970 release. The key issue will undoubtedly be whether the plain meaning of
the guarantee should prevail, or whether it results in an absurdity or defeats
the intentions of the parties. But it is clear to us that Hydro has presented a
prima facie argument that the provisions of the "guarantee"
should be interpreted in its favour.

and John Inglis, as a result of Hydro's letter of June 30, 1970 confirming that
John Inglis's obligations under the contract had been satisfied.[54] Dealing with the first issue, as problems
developed, caused by vibrations following the installation of the first
turbine, much discussion, as we have already seen, took place involving John

our company has every confidence in them. Furthermore, it is our intention to

[57] What was extended by the supplementary guarantee
between Hydro and John Inglis, in our opinion, was the period of the guarantee
(from one year to three years) with respect to the runner blades and stay vanes
and no more. This and this alone is what English Electric's agreement of July
14, 1967 refers to. By standing firmly behind John Inglis's contractual
responsibilities, English Electric did not, in our opinion, assume any
additional legal obligations.[58] We readily conclude that there is no prima
facie or reasonably arguable case against English Electric in contract and
the motions court judge was entirely correct in so deciding (see paras. 26 and
41 reasons for judgment).[59] Given this conclusion, it becomes self-evident,
in our opinion, that English Electric is not entitled to rely upon the release
provisions of the contractual guarantee, at para. 21 of the general conditions,
consequent upon the confirmation (understandably directed only to John Inglis)
by Hydro dated June 30, 1970 that John Inglis was relieved of any further obligations
in connection with the warranties under the contract. Throughout the entire
affair, including the intensive discussions and negotiations that led up to the
execution of the agreement of July 14, 1967, between Hydro, John Inglis and
English Electric, it is clear that, while English Electric was "standing
behind" its design and John Inglis its sole contractual obligation was
created by the extended guarantee of July 14, 1967.

additional legal obligations.[58] We readily conclude that there is no prima
facie or reasonably arguable case against English Electric in contract and
the motions court judge was entirely correct in so deciding (see paras. 26 and
41 reasons for judgment).[59] Given this conclusion, it becomes self-evident,
in our opinion, that English Electric is not entitled to rely upon the release
provisions of the contractual guarantee, at para. 21 of the general conditions,
consequent upon the confirmation (understandably directed only to John Inglis)
by Hydro dated June 30, 1970 that John Inglis was relieved of any further obligations
in connection with the warranties under the contract. Throughout the entire
affair, including the intensive discussions and negotiations that led up to the
execution of the agreement of July 14, 1967, between Hydro, John Inglis and

[60] In London Drugs Ltd. v. Kuehne & Nagel
International Ltd., [1992] 3 S.C.R. 299, 97 D.L.R. (4th) 261, the Supreme
Court in a landmark decision relaxed the strict rules of privity of contract
beyond the established exceptions of agency and trust, so that employees of a
corporation actually performing the contracted work were entitled to the
protection of a limitation of liability clause despite the fact that they were
not personally parties to the contract. This was because "commercial
reality and common sense require that it should" (at p. 415). Critical to
the creation of the new exception is the intention of the contracting parties.
Thus, on the facts of London Drugs at p. 448:… a threshold requirement for employees to obtain the benefit of
their employer's contractual limitation of liability clause is the express or
implied stipulation by the contracting parties that the benefit of the clause
will also be shared by said employees.[61] This essential point was reiterated again in Edgeworth
Construction Ltd. v. N.D. Lea & Associates Ltd., [1993] 3 S.C.R. 206,
by McLachlin J. for the Court at pp. 216-17, 107 D.L.R. (4th) 169. (On the
facts of Edgeworth Construction, the Court concluded that the
contractual provisions and other surrounding circumstances were "entirely
consistent" with the conclusion that the protection was not intended to be
extended beyond the contracting party.)

Pile & Dredge Ltd. v. Can-Dive Services Ltd., [1999] S.C.J. No. 48 (QL)
[now reported 176 D.L.R. (4th) 257], Iacobucci J., writing for a unanimous
court, readily concluded that a waiver of subrogation provision entered into
between sophisticated commercial clients, which expressly extended the benefit
of such waiver to an ascertainable class of third-party beneficiaries, did
confer the benefit of such a provision on the third parties who were expressly
contemplated and included within the precise terms of the waiver provision.[63] Here careful examination of the contract,
including the limitation of liability provision, makes it very clear that John
Inglis alone is responsible for making good any defects (other than the
extended guarantee of English Electric as just reviewed). There is no express
language suggesting that the contract and limitation of liability clause was
meant to benefit anyone else. Likewise, it does not appear that it can be
implied that the limitation of liability clause was meant to benefit English
Electric. The circumstances here are not analogous to those of employees
actually charged with doing the work contemplated by the parties to the
contract, as in London Drugs, or a specifically named beneficiary in a
complex commercial arrangement as in Fraser River Pile & Dredge Ltd.
Rather, similar to Edgeworth Construction, English Electric was a
separate large professional firm which had the ability to protect itself in a
variety of ways, if it chose to do so. Doubtless, it chose not to do so because
of the very limited nature of its contractual relationship with Hydro.

[64] Under these circumstances, it can hardly be
gainsaid that by some mysterious reasoning English Electric became entitled to
the protection of the very contractual provisions that it was so astute to
avoid, simply because it guaranteed John Inglis's performance of the extended
guarantee with respect to the stay vanes and runner blades.[65] In its factum, Hydro argued that "English
Electric cannot, however, rely upon the limitation of liability to protect it
from its own torts, committed independently of the contract". But this
raises an entirely different issue from the question of English Electric's
ability to seek the protection afforded by the provisions of the contract
between Hydro and John Inglis.Liability in Tort[66] We therefore turn to English Electric's
potential liability in tort and the question whether an extension of time for
such a potential cause of action was properly raised in Hydro's application.[67] English Electric, supported by John Inglis,
argues that Hydro has not pleaded a cause of action in tort. This is an issue
of particular significance to English Electric. As we have already observed,
Hydro has no case against English Electric in contract apart from any claim
that might have arisen under English Electric's limited guarantee given on July
14, 1967.[68] For the purpose of this issue, Hydro's
application under s. 14(1) of the Act and the supporting affidavit of
Robert Law constitute the "pleadings" which must be examined to
determine whether or not material facts that raise a claim in tort have been
alleged.

[69] English Electric argues that by its application
Hydro intended to seek leave to sue only in contract. Counsel for English
Electric explain in their factum:English Electric acknowledges that it was
the intention of Hydro to sue in tort and contract eventually, but submits that
Hydro only sought leave in respect of the causes of action framed in contract.
… References were made to the fact and belief of Hydro that it had a right,
separate from the Application, to bring forward an action in tort with respect
to the 1992 failure. …Hydro represented that it was its intention to issue a
claim in tort in any event and therefore wished to have the Application for
leave determined in respect of the action in contract in order that they might
be joined in one pleading.This perception by Hydro changed
dramatically as at July 8, 1997, when we suspect that some research on the
issue of limitation periods threatened to undermine Hydro's confidence in the
view that the limitation period in tort had not expired. Their concern … proved
to be well founded, as recently clarified by this Court in Rarie v. Maxwell
[(1998), 131 Man.R. (2d) 184], namely that Part II of the Act occupies the
whole field of discoverability and that accordingly, judge-made discoverability
has no application in Manitoba.[70] Hydro does not dispute the essential facts
underlying that scenario and those opinions., nor could it in the face of
correspondence between the parties and the case management memoranda that are
part of the record. However, as we will see, it is the factual situation that
is put forward, and not the label put on the facts, that will determine the
sufficiency of the pleadings.

Diplock L.J. in Letang v. Cooper, [1964] 2 All E.R. 929 at 934 (C.A.),
at para. 26, that "[i]t is clear that a cause of action is simply a
factual situation, the existence of which entitles one person to obtain from
the court a remedy against another person".[72] The issue of the sufficiency of pleadings that
is raised in the context of this appeal is not one that has received a great
deal of attention in Canadian decisions. However, in Scotsburn Co-operative
Services Ltd. v. W.T. Goodwin Ltd., [1985] 1 S.C.R. 54, 16 D.L.R. (4th)
161, Dickson J. (as he then was), writing for the majority, cited at p. 65,
without comment but with apparent approval, the English practice and
authorities, including Re Vandervell's Trusts (No. 2), [1974] 3 All E.R.
205 (C.A.), in which Lord Denning M.R. had written at p. 213:It is sufficient for the pleader to state
the material facts. He need not state the legal result. If, for convenience, he
does so, he is not bound by, or limited to, what he has stated. He can present,
in argument, any legal consequence of which the facts permit.

[73] Lord Denning M.R. had expressed the same
principle in slightly different words in an earlier case, Karsales (Harrow),
Ltd. v. Wallis, [1956] 2 All E.R. 866 (C.A.). He had written at p. 869:… I have always understood in modern times
that it is sufficient for a pleader to plead the material facts. He need not
plead the legal consequences which flow from them. Even although he has stated
the legal consequences inaccurately or incompletely, that does not shut him out
from arguing points of law which arise on the facts pleaded.[74] Lord Denning's dicta in Re Vandervell's
Trusts (No. 2) was applied in 384238 Ontario Ltd. v. Canada (1983),
8 D.L.R. (4th) 676 (F.C.A.) (leave to appeal refused, [1984] 1 S.C.R. v), and
in R. v. Imperial General Properties Ltd., [1985] 1 F.C. 344, 16 D.L.R.
(4th) 615 (C.A.) (leave to appeal refused, [1985] 1 S.C.R. ix, 16 D.L.R. (4th)
615n).[75] Not alluded to by the motions court judge are
the recent Canadian cases which have established that a given wrong may give
rise to two different forms of action, one in contract and the other in tort.
See, for example, Central Trust Co. v. Rafuse, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 147, 31
D.L.R. (4th) 481, BG Checo International Ltd. v. British Columbia Hydro and
Power Authority, and Winnipeg Condominium Corporation No. 36 v. Bird
Construction Co., [1995] 1 S.C.R. 85, 121 D.L.R. (4th) 193. It is not
necessary in this appeal to review and consider the trend of the law towards
concurrency in tort and contract that these decisions have heralded. It is
sufficient for our purposes to observe that in those decisions, the Supreme
Court has recognized that a common law duty of care may arise from the facts
pleaded that also support a claim for breach of contract.

[82] English Electric challenges the finding of the
motions court judge that "the designer of the turbines was [English
Electric] and that there is a real basis for arguing it was also the designer
of other components including the outer head cover studs". That was an
allegation put forward in para. 6 of the affidavit: the "turbines were
designed and developed primarily by the Respondent [English Electric]".
While the nature and extent of the role of English Electric in the design of
the turbines and its components, and the legal consequences flowing therefrom,
will likely become live issues at the trial of the action, there was ample
evidence before the motions court judge on Hydro's application to support these
findings and the implicit finding that there was a relationship of sufficient
proximity to create a common law duty of care.[83] In para. 14, it is alleged that "the
designer of the turbines fell below the standard of care expected of engineers
in the design of equipment of this nature". It is not alleged that the
standard of care arises out of or is defined by contractual provisions or
specifications. It is a claim sounding in tort.[84] The inelegant and sometimes inaccurate drafting
of Mr. Law's affidavit is the cause of much, it not all, of the difficulties
that surround this issue. As we have noted above, the affidavit was filed in
support of an application that was originally intended to address the
limitation period affecting Hydro's contractual claims. Mr. Law, in para. 6,
wrongly identified English Electric Company of Canada, Limited as a party to
the contract. He then went on to say that English Electric "assumed the
contractual commitments of [John Inglis] and English Electric Company of
Canada, Limited pursuant to the said Agreement by means of a letter dated June
18, 1965". That assertion is not established on the record before the
court. Further paragraphs of the affidavit refer to the responsibilities of
John Inglis, English Electric Company of Canada, Limited, and English Electric
pursuant to the contract and, in para. 15, to their breach of its terms.

input: Held, a judgment should issue that TB is liable to pay $40,000 by reason of liability imposed under s. 13(1) of the Construction Lien Act. A breach of s. 13(1) does not lead to the conclusion that the person breaching the Act is a trustee. The elements for common law liability as a trustee or as a constructive trustee were different from the liability imposed by the Act. Section 13 of the Act was passed to impose liabilities for breaches of trust by a corporation under s. 8 upon the directors or officers or persons in control of the corporate activities when they conducted themselves in the ways described by s. 13. The standard under s. 13 was very different from the standard under trust law when a stranger to a trust can be found liable as a constructive trustee. The elements necessary for a plaintiff to be successful in an action under trust law were significantly more stringent than the elements under s. 13 of the Act. There is a difference between statutory liability and common law liability. Section 13 was not a restatement of the common law but the creation of an independent statutory scheme. The legislation did not require constructive trusteeship. Accordingly, judgment should issue that TB was liable to pay $40,000 by reason of liability [page291] imposed under s. 13(1) of the Construction Lien Act for the breach of trust of ESD Industries Inc.

input: [5] Put in its simplest form, the question is as to whether the form and content of the judgment should be a declaration that the individual defendant was in breach of trust and that the judgment against him was, by reason of his own breach of trust, or whether the judgment should recite that the corporation was in breach of its trust, and that the defendant was statutorily liable for the corporate breach of trust by operation of the Act. [6] The corporate defendant had been a subcontractor on a project in Ottawa. The plaintiff had been a sub-subcontractor who had provided materials to the job site. Moneys had been paid to the subcontractor by reason of the materials provided to the job site by the sub-subcontractor. The subcontractor had juggled those funds, co-mingled them with other funds from other projects and disbursed all of the moneys without satisfying the debt to the sub-subcontractor. The amounts of money inappropriately disbursed by the subcontractor far exceeded the amount of the claims of the sub-subcontractor and some of the money was taken by the individual personally. [7] Section 8(1)(b) of the Act provides in part: 8(1) All amounts, . . . . . (b) received by a contractor or subcontractor, on account of the contract or subcontract price of an improvement constitute a trust fund for the benefit of the subcontractors and other persons who have supplied services or materials to the improvement who are owed amounts by the contractor or subcontractor.

input: [8] The parties agree that this trust provision applies with respect of the corporate defendant. [9] Section 13(1) of the Act provides: (1) In addition to the persons who are otherwise liable in an action for breach of trust under this Part, (a) every director or officer of a corporation; and (b) any person, including an employee or agent of a corporation, who has effective control of the corporation or its relevant activities, who assents to, or acquiesces in, conduct that he or she knows or reasonably ought to know amounts to breach of trust by the corporation is liable for the breach of trust. Section 13(3) provides: 13(3) Where more than one person is found liable or has admitted liability for a particular breach of trust under this Part, those persons are jointly and severally liable. [page293] [10] The defendant argues that, on a clear reading of the words of those sections, the trust that is created under s. 8 is imposed upon the corporation, and that when one reads s. 13(1) closely, it constitutes a scheme whereby liability can be imposed upon other persons as a consequence of the breaches of trust on the part of the s. 8(1)(b) trustee. [11] The defendant argues that the wording "In addition to the persons who are otherwise liable in an action for breach of trust under this Part", certain other persons as defined in subsections (a) and (b) who assent to, or acquiesce in, conduct that he or she knows or reasonably ought to know amounts to breach of trust by the corporation are "liable for the breach of trust" are specific words which are limited in their meaning. Counsel argues that the additional persons contemplated by s. 13 become statutorily liable for the corporation's breach of trust because they have assented to, or acquiesced in, conduct which they know or reasonably ought to know "amounts to breach of trust by the corporation" and they, therefore, become liable "for the breach of trust". That is to say, the breach of trust by the corporation (italics mine).

The trust created by the <legislation><title>Act</title></legislation> was imposed upon the corporate subcontractor and that <legislation><fragment>s. 13</fragment></legislation> was designed to pierce the corporate veil and thrust liability for the corporate breaches of trust upon the directors, officers or persons in charge who had assented to, or acquiesced in the corporate conduct which they knew, or ought to have known, amounted to breach of trust by the corporation. input: In my opinion, the language and intent of the legislation support the conclusion that a person found liable under s. 13(1) of the Act has in fact been found liable for breach of trust. Section 13 begins with the words, "in addition to the persons who are otherwise liable in an action for breach of trust under this Part" and then goes on to set out the circumstances in which others will be "liable for the breach of trust". It seems to me that the plain meaning of those words is that individuals who fall within s. 13 will be liable for breach of trust in addition to those whose liability is founded under other sections of the Act, with both categories of wrongdoers being in breach of trust. This interpretation is reinforced by s. 13(3) which provides that where more than one person is found liable "for a particular breach of trust under this Part" those persons are jointly and severally liable. It is clear that s. 13(3) applies to individuals whose responsibility is founded under s. 13(1) as well as those, including the corporate contractor trustee, whose responsibility is based on other provisions within Part II of the Act. It follows naturally from this section that if Construc is liable for breach of trust, then Mr. Paniccia is also jointly and severally liable with Construc for the breach of trust. He must, therefore, be liable himself for breach of trust. The intention of the legislation was to set up a trust with respect to moneys received from owners in favour of unpaid trades. It would be inconsistent with that intention if individuals who by their conduct defeat the trust were not liable for breach of trust in the same manner as the corporate vehicles they control.

input: [16] Counsel for the defendant before me takes the position that in deciding St. Mary's the judge erred and that she ought not to have made the jump from s. 13(1) finding individual persons to be liable into a finding that they are, in fact, trustees. [page296] [17] Justice Flinn, in the Harrison decision, sets out the basis upon which he reached his conclusions. Reviewing the facts and information before him [at p. 288 C.P.C.] he set out: Surely, one has to take a hard look at a case in which the plaintiff's claim is now being presented by the third firm of solicitors for the plaintiff, that the cause of action arose over 7 years ago, that the present solicitors have had control of the file since January, 1993, and that the basis of the claim of breach of trust arises out of the allegation that Devran failed to pay Harrison all amounts due pursuant to the work completed by Devran on the project, in the statement of claim described as extras and damages for delay. There is nothing new about those claims. They are itemized and set forth in invoices referred to in the statement of claim and there is no allegation in the material that any further information was obtained on the examination for discovery of representatives of the defendant. Further, counsel for the defendants saw fit to cross-examine the deponent on his affidavit in these matters and notwithstanding the discovery of the defendants, there is nothing in that affidavit which put any meat on the bones of a bald declaration that because Devran didn't pay, the deponent believes that Devran appropriated or converted to its own use part of the moneys.

input: [20] The St. Mary's Cement decision relied on s. 13(3) in support of a finding that s. 13 imposed trust obligations on the persons set out in subsections (a) and (b). Subsection 13(3) provides: 13(3) Where more than one person is found liable or has admitted to liability for a particular breach of trust under this Part, those persons are jointly and severally liable. [21] The above was interpreted as meaning that if directors were to be jointly and severally liable with their trustee company for the corporate breach of trust, then the director must be liable themselves as trustees for breach of the trust. The learned judge then went on to consider that it was the intention of the legislation to set up the trust provided for in s. 8 and that it would be inconsistent with that intention if individuals who, by their conduct defeated the trust, were not liable for breach of the trust in the same manner as the corporate vehicles they controlled. [22] By logical extension, the position taken by the defendant in the matter would be that the wording of subsection (3) simply does not lead to the conclusion that if somebody is to be found jointly and severally liable with the trustee in a breach, then they themselves must be deemed to be a trustee. Similarly, it would be a logical extension of the defendant's position that the further comment by the learned justice on the intention of the legislature would not logically follow. It was the finding of that judge that it would be inconsistent with the intention of the trust provisions of s. 8 if "individuals who by their conduct defeat the trust" were not liable for breach of trust in the same manner as the corporate vehicles they control. It is the logical extension of the defendant's position that this would not be correct and that there is no provision contained in s. 13 that could lead one to that conclusion.

input: [23] A reading of s. 13 makes it quite clear that directors, officers and any person who assents to or acquiesces in the conduct which they knew, or reasonably ought to know, would defeat the trust are, in fact, statutorily held liable for the breach of trust. Looking at the Act, it is difficult to contemplate how such persons could act through the company to defeat the trust and escape personal liability whether or not they themselves are deemed to be trustees. [24] The wording of s. 13 as it stands alone creates a clear and obvious statutory liability for identified persons who conduct their affairs in a described manner. If the individuals are not within the group of described persons, or if their conduct does not meet the standard required for the imposition of liability under s. 13, they escape liability. If, however, the individuals fall within the described group of persons and their conduct falls within the prohibited conduct under s. 13, then they do in fact become liable. [page298] Just who those individuals might be, that is, who are defeating the trust and escaping liability, are not readily identifiable. [25] The plaintiff takes a very different and interesting position. Counsel for the plaintiff argues that the principles of trust law would apply to persons in the position of the individual defendant in the case at bar, and that when one reviews the considerations of the Supreme Court of Canada in Air Canada v. M&L Travel Ltd., [1993] 3 S.C.R. 787, 15 O.R. (3d) 804, Gold v. Rosenberg, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 767, 152 D.L.R. (4th) 385, and Citadel General Assurance Co. v. Lloyd's Bank Canada, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 805, 152 D.L.R. (4th) 411, the persons contemplated in the group created by subsections (a) and (b) would, by reason of their relationship to the corporation and the trust created under s. 8 of the Act, place themselves in the position of being capable of being found liable as constructive trustees. Those cases establish that a stranger to a trust can be held liable for a breach of trust if they knowingly participated in the breach of trust, either as persons in receipt and chargeable with trust property or as persons who knowingly assisted in a dishonest and fraudulent design on the part of the trustee. In the face of either circumstance, a constructive trust would be created and they could be found liable as either persons described as constructive trustees arising from "knowing receipt" or "knowing assistance". Mr. Justice Iacobucci in Air Canada considered at pp. 809-11 S.C.R. the concept of the creation of a constructive trust. He further considered the degree of knowledge that would have to be imputed to such a constructive trustee in order to find liability on either the concept of "knowing receipt" or "knowing assistance".
