[33] It is necessary now to consider
how this approach to interpretation affects the result in this case. [34] The trial judge’s approach to
interpretation in this case is summarized in the following paragraph from his
judgment: [21] I
therefore propose to interpret section 9 and the Mining and Mineral Rights Tax
Act as a whole, according to the contemporary or modern approach which is also
in my opinion the approach mandated by the Interpretation Act. To do so it is
proper for me to consider materials touching on the objectives of the Act and
the objectives of the Legislature in enacting its provisions. To put it
another way, was there a "mischief" which the Legislature was
attempting to rectify. For these purposes I am entitled to have recourse to
the report of a Royal Commission on mineral revenues and to a lesser and very
limited extent, to a statement as to the objects of the legislation as
expressed by the Minister of Mines and Energy in 1975 during debate in the
House of Assembly. [35] He rejected a "plain
meaning" approach to interpretation in the following words: [39] Can it
then be said that in 1995 Archean transferred to Diamond Fields and its
successors, "the right to engage in mining operations" in the context
of the Act. At first blush and on a narrow construction of the wording, one
might conclude that because an exploration license is one entity and a mining
lease is another, that the transfer was not the transfer of the right to engage
in mining operations. However, after review and reflection, I have concluded
otherwise.

[36] The trial judge quoted extensively
from the Report of the Royal Commission on Mineral Revenue (1974)
although he acknowledged that all of the recommendations of that Commission
were not necessarily embodied in the ensuing legislation. [37] He concluded: [40] The
historical background of mining concessions in this province as provided by the
.... Royal Commission and a reading of the legislation which followed, makes it
clear that the legislative provisions for exploratory licences, mining leases
and the tax on royalties, were designed to avoid the undesirable practices of
the past whereby concession holders received substantial royalty payments from
mine operators, without tax liability. These payments were described as
unearned royalties, and it was such royalties at which the legislation was
aimed. [41] Archean
was essentially a prospector. It sold its exploration licences to Diamond
Fields for cash, shares and the right to receive a royalty of 3.0% on net
smelter returns. It now proposes to sell its contractual right to receive the
3.0% royalty, which is the only right which it now has, to a prospective
purchaser. Without the tax liability under section 9, it appears to me that
Archean or its purchaser/successor would be in the same position as were the
receivers of unearned royalties prior to 1975. . . . . . . [43] Clearly the objects of the legislation are that unearned royalties derived from
mining operations within the province, shall be subject to a specific tax
regime in addition to taxes of general application."

[38] The trial judge did not accede to
the argument made on behalf of Archean that the focus of the comments in the
Royal Commission Report on "unearned royalties" and on the scope of
s. 9 was limited to taxation of existing concession holders who had bartered their
rights in the past to other operators in return for royalties which had escaped
taxation. He apparently took the view, a view with which I agree, that focus
on the ills of the past with respect to the non-taxation of specific concession
holders was merely the motivation or justification for recommending a new
taxation regime that would not allow for the repeat of situations where people
could trade on the non-renewable mineral resources of the province without
paying a fair return to the province for that privilege. [39] The trial judge concluded that the
language employed in s. 9 broadly construed in accordance with s. 16 of the Interpretation
Act, could, and should, encompass a situation where the rights of a licence
holder, as opposed to holder of an actual mining lease, are granted or
transferred in return for a royalty payment. This conclusion was primarily
influenced by the fact that under the legislative scheme the only way, short of
an express grant by the legislature, in which a right to engage in mining
operations could be obtained, was through the prior acquisition of an
exploration licence and the fulfillment of the conditions associated with that
licence. He recognized the reality that an exploration licence which has
resulted in the discovery of commercial ore has significant value precisely
because the holder of it controls the mechanism by which a mining lease can be
obtained. While it is true that the "right" of the holder of a
licence to the issuing of a mining lease pursuant to s. 31 of the Mineral
Act, can only be exercised if he or she fulfills certain ancillary
conditions, the fulfillment of those conditions (such as completion of
previous assessment work and the provision of surveys and markings) is within
the control of the holder of the licence.

on the ills of the past with respect to the non-taxation of specific concession
holders was merely the motivation or justification for recommending a new
taxation regime that would not allow for the repeat of situations where people
could trade on the non-renewable mineral resources of the province without
paying a fair return to the province for that privilege. [39] The trial judge concluded that the
language employed in <legislation><fragment>s. 9</fragment></legislation> broadly construed in accordance with <legislation><fragment>s. 16</fragment> of the <title>Interpretation
Act</title></legislation>, could, and should, encompass a situation where the rights of a licence
holder, as opposed to holder of an actual mining lease, are granted or
transferred in return for a royalty payment. This conclusion was primarily
influenced by the fact that under the legislative scheme the only way, short of
an express grant by the legislature, in which a right to engage in mining
operations could be obtained, was through the prior acquisition of an
exploration licence and the fulfillment of the conditions associated with that
licence. He recognized the reality that an exploration licence which has
resulted in the discovery of commercial ore has significant value precisely
because the holder of it controls the mechanism by which a mining lease can be
obtained. While it is true that the "right" of the holder of a
licence to the issuing of a mining lease pursuant to <legislation><fragment>s. 31</fragment> of the <title>Mineral
Act</title></legislation>, can only be exercised if he or she fulfills certain ancillary
conditions, the fulfillment of those conditions (such as completion of
previous assessment work and the provision of surveys and markings) is within
the control of the holder of the licence.

[40] The licence holder therefore has
it within his or her power to exercise the right to obtain a lease, which
cannot be arbitrarily refused in the discretion of the Minister, and, in the
words of s. 31(5)(a) of the Mineral Act, acquire "the exclusive
right to develop, extract, remove, deal with, sell, mortgage, or otherwise
dispose of all the unalienated minerals, or those specified in the lease, in,
on or under the land described in the lease". While the licence itself
confers no right to remove minerals except for very limited purposes (s. 23(2)
of the Mineral Act) the licence in effect is the key that enables the
benefits of a mining lease to be unlocked. [41] Counsel for Archean nevertheless
argues that the words "grant of the right to engage in mining
operations" in s. 9(j)(a) of the Mining and Mineral Rights Tax Act
admit of only one reasonable interpretation, namely, that they are clearly
referable to a present grant of an existing right that would have
the benefit of conferring upon the recipient a present entitlement to
carry on mineral extraction activities". I do not agree. The question in
reality is whether a licencee’s "right to the issuing of a mining
lease" within s. 31(2) of the Mineral Act is the equivalent of "the
right to engage in mining operations" in s. 9(1)(a) of the Mining and
Mineral Rights Tax Act. As noted, the ability of a licencee to obtain a
mining lease (and the right to "develop, extract, remove, deal with,
mortgage, or otherwise dispose of" the minerals in s. 31(5)(a) of the Mineral
Act) is dependent solely on matters within the control of the licencee; it
does not depend on the discretionary decision of the government. Provided the
licencee has complied with the terms of the licence and submits a proper
application with appropriate survey, there is a "right" to a lease
and, by extension, a right to engage in mining operations.

[42] Because the licencee has the legal
means to compel the issuance of a lease, which carries with it the right to
extract minerals, it can be said, without torturing or stretching the language,
that he has a right to engage in mining operations, albeit at some time in the
future. While it is true that the right cannot be exercised at that moment,
that is, at any time during the currency of the licence and before a lease is
issued, it is nevertheless a present right in a similar way to rights in
property and trust law that may be vested in interest but only enjoyable at a
later time. [43] In a sense, the "right to
engage in mining operations" in s. 9(1)(a) of the Mining and Mineral
Rights Tax Act can be said to be broader in its formulation than the
"right to develop, extract, remove ... minerals" in s. 31(5)(a) of
the Mineral Act. I agree with counsel for the respondents that the
notion of "engaging" in mining operations is a larger concept than
that of extracting minerals. The "right to engage" connotes possible
commencement or arrangement of affairs in the future rather than the actual
development or extraction. The phrase "right to extract minerals" is
specifically used in other parts of the legislation. See, for example, the
definition of "operator" in s. 2(j) of the Mining and Mineral
Rights Tax Act, which defines an operator as a person who "(i) has the
right to extract minerals, and (ii) carries out mining operations ..." The use of the different phrase "right to engage in mining
operations" in s. 9(1)(a) is some indication that a different and broader
concept was contemplated, instead of a reference strictly to an existing mining
lease and the present right to extract minerals, as was submitted by counsel
for Archean.

[44] Finally, as far as the textual
analysis in the context of the legislation itself goes, it is not without
significance that s. 8 of the Mining and Mineral Rights Tax Act appears
to allow an operator to deduct from its net income derived from mining
operations, for the purpose of paying a tax on the right to mine, the amount of
royalties paid to a person "for the grant of the right to engage in mining
operations". Thus it appears that if a mining company employs a separate
prospecting company to stake claims and then takes a transfer of the licence
under which the claims were staked in return for a royalty payment to the
prospector, it can deduct the royalty so paid as an expense, for the purposes
of calculating the tax it would otherwise pay on the right to mine. The amount
of tax that would otherwise be payable by the mining company would therefore be
reduced. It would be odd if the province were to be thereby deprived of such
tax revenue in the hands of the mining company and still not be able to recoup
it in the hands of the person to whom the royalties were paid. Otherwise the
overall return to the province would not be maximized. [45] In light of the recommendation of
the Royal Commission which led to the new legislation that "all persons
who derive income from mining [should] become subject to tax" and in light
of my conclusion that one of the objects of the legislation is to take account
of the societal imperative of a fair return to the owner of the resource (the
province) in s. 9's provision for incremental shares of royalties payable by
ultimate concession holders on the exploitation of the resource, it would be
inconsistent with such broad objectives to interpret the words in s. 9(1)(a) in
the narrow manner advocated by Archean. I agree with counsel for the
respondents that the effect of Archean’s argument would lead to an unreasonable
and impractical result, namely that a person transferring a licence the day
before it matured into a lease would not pay tax, while the same person
transferring the licence a day after it had matured, by fulfillment of the
conditions for the issuance of a lease, would pay tax. This would easily lead
to a formalistic manipulation of the documentation and its timing to avoid tax
that might otherwise be payable. It would frustrate the overall intent of the
legislation.

[46] I conclude, therefore, that the
reasoning of the trial judge that the right to engage in mining operations
encompasses the right pursuant to a licence to obtain a mining lease is not
inconsistent with the text of the legislation when read in its proper context. It is also consistent with the broad objective sought to be achieved by the legislation
as a remedy for the ills identified by the Royal Commission report that
precipitated it. The interpretation given by the trial judge can therefore be
justified in terms of its plausibility (its compliance with the legislative
text) and its efficacity (its promotion of the broad legislative purpose). In
my view, it is an interpretation that is also acceptable in the sense that the
outcome is reasonable and just. It ensures that people who trade on the
non-renewable mineral resources of the province pay a fair return to the
province. Whilst in some cases it would be unfair to give to a taxation
statute an interpretation at variance from that which might reasonably be
relied upon by the taxpayer in ordering his or her affairs, this is not one of
those cases. It is highly unlikely that Archean would not have engaged in its
search for minerals in this case if it knew in advance that the tax imposed
under s. 9 might potentially apply to it. Nor has it been suggested that
Archean would only have contemplated the sale of its right to the royalties to
a third person if they were not subject to any tax.

social and legal values of protection of vested property rights affect the

legislation is that it attempts to obtain for the province a fair return for

trial judge, and his decision resulting therefrom, can be justified in terms of

W.W. Marshall, J.A. O’Neill, J.A.: [52] This is an appeal from a decision
of the Trial Division ordering that a declaration be issued as requested by the
respondents, the defendants at trial, that the “Net Smelter Royalty” payable to
the appellant, the plaintiff at trial, is taxable under s. 9(1)(a) of the Mining
and Mineral Rights Tax Act, R.S.N. 1990, c. M.-16 (the Act). [53] The facts are not in dispute. [54] The Appellant, Archean Resources
Ltd. (“Archean”) is and was a Newfoundland prospecting company, engaged in the
business of mineral exploration. Archean’s principals, Albert Chislett and
Chris Verbiski, are the co-discoverers of the Voisey’s Bay nickel-copper-cobalt
ore bodies (the “Voisey’s Bay Property”). [55] Archean holds a contractual
royalty entitling it to receive 3% of net smelter returns respecting mineral
production from the Voisey’s Bay Property (“the Net Smelter Royalty”). [56] Archean acquired the Net Smelter
Royalty pursuant to a mineral option agreement, (the Labrador Option
Agreement), in consideration of the transfer of certain mineral exploration
licences to Diamond Fields Resources Inc. (“DFRI”). The Net Smelter Royalty
entitlement under the Labrador Option Agreement was itself negotiated and
concluded in 1993. [57] The mineral licences covering the
Voisey’s Bay Property were acquired by DFRI upon exercise of the option
conferred by the Labrador Option Agreement.

In order to reflect accurately recent taxation case law, it is
necessary to distinguish between literal and strict interpretation. As a rule,
taxation statutes are no longer subject to a strictly literal construction. They are interpreted in the same way as other types of legislation (according
to the contextual, purposive or historical approach, etc.) But if after a
thorough effort there are still reasonable doubts as to the enactment’s
meaning, the statute will generally be applied to limit its effect and favour
the tax payer. [68] In Driedger, at p. 131, the
modern rule of statutory interpretation is set out: There is only one rule in modern interpretation, namely, courts
are obliged to determine the meaning of legislation in its total context,
having regard to the purpose of the legislation, the consequences of proposed
interpretations, the presumptions and special rules of interpretation, as well
as admissible external aids. In other words, the courts must consider and take
into account all relevant and admissible indicators of legislative meaning. After taking these into account, the court must then adopt an interpretation
that is appropriate. An appropriate interpretation is one that can be
justified in terms of (a) its plausibility, that is, its compliance with the
legislative text; (b) its efficacy, that is, its promotion of the legislative
purpose; and (c) its acceptability, that is, the outcome is reasonable and
just.

[69] The trial judge concluded from his
perusal of the authorities that the traditional strict and literal
interpretation of taxing statutes has “yielded to the doctrine that taxing
statutes are to be treated in the same manner as other legislation, with the
proviso that in cases of reasonable doubt, the enactment is construed in favour
of the subject”. [70] The appellant acknowledges in its
argument that the literal approach to the interpretation of statutes no longer
applies and that the “proper interpretative approach to taxing statutes” is
that stated in Stubart Investments Ltd. v. The Queen (1984), 10 D.L.R. 1
(S.C.C.), but that the approach mandated there is “nevertheless subject to the
‘plain meaning’ rule that when statutory language is clear, it should be given
its plain and ordinary meaning, and resort to interpretative devices or
extrinsic aids is inappropriate”. [71] In Stubart, Estey J. for
the majority of the Supreme Court of Canada said at p. 32: While not directing his observations exclusively to tax
statutes, the learned author of Construction of Statutes, 2nd
Ed. (1983), at p. 87, E.A. Dreidger, put the modern rule succinctly: Today there is only one principle or
approach, namely, the words of an act are to be read in their entire context
and in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the scheme of the
Act, the object of the Act, and the intention of Parliament.

... where a legislative provision is clear and plain, the
meaning governs and the courts may not, under the guise of interpretation,
second guess the wisdom of the legislature by adopting implausible constructions
not in harmony with its intent and object or attempt to fill gaps in the
legislative scheme. Later, Marshall J.A., on p. 231, adopted the words of Denning
L.J. in Asher v. Seaford Court Estates, [1949] 2 K.B. 481 (C.A.) on the
obligation placed upon a trial judge in interpreting a statute where there is
an ambiguity: He must set to work on the constructive task of finding the
intention of Parliament, and he must do so not only from the language of the
statute, but also from a consideration of the social conditions which gave rise
to it, and of the mischief which it was passed to remedy, and then he must
supplement the written word so as to give “force and life” to the intention of
the legislature. [74] The appellant’s position was that
the language of s. 9(1)(a) is “clear and unambiguous” and does “not admit of
the remedial and liberal construction imposed by” the trial judge. Further, it
argued that the statutory provisions applicable to the required analysis were
themselves, “plain and unambiguous”. [75] By way of summary, Archean’s
submission was that “in cases of clear and unambiguous statutory language, the
scheme, object and intention of Parliament as adverted to in Stubart are
apparent and yield the proper meaning based on the plain and ordinary meaning
of the statutory language”.

It is sometimes said that the courts should not look to
extrinsic materials, even though the materials otherwise would be admissible,
unless the legislation to be interpreted is ambiguous or unclear. It is
arguable that this constraint is pointless and misleading and should be
abandoned. The constraint is pointless because, given the plasticity of
language and the complexity of law, virtually all legislation is ambiguous in
that it is susceptible of more than one reading. There is little point in a
test that virtually all legislation meets. The constraint also is misleading
in that it perpetuates the empty rhetoric of the plain meaning rule. Under
current judicial practice, to say that a provision is not ambiguous, that its
meaning is clear or “plain”, is a conclusion reached at the end of
interpretation, not a threshold test. It is a judgment that can appropriately
be made only in light of all the available evidence of legislative meaning. [79] The whole thrust of this argument
is that the plain meaning of a word, words or expressions, however “plain” they
may appear to be, can only be ascertained when looked at and examined in the
light of the context in which they are used which must include the whole
purpose and object of the statute in which they appear. This argument finds
further support in R. v. Adams, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 707. There, Sopinka
J., for the Supreme Court of Canada, said at p. 719:

In approaching the interpretation of any statutory provision,
it is prudent to keep in mind the simple but fundamental instruction offered by
the court in Reigate Rural District Council v. Sutton District Water Co.

the object with which the statute was passed, because it enables one to

continued to be followed by this Court to the present time. [80] The respondents’ position is that

... Elmer Driedger in Construction of Statutes, (2nd
ed., 1983) best encapsulates the approach upon which I prefer to rely. He
recognizes that statutory interpretation cannot be founded on the wording of
the legislation alone. At p. 87 he states: ... Today there is only one
principle or approach, namely, the words of an Act are to be read in their
entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with
the scheme of the Act, the object of the Act, and the intention of Parliament. [81] In R. v. Gladue, [1999] 1
S.C.R. 688, the Court was considering an amendment to the Criminal Code
codifying, for the first time, the fundamental purpose and principles of
sentencing and specifically dealing with s. 718.2(e), the effect of which the
Court found was to alter the method of analysis to be used in determining a fit
sentence for an aboriginal offender. The decision of the Court was delivered
by Cory and Iacobucci JJ. The following is to be found at p. 704: As this Court has frequently stated, the proper construction of
a statutory provision flows from reading the words of the provision in their
grammatical and ordinary sense and in their entire context, harmoniously with
the scheme of the statute as a whole, the purpose of the statute, and the
intention of Parliament. The purpose of the statute and the intention of
Parliament, in particular, are to be determined on the basis of intrinsic and
admissible extrinsic sources regarding the Act’s legislative history and the
context of its enactment: Rizzo & Rizzo Shoes Ltd. (Re),
[1998] 1 S.C.R. 27, at paras. 20-23; R. v. Chartrand, [1994] 2
S.C.R. 864 at p. 875; E.A. Driedger, Construction of Statutes (2nd
Ed. 1983) at p. 87; Driedger on the Construction of Statutes (3rd
Ed. 1994) by R. Sullivan, at p. 131.

In its decision the Court considered the wording of s. 718(2)
and the general scheme of the part of the Criminal Code in which it
appears, its legislative history, the social context surrounding its enactment,
including the “overrepresentation” of aboriginal Canadians in penal
institutions. [82] In my view, the law is clear that,
faced with the task of interpreting words or expressions in a statute, the
court or judge must, before coming to a conclusion as to what these specific
words or expressions means, consider them in “their entire context, harmoniously
with the scheme of the statute ... its purpose and the intention of the
legislature”. Further, the statute must be considered in the light of s. 16 of
the Interpretation Act (assuming the court is dealing with a
Newfoundland statute), which requires that the Act and every provision thereof
be considered remedial and shall receive the liberal construction and
interpretation that best assures the attainment of the objects of the Act and
provisions, according to its true meaning. [83] The trial judge, having set out
the facts and referred to the various rules of interpretation already
canvassed, continued: I therefore propose to interpret section 9 and the Mining and
Mineral Rights Tax Act as a whole, according to the contemporary or modern
approach which is also in my opinion the approach mandated by the
Interpretation Act. To do so it is proper for me to consider materials
touching on the objectives of the Act and the objectives of the Legislature in
enacting its provisions. To put it another way, was there a “mischief” which
the Legislature was attempting to rectify. For these purposes I am entitled to
have recourse to the report of a Royal Commission on mineral revenues and to a
lesser and very limited extent, to a statement as to the objects of the
legislation as expressed by the Minister of Mines and Energy in 1975 during

the argument of the appellant that the plain meaning rule should be applied in
the interpretation of the Act. [85] The trial judge reviewed the
pre-1975 mineral concession regime in the Province and set out some of the
observations of the report of the “Royal Commission on Mineral Revenue” which
was presented in December 1974. He concluded: It is clear from the Commission’s observations and
recommendations, that one of the major ills of the pre-1975 concession system
was that the concession holders who had the right to explore and mine, but did
not usually do so, were in receipt of significant sums of “unearned” income
which was not subject to mining taxes. Though all of the recommendations of

According to the general rule which provides that the burden of
proof lies with the plaintiff, in any proceeding it is for the party claiming
the benefit of a legislative provision to show that he is entitled to rely on
it. The burden of proof thus rests with the tax department in the case of a
provision imposing a tax obligation and with the taxpayer in the case of a
provision creating a tax exemption. While I agree with the principle, I cannot see its application
here in light of the very clear findings made by the trial judge. Obviously,
if at the end of his very thorough examination of the circumstances and the
law, the trial judge was not able to decide whether Archean was liable for the
tax, then since the burden of proof would be on the government, the tax on the
royalty would not be applicable. Clearly, that is not the case here. [88] The trial judge, having referred
to the “historical background of mining concessions” in the province as
provided by the 1973 Royal Commission, and a reading of the legislation which
followed, concluded that the legislative provisions for exploratory licences,
mining licences and the tax on royalties were designed to avoid the undesirable
practices of the past whereby concession holders received substantial royalty
payments (described as “unearned royalties”) from operators, without tax
liability, and that it was these royalties at which the legislation was aimed.

[89] In his analysis, the trial judge
stated, in my view correctly, that the interpretation of s. 9 of the Act was
the real issue. He said: Can it then be said that in 1995 Archean transferred to Diamond
Fields and its successors, “the right to engage in mining operations”, in the
context of the Act. At first blush and on a narrow construction of the
wording, one might conclude that because an exploration licence is one entity
and a mining lease is another, that the transfer was not the transfer of the
right to engage in mining operations. However, after review and reflection, I
have concluded otherwise. [90] Earlier in his judgment, the trial
judge had referred to the several provisions of the Mineral Act, R.S.N.
1990, c-M 12, and set out several of the relevant sections of that Act. He
noted that the Mineral Act provided for a system whereby persons, on
complying with stipulated procedures, could be granted exploration licences
authorizing the recipient to engage in mineral exploration on specified areas. He noted that Archean obtained a significant number of exploration licences in
areas of Labrador and had begun exploration. He added: It has been explained to me that
exploration companies such as Archean rarely have the expertise and capital to
develop promising fields and therefore they seek out or may be approached by,
junior mining companies who may wish to purchase their interests. Such
companies in turn seek to involve what are referred to as senior mining
companies, which have the technical and financial resources to develop mines.

most significant nickel/copper/cobalt deposits in the world. [91] Exploration licences are issued

the area of land described in the licence from the date of issuing for the
period of (a) in

the case of a licence covering reserved lands, 4 years. (2) A licence confers no right to remove minerals except
for the purpose of sampling, assaying and testing, and a licensee who removes
or sells minerals in contravention of this section (a) commits
a material breach of the terms of the licence; and (b) is
guilty of an offence under this Act. [92] It is not necessary to set out the
various steps in the Mineral Act whereby mineral exploration licence may
be obtained. Suffice it to say that, subject to the terms under which a
licence is issued, the licencee has the exclusive right to explore for minerals
in the area described in the licence but, as set out in s. 23(2), has no right
to remove minerals except for “sampling, assaying and testing”.

[93] Section 24 of the Mineral Act
permits the transfer of an exploration licence and is as follows: 24. Nothing in this Act shall prevent the holder of a licence
from transferring, assigning, mortgaging, pledging or conveying that licence to
another person if section 6 is complied with, but a transfer, assignment,
mortgage, pledge or conveyance of the minerals in, on or under part of the area
covered by the licence is not valid unless the written approval of the minister
is obtained and is filed with the document presented for registration under
section 6. Section 6 deals with the registration of, inter alia,
transfers, assignments, mortgages and agreements relating to minerals and
rights with respect thereto. It is not relevant for our purposes. [94] On what basis can it be said that
Archean’s transfer of its mineral exploration licences to DFRI, as permitted by
s. 24 of the Mineral Act, was a “grant ... of the right to engage in
mining operations”, as contemplated by s. 9 of the Act, so as to attract tax on
the royalty payable thereunder, which here would be when mining operations
commence? Obviously, at the time the transfer was made to DFRI, nobody,
including Archean, had the right to engage in mining operations on the lands
covered by the exploration licences and it follows that, there being no right to
engage in mining operations, there could be no grant of mining operations.

[95] Earlier in his decision, in
considering the arguments of counsel, the trial judge had stated that although
an exploration licence does not, in itself, entitle the holder of it to a
mining lease, on compliance with s. 31 of the Mineral Act, which would
include the licence holder having complied with all the terms of the licence
during its currency, a mining lease would be granted. [96] There is no suggestion that any of
the requirements in s. 31 are not reasonably capable of completion by the
holder of a licence. Further, upon compliance with the Mineral Act, the
holder of the licence has under s. 31, “a right to the issuing of a mining
lease ...”. [97] Clearly, the option agreement
anticipated that on completion of the transfer of the exploration licences,
mining operations would be carried on since part of the payment for the
transfer, the royalty, could only come into existence on the carrying out of mining
operations producing “net smelter returns”. In effect then, what was being
transferred from Archean for good and valuable consideration was the right,
albeit after compliance with certain statutory provisions under the Mineral
Act, to obtain a mining lease and “the right to engage in mining
operations”. [98] With respect to the question posed
by the appellant as to whether Archean was within the “mischief” to which the
Act was directed and in particular, whether Archean can be properly classified
as an earner of unearned income, it can fairly be said that that question has
already been answered in the remedial and liberal interpretation given to s.
9. True, as argued by the appellant, s. 9(1) was enacted “in response to the
recommendations of the Royal Commission” to which reference has already been
made. Archean argues, with some justification, that it is in a completely
different position from that of the several companies and groups referred to
earlier which had acquired mining rights from the Province and had granted or
subleased them to mine operators in exchange for royalties and other
consideration, which in effect, were “unearned”. In that regard, Archean did
not acquire a right to mine, it acquired prospecting or exploration rights and
actually discovered a valuable mineral property. It could have, had it wished,
applied for and obtained a mining lease. It chose to transfer its exploration
licences to another group which would then enable that other group to apply for
and obtain a mining lease. It was this choice which set up the right in
Archean to receive, when mining operations would begin, a royalty.

[99] Whether Archean would be a
recipient of “unearned royalties” is not important for our purposes. The Act
is cast broadly and imposes a tax on any person who receives “money by way of
rental, royalty or similar payment” in consideration of a grant to another of
“the right to engage in mining operations ...”. The Act does not in any way
limit the tax to those who had, in the past obtained mining concessions even
though they had been identified by the commission as the principal reason why
the Crown was not receiving appropriate revenues from mining operations in the
Province. [100] Although there were several
references as set out earlier to concession holders as landlords, that word, in
my view, was used in an illustrative sense and should not be taken as an
indication that some property rights must be maintained before the tax becomes
applicable under s. 9(1)(a) of the Act. The tax is payable on the royalty
received even where that royalty is payable strictly on a contractual basis, as
here. [101] The third issue raised by the
appellant in its factum can also be disposed of readily. I have already
concluded, as did the trial judge, that the transfer of the exploration licence
was a transfer of the right to engage in mining operations so as to bring
Archean within the purview of s. 9 of the Act. Reference has already been made
to the “first blush”, “narrow construction”, and “might conclude”, statement
by the trial judge. Certainly, on a proper interpretation of the Act, it
cannot be said that there was any reasonable uncertainty resulting from lack of
explicitness in the statute so that this Court could conclude that Archean was
not liable for the tax.

HONOURABLE MADAM JUSTICE PAPERNY ____________________________________________________ I. INTRODUCTION[1] Alberta, like many other provinces in Canada (British Columbia,
Manitoba, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia), has introduced an
administrative licence suspension program for motor vehicle operators involved
in drinking and driving. Essentially, the program provides for a 90 day licence
suspension by a peace officer who has reasonable and probable grounds to
believe that the person drove a motor vehicle while his ability to do so was
impaired by alcohol. The appellants ask this Court to declare the program
unconstitutional. II. FACTS [2] On April 6, 2001, Thomson was stopped at a Check Stop by the Calgary
police and charged with impaired driving and operating a motor vehicle with
more than 80 milligrams of alcohol in 100 millilitres of blood. He was served
with a notice of suspension which effected a 90 day driver’s licence suspension
starting 21 days after the issuance of the Notice. He filed an originating
notice seeking a declaration that the Administrative Licence Suspension (“ALS”)
program was invalid, illegal and of no force or effect and sought judicial
review of the legal validity of the ALS program. His suspension was stayed
pending final determination of the judicial review.

[3] On May 10 and 11, and August 16, 2001, Slatter J. heard 270 applications
challenging the constitutional validity of the ALS program found in the Traffic
Safety Act, S.A. 1999, c. T‑6.4 (“Act”). Three of the
applications were treated as representative cases and in a written judgment, Gonzalez
et al. v. Alberta (Driver Control Board), [2001] 11 W.W.R. 628, the
chambers judge found the program constitutional. Most of the 270 applicants
appealed to this Court. Ten of those appeals, involving approximately 190
individuals, were consolidated under one style of cause. Pending this appeal,
trial courts have stayed approximately 1,000 licence suspensions issued under
the legislation. None of the named applicants in Gonzalez have appealed,
but as these are effectively representative cases, the appellants here rely on
certain facts giving rise to allegations that ss. 8 and 10(b) of the Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms were breached. One individual brought an
application to the Court of Queen’s Bench as a court of competent jurisdiction
under s. 24(1) of the Charter and bypassed an appeal of his suspension
to the Board. [4] The appellants also ask this Court to reconsider two previous decisions
which held that driving was not a liberty interest protected by s. 7 of the Charter.

III. THE LEGISLATION [5] The Traffic Safety Act is a comprehensive legislative scheme
covering virtually all aspects of the regulation of highways and motor vehicles
in Alberta. The Act was fully proclaimed in force on May 20, 2003,
after the hearing of this appeal. The Act replaces and consolidates the
Highway Traffic Act, the Motor Vehicle Administration Act, the Motor
Transport Act and other related legislation, and merges the Alberta Motor
Transport Board and the Driver Control Board, continuing them as the Alberta
Transportation Safety Board. [6] A general description of the Act follows: Part 1 -
General administration - establishes the Registrar of Motor Vehicle Services,
empowers municipalities to pass bylaws and the Lieutenant Governor in Council
to make regulations. Part 2 -
Alberta Transportation Safety Board - establishes the right to appeal to the
Board on matters related to driver conduct including the cancellation or
suspension of various licences and permits. It also provides for further appeal
to the courts. Part 3 - Motor
Vehicle Administration - provides for the licensing and registration of drivers
and vehicles, establishes equipment standards for vehicles, and other
provisions relating to vehicle safety. Part 4 -
Disqualification from Driving- creates two divisions for disqualifications from
either offences or judgments. The administrative licence suspension is in Part
4.

The provisions of the Schedule are for all relevant purposes identical with s.

Driver Control Board but by the Alberta Transportation Safety Board. In this
judgment, we refer to the corresponding identical provisions in the Traffic
Safety Act, and refer to the Board whether that be the Alberta
Transportation Safety Board or the previous Driver Control Board. IV. ADMINISTRATIVE
LICENCE SUSPENSIONS [8] The operation of the program is triggered when a peace officer
reasonably suspects an individual of “alcohol-related driving”. This is defined
as driving with more than 80 milligrams of alcohol in 100 millilitres of blood,
or refusing to provide a breath sample when demanded. Where a peace officer has
reasonable and probable grounds to believe a person drove a motor vehicle while
under the influence of alcohol, or refuses, without reasonable excuse, to
provide a breath sample, the officer is required to take possession of the
driver's licence on behalf of the Registrar of Motor Vehicle Services and issue
a temporary licence valid for 21 days. Thereafter, an automatic three-month
suspension of the licence occurs under s. 88(5), or where bodily harm or death
has resulted, a six-month suspension under s. 88(6). This transitional period
is designed to afford the driver an opportunity to make alternate
transportation arrangements pending his suspension and, if he chooses, to
launch an appeal to the Board.

6. Is Charter relief available under s. 24? VI. STANDARD OF REVIEW [14] This appeal challenges the constitutional validity of provincial
legislation on pure questions of law and as such, the standard of review is
correctness. VII. ANALYSIS Issue 1. Reconsideration of s. 7 Charter decisions [15] The appellants sought leave to re-argue that driving a motor vehicle is
a liberty interest guaranteed under s. 7. This Court declined to grant leave in
reasons issued separately at 2003 ABCA 112. We remain bound by our previous
decisions in R. v. Neale and Yehia v. Alberta (Solicitor General),
which accord with the weight of appellate authority across the country that
driving a motor vehicle is not a liberty interest protected by s. 7. Issue 2. Does the ALS program constitute valid Provincial
Legislation? [16] The appellants submit the ALS program is, in its purpose and effect,
criminal law and therefore, ultra vires the jurisdiction of the
Province. The intervener, the Attorney General of Alberta, and the respondent,
the Board, submit that the program is a valid regulatory licencing program
within provincial jurisdiction over property and civil rights. A.
Characterization - the pith and substance of the law [17] Resolving the first issue requires a division of powers analysis as
outlined by the Supreme Court of Canada in Reference re Firearms Act
(Canada), [2000] 1 S.C.R. 783. The first stage of the analysis is to
determine the “pith and substance” or essential character of the law by
examining the purpose of the subject legislation, and its legal effect. A law’s
purpose is often stated in the legislation, but may also be ascertained by
reference to extrinsic material such as Hansard: Firearms Reference at
para. 17. The purpose of legislation may also be determined by looking at the
problems it is intended to address – the so‑called “mischief” approach: R.
v. Morgentaler, [1993] 3 S.C.R. 463 at 483-4.

[18] Determining the legal effects of a law involves considering how the law
will operate and how it will affect Albertans. Whether the law is efficacious is
not relevant to the analysis: see Firearms Reference at para. 18. In
some cases, the effects of the law suggest a purpose other than that which is
stated. Where the effects of the law diverge substantially from the stated aim,
it is sometimes said to be “colourable”. B.
Classification - the division of federal and provincial powers [19] The second stage is to classify that essential character by reference to
the heads of power under the Constitution Act, 1867 to determine whether
the law is within the jurisdiction of the enacting government. If it is, then
the law is valid. [20] The appellants submit the ALS program is a matter related to criminal
law under s. 91(27) of the Constitution Act, 1867. The respondent and
intervener submit the legislation, as a matter related to property and civil
rights, falls within provincial jurisdiction under s. 92(13) of the Constitution
Act, 1867. [21] Classification of legislation as criminal law, as a general rule,
requires that the legislation possess three prerequisites: a valid criminal law
purpose, backed by a prohibition and a penalty: see Firearms Reference
at para. 27. [22] Classifying the legislation also recognizes, as Dickson, C.J.C. stated
in General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. City National Leasing, [1989]
1 S.C.R. 641 at 669, that “overlap of legislation is to be expected and
accommodated in a federal state”. Laws mainly in the jurisdiction of one level
of government may overflow into, or have “incidental effects” upon, the
jurisdiction of the other level of government. It is a matter of balance and of
federalism: no one level of government is isolated from the other, nor can it
usurp the functions of the other: see Firearms Reference at para. 26.

[23] Thus, the double aspect doctrine permits both levels of government to
legislate in one field for two different purposes: Provincial Secretary of
Prince Edward Island v. Egan, [1941] S.C.R. 396. Where the resulting
provincial and federal legislation truly conflict, federal legislation is
paramount. C.
Application to this appeal a) Characterization [24] The stated purpose of the ALS program is contained in the extrinsic
material filed by the intervener. Motor vehicle injuries and deaths caused by
impaired driving exact a huge societal toll in Alberta. The evidence is overwhelming
and undisputed. The extent of human suffering and loss, both personal and
economic, continues to escalate. The evidence demonstrates that in Alberta,
alcohol-involved motor vehicle accidents causing injury have remained at a
higher level than, for example, in Ontario. Licence suspensions and
specifically ALS programs are important instruments in provincial government
efforts to combat a persistent and pressing public health and safety issue. The
evidence supports the conclusion that the ALS program is designed to provide an
immediate response to the identified problem. This is accomplished by
immediately suspending the licence of impaired drivers. The immediacy of the
suspension enhances specific deterrence by providing an immediate consequence
to socially irresponsible behaviour. The timing of the suspension also acts as
a general deterrent by reinforcing the significant consequences to the public.
While these objectives are also largely present in post-conviction licence
suspension legislation, only the ALS program satisfies one of the most
important elements of deterrence – swiftness. The key feature of the ALS
program remedies what, from a public safety and deterrence perspective, is seen
as a lacuna in post-conviction suspension, that is, the inevitable delay in the
imposition of a licence suspension when, and if, the driver is convicted of a
criminal driving offence. The ALS program provides for the suspension of a
licence regardless of the outcome of subsequent criminal proceedings.

b) Classification [25] That the province has the jurisdiction to issue, suspend or cancel
licences and regulate highway traffic safety by means of the administration of
motor vehicle licences is well recognized. A long line of Supreme Court of
Canada decisions has held that both the provincial and federal governments may
legislate where criminal conduct and public safety overlap. Specifically, the
imposition by a province of an automatic licence suspension upon a Criminal
Code conviction for impaired driving was upheld by the Supreme Court of
Canada in Egan, (supra). Similarly, provincial legislation suspending a
driver’s licence upon refusal to provide a breath sample was upheld in Re
Validity of Section 92(4) of the Vehicles Act, 1957 (Sask.), [1958] S.C.R.
608. Even where the provincial suspension provisions were more severe than the Criminal
Code provisions, the provincial scheme has been upheld and not considered
punishment within the exclusive federal sphere: Ross v. Registrar of
Motor Vehicles, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 5. [26] The objective of the ALS program is public safety. The means chosen to
achieve it is through licence suspensions. Licence suspensions are
administrative in nature and while suspension of a licence may create a
significant inconvenience, it does not violate a person’s liberty rights nor
does it criminalize anti-social behaviour. Driving a motor vehicle remains a
privilege in a civil society and while often taken for granted, carries with it
obligations and qualifications which, if violated, may result in licence
suspension or revocation.

[27] The cases make clear that licence suspension has a legitimate place in a
provincial safety program. Both provincial and federal governments can
legislate where public safety and criminal law overlap. Compliance with
provincial legislation does not result in conflict with federal legislation and
vice versa. Further, the existence of sanctions in the federal Criminal Code
does not so fully occupy the field that provincial safety programs suspending
licences are precluded. [28] The appellants seek to distinguish the cases of provincial licence
suspensions post-conviction from the case on appeal. The ALS program operates
prior to conviction and therefore, it is argued, its legal purpose and effect
is to fill what is characterized as a gap in the criminal law. The evidence
supports the conclusion that the ALS program’s key feature is an almost
immediate suspension in order to obtain a greater deterrent effect. However, I
find nothing objectionable in the Province’s articulated goal of enhancing
public safety through deterrence by suspending licences of those involved in
alcohol-related driving faster than might be the result under criminal law. [29] The ALS program attempts to remove the delay in the suspension of a
driver’s licence which occurs in the criminal law context. The evidence
supports the conclusion that the effect of the delay undercuts the suspension’s
deterrent effect and accordingly, at best, does nothing to mitigate the risk
or, at worst, increases it. The primary concern of provincial legislatures is
one of public safety as distinct from deterring or punishing criminal
behaviour. Where the province perceives that more can be done to increase
highway and public safety in general, it is entitled to act accordingly. The
objectives of the criminal law, as distinct from civil law, include deterring
and sanctioning criminal behaviour. Criminal consequences are penal and may result
in a deprivation of a liberty. Thus, criminal law aims to strike a careful
balance of the individual’s rights and interest and broader societal goals.
Where, as here, the consequences of the behaviour are civil in nature, the
stringent procedural safeguards required under the criminal law are of less
significance and the balance shifts somewhat in favour of the societal goal of
deterrence and safety.

[30] In the criminal law context, swiftness must yield to procedural
safeguards. In a civil context, the balancing of societal interests against
individual privilege changes the balance in favour of the former. [31] The appellants also raised arguments intended to demonstrate that the
program does not accomplish the goal of public safety. However, as noted in the
Firearms Reference, within its constitutional sphere, the legislators
are the judges of whether a measure is likely to achieve its intended purpose.
The intention here is to bring home to the driver and the public the immediate
negative consequences of drinking and driving. Whether or not more drivers are
actually deterred by the system is not relevant to determining legislative
validity under a division of power analysis. [32] As noted by the chambers judge, the validity of Alberta’s ALS program is

Issue 3: Does the ALS program offend s. 11(d) of the Charter? [33] The appellants argue the ALS program violates the presumption of
innocence under s. 11(d) of the Charter because it creates a burden on
the applicant to prove his or her innocence before the Board. They submit that
in appealing a licence suspension, the burden is on the applicant to offer
evidence or make representations to satisfy the Board that no alcohol-related
driving occurred or a sample was reasonably refused and as such, the appellant
is not presumed innocent. [34] The chambers judge held that an appellant under the ALS program must
satisfy the Board that he did not engage in alcohol-related driving in order to
have the suspension automatically set aside under s. 39(4). Similarly, he held
that the Crown must satisfy the Board that alcohol-related driving has occurred
to maintain the suspension under s. 39(5). He held that if the Board is not
satisfied on a balance of probabilities as to the presence or absence of
alcohol-related driving, the suspension should be lifted. I agree. In my view,
this does not create a reverse onus. However, even if it could be said that a
reverse onus exists, it would not violate s. 11(d) given the civil nature of
these proceedings.

[35] Section 11(d) of the Charter provides: 11. Any person
charged with an offence has the right(d) to be
presumed innocent until proven guilty according to law in a fair and public
hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal; [36] In order to receive the protection of s. 11(d) of the Charter, a
person must be “charged with an offence”. The rights in s. 11(d) do not apply
to administrative or civil proceedings, but are guaranteed for persons
prosecuted by the state for public offences involving punitive sanctions: Blencoe
v. British Columbia (Human Rights Commission), [2000] 2 S.C.R. 307; R.
v. Wigglesworth, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 541. [37] Section 11(d) does not apply to a hearing before the Board. A driver
subject to a suspension under the ALS program is not charged with a criminal or
quasi-criminal offence; a driver faces a withdrawal of a privilege, not a
punitive sanction; cannot be compelled to give evidence; and is not, at the end
of the day, found guilty of an offence. I agree with the decision of Melvin J.
in Willock v. British Columbia (Superintendent of Motor Vehicles)
(2000), 23 Admin.L.R. (3d) 111 (B.C.S.C.), that s. 11(d) is not violated by the
process and procedures for an appeal hearing under a provincial ALS program.

Issue 4: Does the ALS program offend s. 13 of the Charter? [38] The appellants argue that an appeal before the Board requires revealing
the appellant’s entire case prior to defending the subsequent criminal charges.
This, they argue, violates s. 13 of the Charter. [39] Section 13 of the Charter provides: 13. A witness
who testifies in any proceedings has the right not to have any incriminating
evidence so given used to incriminate that witness in any other proceedings,
except in a prosecution for perjury or for the giving of contradictory
evidence. [40] A hearing before the Board, practically speaking, will occur before a
first appearance in a criminal court. If any evidence is put before the Board,
there is no provision in the legislation prohibiting the evidence from being
used in the subsequent criminal trial. Additionally, the appellants argue, if
an appellant reveals a good defence, for example, based on a defect in the certificate
of analysis, the Crown will have time to remedy the defect prior to the
criminal proceedings. [41] As seen in s. 39(4) of the Act, an appellant cannot be compelled
to give evidence before the Board. Even if an appellant chooses to testify, the
appropriate forum for raising the protection of s. 13 is during the criminal
proceedings, not before the Board. As the chambers judge pointed out, there is
no need to include in the ALS provisions a prohibition against the use of the

[42] As for the appellant revealing his or her defence prior to the criminal
proceedings, that complaint is essentially about the claimed loss of a tactical
advantage. Section 13 does not provide protection against any such loss.
Instead, it protects the right against self incrimination. Further, the Charter
itself does not guarantee the right of an individual to avail himself or
herself of all potential or strategic advantages. The ALS program does not
violate s. 13. Issue 5: Does the ALS program authorize Charter breaches? [43] The appellants argue that even if valid under a division of powers
analysis, the program is unconstitutional because no procedural or
constitutional safeguards are required to be recognized by the Board during its
hearings. Thus, they submit, the legislation is an unlawful delegation of
authority to infringe the Charter. This submission was cast more broadly
in oral argument to suggest the legislation is invalid as it authorizes conduct
that is contrary to the Charter. In considering whether legislation
“authorizes” such conduct, it is necessary to determine: (a) whether the legislation itself authorizes infringement;(b) if not, whether the necessary effect of the legislation
authorizes infringement; or(c) if the alleged infringement relates to a person exercising
the delegated discretion. In the third example, the
legislation does not fail but the infringement may warrant Charter
relief.

A.
Analytical framework [44] Legislation may be unconstitutional on its face because it violates a Charter
right and is not saved by s. 1. In such cases, the legislation will be invalid
and declared of no force or effect pursuant to s. 52(1) of the Constitution
Act, 1982. On the other hand, the Charter may be infringed, not by
the legislation, but by the actions of a delegated decision‑maker in
applying it. In the second case, the legislation remains valid, but a remedy
for the unconstitutional action may be sought pursuant to s. 24(1) of the Charter:
Eldridge v. British Columbia (Attorney General), [1997] 3 S.C.R.
624 at para. 20. [45] As a corollary, s. 32 limits Parliament and legislatures from granting
power or authority to a delegate to act in a manner which would result in an
infringement of the Charter: Slaight Communications Inc. v. Davidson,
[1989] 1 S.C.R. 1038 at para. 87. [46] In determining whether the law infringes a Charter right, the
first step requires examination of the purpose and effect of the challenged
legislation. More specifically, the analysis, as undertaken in Little
Sisters Book and Art Emporium v. Canada (Minister of Justice), [2000] 2
S.C.R. 1120 at para. 125, requires determination of whether there is anything
“on the face of the...legislation, or in its necessary effects” which
contemplates or encourages infringement of Charter rights.

B. Purpose
and effects of the legislation [47] The appellants’ submission parallels their argument advanced under the
division of powers; that the legislation is a direct attempt to truncate or
eliminate important Charter protections under the guise of public
safety. I have earlier concluded that the Act has as its purpose the
regulation of highways and the increase of safety on them. Nothing on the face
of the impugned provisions infringes or authorizes infringement of any section
of the Charter including ss. 8 and 10(b). The absence of certain
procedural protections present in the criminal law does not alter the character
or purpose of the legislation. [48] The unconstitutional effects alleged by the appellants must be the
necessary effects resulting from the legislation itself. An infringement of the
Charter by the actions of a delegated decision‑maker in applying
the legislation, as distinct from the legislation itself, does not render the
legislation invalid. In Little Sisters, for example, Binnie, J., for the
majority found, at para. 125, that the differential treatment based on sexual
orientation was not a necessary effect of the Customs legislation but was a
differentiation made at the administrative level in the implementation of the
legislation. The source of the Charter violation of s. 15, therefore,
was not the legislation itself. [49] The appellants submit that the necessary effect of the legislation
requires the Board to consider evidence obtained contrary to the Charter.
This, they submit, is in effect authorization to breach the Charter.
Section 39(3) of the Act makes it mandatory for the Board to review the
police report, the certificate of analysis and any sworn or affirmed
statements. It does not explicitly state that the Board has discretion whether
or not to consider the police report or the certificate if, for example, the
evidence was obtained improperly as a result of infringing the right to legal
counsel or as a result of an unreasonable search and seizure. By implication,
the appellants submit, the Act authorizes the Board to condone police
violations of the Charter rights guaranteed by ss. 8 and 10(b).

[50] This submission fails for two reasons. The first is that the argument
assumes that the ability of a court or a tribunal to consider evidence obtained
in violation of the Charter implicitly or explicitly “authorizes” Charter
violations. This assumption is incorrect. Secondly, the submission fails to
recognize the important distinction between Charter rights as they apply
in a criminal context and their scope and application in civil and
administrative proceedings. [51] As to the first submission, s.39(3) of the Act does not mandate
acceptance of evidence obtained contrary to the Charter. Moreover, the
Supreme Court of Canada in Mooring v. Canada (National Parole Board),
[1996] 1 S.C.R. 75 has made it clear that evidence obtained in breach of a Charter
right may nevertheless by considered by a tribunal. How it is to be considered
need not be mandated by the legislation and its admissibility is properly
determined by the board or tribunal. In Mooring, the court held the
National Parole Board was not required to treat s. 24(2) Charter cases
excluding evidence as determinative because it did not possess the power nor
was it required to exclude evidence under s. 24(2). [52] The necessary effect of the Board giving consideration to evidence
obtained contrary to the Charter is not authorization to breach the Charter
any more than it would be the necessary effect of a court admitting evidence
obtained in breach of Charter rights. As delegated authorities, the Charter
applies to police or peace officers. They are not authorized, for example, to
conduct unreasonable search and seizures contrary to s. 8. Nevertheless,
whether intended or otherwise, breaches have occurred and may reoccur. Those
breaches, however, do not invalidate legislation but may give rise to a Charter
remedy. Where a Charter remedy is not granted, the subsequent
consideration of evidence improperly obtained does not constitute an ex post
facto authorization to breach a Charter right.

[53] As to the second concern, the application of the Charter to the
admission of evidence in civil and administrative proceedings is distinct from
that in the criminal law. The tribunal is governed by the duty of fairness, as
it may apply in each case. Its decision to consider evidence is determined
subject to that duty. Issue 6: Availability of Charter
relief [54] The appellants point to several cases where Charter breaches have
been found in criminal proceedings flowing from roadside detentions conducted
simultaneously under the Criminal Code and the ALS program. They give
the example of breath samples being obtained in contravention of ss. 8 or
10(b). They submit that the legislation fails to provide a remedy and that such
remedy must be available through a court of competent jurisdiction under s.
24(1). I disagree. [55] Section 24(1) of the Charter provides: 24. (1) Anyone
whose rights or freedoms, as guaranteed by this Charter, have been infringed or
denied may apply to a court of competent jurisdiction to obtain such remedy as
the court considers appropriate and just in the circumstances. [56] In criminal proceedings, a person appealing a licence suspension would
be seeking to exclude evidence as provided by the Charter at s. 24(2): 24(2) Where,
in proceedings under subsection (1), a court concludes that evidence was
obtained in a manner that infringed or denied any rights or freedoms guaranteed
by this Charter, the evidence shall be excluded if it is established that,
having regard to all the circumstances, the admission of it in the proceedings
would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.

However, that remedy is not
available under this legislation. A. The
Board is not a court of competent jurisdiction [57] Statutory tribunals may be courts of competent jurisdiction to grant Charter
remedies: Weber v. Ontario Hydro, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 929. In this
case, it was conceded the Board is not a court of competent jurisdiction and is
not authorized by the legislation to exclude evidence as a result of a breach
of Charter rights. [58] As Binnie J. noted in Little Sisters at para. 137, there
is potential for Charter abuse in the administration of a legislated
scheme, however, “a rule requiring Parliament to enact in each case special
procedures for the protection of Charter rights would be unnecessarily
rigid.” He noted that there are various methods to ensure respect by the public
service for the Charter rights of citizens. One such example is the
imposition of the duty of procedural fairness which applies to guide the Board
when dealing with the rights, privileges and interests of individuals. While
distinct from a s. 24(2) remedy, the duty in a particular circumstance may
require a tribunal not to consider evidence. B. The duty of fairness [59] Historically, the common law required tribunals, including
administrators, to observe the principles of natural justice. Natural justice
requires a tribunal, when reaching a decision, will
do so with procedural fairness. Natural justice has two main rules: audi
alteram partem - the requirement that a person know the case against him or
her and be given the opportunity to answer it; and nemo judex in sua causa
debet esse – the rule against bias.
For administrative tribunals, the principles of natural justice have been
extended and described as a duty to be fair.

[60] The Supreme Court of Canada has repeatedly affirmed as a general common
law principle that “there is a duty of procedural fairness lying on every
public authority making an administrative decision which is not of a
legislative nature and which affects the rights, privileges or interests of an
individual”: Nicholson v. Haldimand‑Norfolk Regional Board of
Commissioners of Police, [1979] 1 S.C.R. 311; Martineau v. Matsqui
Institution Disciplinary Board (No. 2), [1980] 1 S.C.R. 602; Attorney
General of Canada v. Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, [1980] 2 S.C.R. 735;
Cardinal v. Director of Kent Institution, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 643 at
653. Clearly, the suspension of a driver’s licence affects an individual’s
privileges and interests and the Board here is obligated to exercise a duty of
fairness. a) Content of the duty of fairness [61] The content of the duty of fairness is flexible and variable depending
upon the context of the particular statute involved and the rights, privileges
or interests affected. “[T]he purpose of the participatory rights contained
within the duty is to ensure that administrative decisions are made using a
fair and open procedure, appropriate to the decision being made and its
statutory, institutional and social context, with an opportunity for those
affected to put forward their views and evidence fully and have them considered
by the decision-maker.”: Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and
Immigration), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817 at para. 22.

[62] The several criteria to determine what procedural rights the duty of
fairness requires in the circumstances of the operation of this civil law
program, as set out in Baker at paras. 23-28, include: (1) the nature of
the decision being made and process followed in making it; (2) the nature of
the statutory scheme and the terms of the statute pursuant to which the body
operates; (3) the importance of the decision to the individual or individuals
affected; (4) the legitimate expectations of the person challenging the
decision; (5) the choices of procedure made by the agency itself. The list is
not exhaustive. b) The content of the duties of the Board [63] As noted in Horsefield, the Ontario ALS program is an example
where the common law duty of fairness may be overridden by the legislature. The
Ontario program does not provide a right to a suspension hearing. In Alberta,
the legislation recognizes the existence of the duty by providing, for example,
the right to a hearing before the Board to confirm or cancel a driver’s licence
suspension or disqualification. [64] While the effect of the ALS statute is licence suspension in the
interest of public safety, the Board does not determine whether safety was at
issue vis a vis the driver in question. It is restricted to satisfying
itself that the statutory conditions for suspension are present. The evidence
it is to consider is set out in s. 39(3)(a)-(d) of the Act. Discretion
is granted to the Board to determine whether a person had a reasonable excuse
for failure to comply with a demand for a breath sample, whether statements and
other information are relevant, and at an oral hearing, whether evidence and
information given or presented is relevant and therefore to be considered.
Parenthetically, where the “defence” of reasonable excuse is proffered, the
Board must be satisfied to a civil standard. It is therefore possible to have
different results before the Board and a court of law dealing with criminal
charges arising from the same event. This possibility, however, does not render
the legislation unconstitutional.

a) inform the
appellant of the case against him or her,b) permit the
appellant a meaningful opportunity to answer the case against him or her,c) give full
and fair consideration to the issues, d) consider
the source of the evidence or information including whether it was gathered in
a manner contrary to the Charter or Charter values,e) consider
relevant evidence and information, and as a corollaryf) not
consider irrelevant or unreliable evidence or information,g) not act
arbitrarily, for an improper purpose or with malice. [69] Although the Board does not have the power under s. 24(2) to exclude
evidence obtained in breach of Charter rights, the manner in which
evidence was obtained remains a factor which must be considered when the Board
exercises its duty of fairness. At a minimum, relevance and reliability remain
necessary considerations before information or evidence is to be considered.
Fairness may preclude consideration of information which is not reliable or
relevant. Where the manner of obtaining the evidence raises issues of its
reliability or relevance, the Board must decide whether it should consider such
evidence and may decide it is not fair to do so. Again, as in Mooring,
the Board here is not required to apply the traditional rules of evidence but
is required to fulfill its fairness obligations while considering “evidence and
information” which is “relevant” to satisfy itself that a person consumed
alcohol, the concentration exceeded .08, drove a motor vehicle, or refused to
supply a breath sample without reasonable excuse. In acting in accordance with
these principles, the Board does not infringe Charter values nor is it
acting on the basis of “unconstitutional evidence”.

[70] Where the Board fails to meet its procedural fairness obligations or
otherwise acts in contravention of the Charter, then resort may be had
to judicial review: Campeau Corp. v. City of Calgary (1978), 12
A.R. 31 (C.A.). Such procedure was appropriately invoked by at least one
appellant in the case at bar. Mr. Hay’s licence suspension was properly quashed
by the chambers judge and remitted back for a consideration by the Board in
accordance with its obligation of procedural fairness. [71] As noted above, it is indeed conceivable that a driver could have his or
her licence suspended after the Board has considered improperly obtained
evidence and then, at a subsequent trial, be acquitted of any charges under the
Code because the same evidence was excluded under s. 24(2) of the Charter.
This result is not incongruous, unreasonable or a legitimate basis for avoiding
the Board and seeking remedy from a court of competent jurisdiction. The loss
of a driver’s licence through the ALS program is a civil consequence and
distinct from any criminal conviction or criminal penalty. [72] In this regard, I agree with the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal in Nova
Scotia (Attorney General) v. Selig (1996), 141 D.L.R. (4th)
462, which held that the act of suspension and act of sustaining the suspension
after review are lawful acts performed pursuant to valid provincial
legislation. A subsequent acquittal on charges under the Criminal Code
arising out of the same circumstances does not make the administrative licence
suspension unlawful or void because the Board, in the exercise of its duty of
fairness, considered the impugned evidence and, on that basis, confirmed the
licence suspension.

[73] The objective of the ALS program is public safety. The consequences of a
breach of the statute are civil - a licence suspension. A breach does not
threaten a liberty interest nor result in the consequences of a criminal
conviction. The substantive and procedural differences between criminal law and
civil law flow from their respective social purposes. The potential deprivation
of a liberty interest in a criminal law context engages a plethora of rights
and procedural safeguards that are not justified in a civil law context where
the jeopardy is civil only and there are significant countervailing societal
concerns at stake. The Legislature here has attempted to strike a balance
between procedural safeguards and public safety. It has done so in a manner
that accords with its legislative authority. VIII. CONCLUSION [74] The ALS program is administrative in nature and designed to enhance
public safety on highways. As such, it is intra vires the Province of
Alberta and does not offend the Charter. The appeal must be dismissed.[75] As requested by counsel, in order to provide time to deal with the
consequences of this decision, including the numerous stays of the licence
suspensions and the Criminal Code charges granted pending this appeal,
the suspensions will not commence until one month from the date of this
decision. APPEAL HEARD on March
5 and 6, 2003 REASONS FILED at Calgary,
Alberta,this 9th day of September, 2003

input: Date: 20030910 Docket: T-1459-97 Citation: 2003 FC 1056 Ottawa, Ontario, September 10, 2003 Present: The Honourable Madam Justice Tremblay-Lamer BETWEEN: ITV TECHNOLOGIES, INC. Plaintiff AND WIC TELEVISION LTD. Defendant AND: WIC TV AMALCO INC. and GLOBAL COMMUNICATIONS LIMITED Plaintiffs by Counterclaim AND ITV TECHNOLOGIES, INC. Defendant by Counterclaim REASONS FOR ORDER AND ORDER [1] This action springs from the use of the letters ITV by the plaintiff in its corporate name, business name and in the domain name for its web site, despite the objections of the defendant, which has several trade-marks registered incorporating the initials ITV. [2] The plaintiff, defendant by counterclaim, ITV Technologies Inc., (hereinafter "ITV Technologies") is a corporation with an office in Vancouver, British Columbia. [3] The defendant, plaintiff by counterclaim, WIC Television Ltd., (hereinafter "WIC") is a corporation with an office in Vancouver, British Columbia. It is in the business of television broadcasting, program production and multi-media communications.

input: [8] ITV Technologies filed its statement of claim on July 4, 1997. In its claim, ITV Technologies seeks to have WIC's trade-marks expunged on the grounds that they were not registrable and are no longer distinctive of WIC's wares and services. In its counterclaim, WIC sues ITV Technologies for passing off contrary to subsection 7(b) of the Act, for trade-mark infringement contrary to section 20 of the Act, and for depreciation of the goodwill attached to its registered trade-marks, contrary to section 22 of the Act. The injunction was terminated at a further hearing three weeks later on the basis that WIC could not show irreparable harm. [11] In 2000, WIC sold the ITV business and trade-marks to Global. input: [13] In my view, when considering the contents of a web site, the original is found on the Internet and provides better evidence than a print copy. The Court was able to see the documents as they existed on the Internet, and could witness such features as hyperlinking and interactive streaming that could not have been realistically reproduced on paper. [14] There was the initial concern that the documents being retrieved on the Internet at trial would not be an accurate representation of how they appeared at the relevant time period. Given that web sites are continually changing and evolving, a web site which appears on the Internet today would not necessarily look the same as it did for example, in 1997. In order to look into the past, both parties relied on the web site www.archive.org, which contains a digital library of Internet web sites. By using the Way Back Machine, the parties were able to access the web sites as they had existed at the relevant time period. I am satisfied that this web site is reliable, and that the Court could rely on its digital library for an accurate representation of the web sites at the relevant time period. [15] Overall, I am of the view that the use of the Internet at trial was beneficial and on several occasions, provided evidence which could not have otherwise been before the Court. For example, the Internet was used by counsel for WIC to confirm that the print copy of the meta tags (key information on a web site) was in conformity with the information found on ITV Technologies' web site. This would not have been possible without access to the Internet.
