input: [37] The failure to refer, in assessing costs, to the overriding principle of reasonableness, can produce a result that is contrary to the fundamental objective of access to justice. The costs system is incorporated into the Rules of Civil Procedure, which exist to facilitate access to justice. There are obviously cases where the prospect of an award of costs against the losing party will operate as a reality check for the litigant and assist in discouraging frivolous or unnecessary litigation. However, in my view, the chilling effect of a costs award of the magnitude of the award in this case generally exceeds any fair and reasonable expectation of the parties. [38] In deciding what is fair and reasonable, as suggested above, the expectation of the parties concerning the quantum of a costs award is a relevant factor. See Toronto (City) v. First Ontario Realty Corp. (2002), 59 O.R. (3d) 568, [2002] O.J. No. 2519 (S.C.J.) at p. 574 O.R. I refrain from attempting to articulate a more detailed or formulaic approach. The notions of fairness and reasonableness are embedded in the common law. Judges have been applying these notions for centuries to the factual matrix of particular cases. [39] Turning to what the quantum should be in this case, I would give consideration to the fact that the costs in the earlier proceeding were fixed in the amount of $97,563 by Lax J. While I accept, as the motions judge did, that there were differences between the two proceedings, the foundation upon which the two applications were prosecuted was based on the control of the Public Accountants Council of Ontario by the Chartered Accountants. The fact that all parties were satisfied to have the same evidentiary record in both cases suggests that there was much in common between the two applications.

input: [40] No doubt there was much more work to be done in respect of the second application. However, having expended partial indemnity costs of nearly $100,000 in response to the first application, I am confident that counsel were not starting tabula rasa when served with the application for judicial review. They would have been fully informed of the licensing application procedure, the make up and operation of the Public Accountants Council, the statutory regime and the issues that divided the Institute of Chartered Accountants for Ontario and the Certified General Accountants of Ontario. I simply cannot accept that counsel for the respondents did not take advantage of the work already done on the first application to better inform themselves in their approach to the second. [41] I also take into account the other factors referred to in para. 29 above, i.e., the respondents filed no evidence; conducted no cross-examination; and advanced substantially the same arguments in support of the motions to quash. [page303] [42] Finally, I consider that there is no proportionality between the costs claimed on a substantial indemnity scale and a partial indemnity scale. [43] These factors suggest that the amounts claimed on a partial indemnity basis call for a significant reduction. The appellants submitted that the award to each of the three groupings of respondents should be $2,500 for a total of $7,500. I do not accept that submission.

input: [44] In my view, a fair and reasonable award, taking into consideration all the factors discussed above, would be: Public Accountants Council of Ontario $ 30,000.00 Individual Respondents $ 20,000.00 Institute of Chartered Accountants of Ontario $ 13,000.00 Total $ 63,000.00 These figures are inclusive of disbursements and Goods and Services Tax. Disposition [45] In the result, I would allow the appeal, set aside the costs award of the motions judge and in its place substitute the award set out in para. 44 above. [46] I would also order that the appellants are entitled to their costs of the motion for leave to appeal and the appeal, fixed on a partial indemnity basis in the total amount of $12,000, including disbursements and Goods and Services Tax. Wade For the respondent Via Rail Canada Inc.:Catherine A. Lahey Avocats à l’audience : Pour l’appelante : David M. Brown, c.r. Pour l’intimée la Commission de la santé, de la sécurité et de l’indemnisation des accidents au travail du Nouveau- Brunswick,John P. Barry, c.r.Deidre L. Wade Pour l’intimée Via Canada Inc.,Catherine A. Lahey THE COURT The appeal is dismissed without costs. LA COUR Rejette l’appel sans dépens. The judgment of the Court was delivered
by ROBERTSON, J.A. I. Introduction [1] This
is the first time this Court has been presented with an appeal involving a
worker’s right to benefits for psychological injuries suffered in the
workplace, as provided for under the Workers’ Compensation Act, R.S.N.B.
1973, c. W-13. The essential facts are as follows. [2] The
appellant and her co-workers had been unsuccessful in convincing their employer
to make changes to their work environment (noise and lighting problems). The
impasse led to a verbal confrontation in which the appellant’s supervisor
castigated her in a manner best described as a bombastic rant, punctuated by
yelling. The appellant’s physician described the event as “emotionally
traumatizing.” The appellant did not return to work and was subsequently
diagnosed as suffering from a “major” and “resistant” depression. After
exhausting benefits under the employer’s disability plan and the federal
unemployment insurance regime, the appellant filed a stress-related claim with
the respondent Commission. The claim was rejected on the basis that the
psychological injury complained of did not qualify as an “accident”, as that
term is defined in s. 1 of the Act. Subject to one exception, that
definition expressly excludes “the disablement of mental stress or a
disablement caused by mental stress...” The exception requires the claimant to
establish that the disability arose as a result of “an acute reaction to a
traumatic event…”. The Commission ruled against the appellant on this point, as
did the Appeals Tribunal established under the Workplace Health, Safety and
Compensation Commission Act, S.N.B. 1994, c. W-14. For the reasons that
follow, I conclude that the Appeals Tribunal did not err in the result. That
said, this Court must address certain issues that eluded the Appeals Tribunal.

input:
[3] As
to the proper review standard, there is no consensus on whether the Appeals
Tribunal’s decision involves a question of fact or law. The two respondents
contend that the Appeals Tribunal approached the issue as a question of
causation and, correlatively, a question of fact. With respect, I disagree. [4] In
my opinion, the Appeals Tribunal rejected the appellant’s appeal because the
confrontation did not qualify as a traumatic event. I agree with the appellant
that the Appeals Tribunal failed to acknowledge the Commission’s reasons for
rejecting the appellant’s claim. Those reasons are tied to two policy
directives that outline the criteria to be applied by Commission staff when
assessing stress-related claims. Specifically, the appellant questions the
Commission’s application of a tri-partite objective test. It is trite law that
Commission policies are non-binding and that it is the responsibility of the
Appeals Tribunal, and ultimately this Court, to rule on the proper
interpretation of the Act. This includes the articulation of a legal
framework through the identification of relevant criteria. However, claimants
have a right to know whether the Commission’s policy directives are consistent
with the provisions of the Act when properly construed. I recognize the
right of the Appeals Tribunal to conduct what amounts to a de novo
hearing and to make independent findings of fact based on fresh evidence. However,
it makes no sense that the Commission would be able to formulate and apply a
tri-partite objective test, together with its own definitions of critical
statutory terms when assessing a disability claim, and then turn around and
abandon that legal framework on appeal by re-characterizing the issue as a
question of fact.

[5] I am
of the view that the appellant’s primary challenge represents a pure question
of law for which the review standard would have been correctness had the
Appeals Tribunal dealt with the interpretative issue and, correlatively, the
correctness of the Commission’s policy directives under attack. Deference
cannot be accorded a tribunal’s failure to address a pertinent interpretative
issue. In fairness to the Appeals Tribunal, there is an explanation for the
omission. [6] The
Commission did not participate in the one and one half hour hearing before the
Appeals Tribunal and neither the appellant nor the respondent employer was
represented by legal counsel. The appellant retained a “labour consultant” who
raised, but did not aggressively pursue, the validity of the Commission’s
policy directives. The employer sent a claims officer and the local office
manager to defend its position. Only after the appeal to this Court was filed
did the Commission elect to intervene as a party. Before this Court, all three
parties elected to be represented by legal counsel. II. Background [7] The
appellant had been working for the respondent, Via Rail Canada Inc., for 15
years before commencing work, on October 15, 2001, at its call center in Moncton, New Brunswick. Shortly
after moving into premises under renovation, the appellant and other employees
complained of poor working conditions. Specifically, they complained of noise
levels and poor lighting conditions. Over the ensuing seven months the
employees’ repeated requests for workplace modifications went unanswered by
their immediate supervisor. In July of 2002, the appellant spoke directly with
her supervisor’s superior with a view to having management address the
employees’ concerns. On learning that the appellant had approached upper
management over the poor working conditions, the supervisor called the
appellant into his office on July 15, 2002. The appellant described the meeting as one in
which “[the manager] threatened and intimidated me for going over his head to
the Director concerning the fixing of the working conditions…” The appellant
also characterized the encounter as a traumatic event which resulted in her
leaving her employment. In her statement of facts, the appellant states that
she “went off work on July 15th 2002 as a result of a disability
flowing from the noise level in the workplace, the excessive and difficult
lighting at the workplace and the inappropriate actions of the manager...”

[8] Following
the confrontation with her supervisor, the union representing the appellant
pursued a grievance against her employer with respect to its refusal to pay the
appellant for the six hours not worked on July 15, 2002. Eventually, that
grievance was abandoned. From July 19, 2002 until September 7, 2002, the appellant received
disability benefits under an employer-funded short term disability plan
administered by a private insurer, Great West Life. The insurer agreed to
provide the benefits until such time as the appellant could seek and obtain
benefits from the Commission. Apparently, Great West Life decided to
discontinue payment of the benefits after concluding that the appellant’s
illness was work-related. This finding was based on a medical report submitted
on the appellant’s behalf. Great West Life also indicated that as physical
alterations had been made to her work environment, there was nothing to prevent
the appellant from going back to work. On the basis of this evidence, the
insurer advised her to pursue a compensation claim with the Commission.
However, the appellant sought and obtained benefits under the Employment
Insurance Act, S.C. 1996, c. 23. She received benefits for a total of 15
weeks, ending on December 5, 2002. Finally, the record does disclose that the
appellant’s supervisor no longer holds that position and that Via Rail made the
requested environmental modifications to the workplace.

[9] On December 23, 2002, the appellant applied
for workers’ compensation benefits. On January 22, 2003, an adjudicator
rejected her claim on the basis that the appellant’s condition related to the
“usual stresses and strains of the workplace” and not an acute reaction to a
traumatic event. Subsequently, the appellant sought a reconsideration of her
claim. The matter was reviewed and on October 27, 2003 the same adjudicator
confirmed the original decision to reject the appellant’s claim. The rejection
letter of October 27, 2003 states that in order for the appellant to qualify
for benefits she had to establish that she suffered an acute reaction to a
traumatic event and that to come within the exception to the general rule three
tests had to be met: (1) the condition must be an acute reaction to a traumatic
event and not due to chronic or cumulative stress; (2) the event must directly
produce a condition which meets established diagnostic criteria; and (3) the
claim must also arise out of and in the course of employment. Applying those
criteria, the adjudicator wrote: With respect to the first test, [the
appellant’s] mental stress was the result of a combination of factors or an
accumulation of factors and not the result of an acute incident. Secondly she
was diagnosed with an adjustment disorder July, 2002. Dr. Nasri, indicates [the
appellant] had a problem with her mood sometime in October, 2001 and suffered
from major depression. An adjustment disorder does not meet the requirement of
the second test which is that the event must directly produce a condition which
meets established diagnostic criteria.

[13] I
start with the proposition that the issue of causation in the context of the Workers’
Compensation Act may involve a question of law, a question of fact or even
a question of mixed law and fact (the application of a legal test or framework
to primary facts). The proper characterization depends on the circumstances of
each case. In the typical compensation case, the issue of causation must be
addressed because the Act’s definition of “accident” imposes a
requirement that it have arisen “out of and in the course of employment…” This
requirement reflects the Act’s primary objective, which is to make
no-fault insurance benefits available to those who suffer injuries in the
workplace. The Act was not intended to serve as a general compensation
scheme that embraces non-occupational injuries. In furtherance of that object,
the Act requires that the injury be caused by some event or condition
tied to the workplace. Note that the expression “arising out of and in the
course of employment” contains two distinct but interrelated concepts. The
general understanding is that if the injury occurs at work, it “arose in the
course” of the employment. This requirement deals with the time, location and
activity surrounding the accident (the “when”, “where” and “what” of the injury
so to speak). If, however, the injury is caused purely by natural phenomenon
(e.g., an aneurism) such that the injury would have resulted irrespective of
the employment situation, it cannot be held that the injury “arose out” of the
employment. This is the “how” of the injury. Note also that s. 7(2) of the Act
provides that once it is established that the accident arose out of the
employment it is presumed that the accident occurred in the course of
employment and vice versa. See generally Douglas G. Gilbert & L.A.
Liversidge, Workers’ Compensation in Ontario, 3rd ed. (Aurora, Ont: Canada
Law Book Inc., 2001), at 19, and Terence G. Ison, Workers’ Compensation in Canada, 2nd ed.
(Toronto: Butterworths, 1989), at 35.

[14] As
Justice Drapeau (as he then was) explained in Martin v. Commission de la santé,
de la sécurité et de l’indemnisation des accidents au travail (N.-B.) (1998), 205 N.B.R. (2d)
319 (C.A.) at para. 14: “[t]he
existence of a causal link between disability by reason of a personal injury
and an accident arising out of and in the course of employment is a question of
fact.” In cases where an employee has suffered a physical injury on the job
site, it is not difficult to establish causation within the framework of the Act.
The more difficult cases involve an employee alleging disability tied to an
occupational disease. For example, in Martin, the issue was whether a
worker’s medical problems were caused by his exposure to toxic fumes at his
workplace. See also Moyer v. Workplace Health, Safety and Compensation
Commission (N.B.) (2004), 277 N.B.R. (2d) 111 (C.A.) and Athey v. Leonati,
[1996] 3 S.C.R. 458 at 466-67 dealing with causation in the context of a
negligence suit. [15] I
agree that the causation issue in the typical compensation case involves a
question of fact. But this does not mean that the causation issue cannot
involve a question of law. Recall that causation is a theoretical construct
that can involve pure questions of law (see Snell v. Farrell, [1990] 2
S.C.R. 311 at 326-30). A decision of this Court that reflects the understanding
that the causation issue may involve a question of law is Keddy v. Workplace
Health, Safety and Compensation Commission (N.B.) et al. (2002), 247 N.B.R.
(2d) 284 (C.A.). In that case, the central issue was whether the Appeals
Tribunal erred in concluding that s. 11(1) of the Workers’ Compensation Act
barred the claimant’s tort action against a hospital. The legal question posed
was whether a worker who was injured while receiving medical treatment for a
work-related injury was acting within the course of his or her employment at
the time of the subsequent injury. A positive response to that question has the
effect of barring any tort claim that the claimant may have against either
employer, provided both employers are covered by the legislation, which they
were in Keddy. As a matter of interpretation and policy, the Appeals
Tribunal answered the question in the positive and, therefore, the tort claim
against the nurse and hospital was barred under s. 11(1). This Court ruled that
the issue was a question of law for which the review standard was correctness,
but that the Tribunal had not erred in its determination. Note that Keddy
was not a case in which it had to be determined whether the employee had sought
medical treatment for the work injury or whether the medical injury arose from
the treatment of the work injury. Rather, the Keddy case raised a broad
policy issue of precedential significance and one that other tribunals and
courts have had to address (see Kovach v. Workers’ Compensation Board,
[1996] B.C.J. No. 2388 (C.A.) (QL) and Pasiechnyk v. Saskatchewan (Workers’
Compensation Board), [1997] 2 S.C.R. 890). As explained in Canada (Director of
Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc., [1997] 1 S.C.R. 748 at para. 37 the fact
that a case is of true precedential significance is a litmus test for deciding
whether the issue being addressed involves a question of law.

[16] In
the present case, the disability for which the appellant claims compensation is
rooted in her workplace. The poor working conditions, together with the
appellant’s encounter with her supervisor, are the factors underscoring her
disability claim. Specifically, the appellant argued that the confrontational
encounter with her supervisor led to her inability to work. In the words of her
doctor, that incident was the “straw that broke the camel’s back.” While both
the Commission and the Appeals Tribunal rejected the idea that the encounter
qualified as a traumatic event, it is agreed that the stress for which the
appellant is seeking compensation was work-related. In short, no one denies
that the appellant suffered stress “arising out of and in the course of
employment.” Hence, the issue of factual causation does not present a barrier
to her compensation claim. However, that is not sufficient for purposes of
establishing a valid claim. [17] The
causation issue arises twice in the assessment of stress-related claims. On the
first occasion the decision-maker is required to decide whether the stress (the
alleged traumatic event) arose out of and in the course of employment. Assuming
this to be so, the decision-maker must then decide whether the work-related
incident qualifies as a traumatic event. If the incident so qualifies, the
causation issue arises a second time. The decision-maker must now decide
whether the traumatic event caused an acute reaction leading to the claimant’s
inability to work.

[18] When
I read the Appeals Tribunal’s reasons, reproduced at paragraph 9 of these
reasons, I am left with the impression that the appellant’s appeal was
dismissed because her inability to work was the cumulative effect of a number
of stressors being experienced within and outside the workplace, rather than a
single incident which caused an acute reaction. In short, the Appeals Tribunal
held that the appellant’s confrontation with her supervisor was not a traumatic
event. Rather, her claim was for chronic stress, a topic addressed below. In
these circumstances, the respondents’ argument that the issue before this Court
relates to causation and, therefore, a question of fact, is, with great
respect, wrong. This leaves for consideration the appellant’s argument. [19] Counsel
for the appellant recognizes that the terms “traumatic event” and “acute
reaction” are subject to interpretation. Therefore, their meaning qualifies as
a question of law. Specifically, counsel seized on the fact that the
appellant’s claim was rejected after the adjudicator applied the Commission’s
policy pertaining to stress-related claims. When one looks at Policy 21-103
(“Conditions for Entitlement-Stress”) it is evident that the Commission applies
a tri-partite test when assessing stress-related claims. Moreover, the
Commission has adopted its own definitions for the terms “traumatic event”,
“acute reaction” and “post-traumatic stress disorder.” Policy 21-103 also
speaks of an objective test for assessing stress claims. Finally, Policy
21-103.01 provides Commission staff with guidelines to be considered in cases
involving post-traumatic stress syndrome.

[20] Counsel
for the appellant argues that the application of these policies constitutes an
error of law in the sense that they contradict the proper meaning of the
expression “acute reaction to a traumatic event.” Counsel also contends that
the Appeals Tribunal applied those policies when deciding whether the
appellant’s disability came within the exception to the general rule. With
respect to the latter submission, the Appeals Tribunal’s reasons do not support
the argument that the Tribunal expressly or implicitly accepted and applied
either of the two policies in question. It is clear to me that the Tribunal
considered that a determination as to what qualifies as a traumatic event is a
question of personal judgment more akin to a question of fact. There is a reason
why this is so and one that underscores a fundamental problem in the administrative
appeals process. [21] When
one looks at the record below (“Statement of Facts”), it is evident that the
Commission did not participate in the hearing, thus leaving carriage of the
appeal to the appellant’s employer, Via Rail. At that hearing, the appellant
was represented by a “labour relations consultant”, who apparently has no
formal legal training. The same appears to be true of the two representatives
appearing on behalf of Via Rail: a claims officer and the local manager. In
these circumstances, it is not surprising that the Appeals Tribunal was not
presented with any legal arguments, save one, dealing with the interpretation
of the expression “acute reaction to a traumatic event.” To the credit of the
appellant’s advisor, he did question the validity of the policy in question and

[22] In
brief, I recognize the Appeals Tribunal’s right to conduct a de novo
hearing and to make independent findings of fact based on evidence not
presented to the Commission. However, that does not mean that the Appeals
Tribunal is free to disregard the Commission’s reasons for rejecting a claim.
Those reasons may raise questions of law. It makes no sense, for example, that
the Commission would formulate and apply a tri-partite test, together with its
own definitions of critical statutory terms, when assessing disability claims
and then turn around and abandon that legal framework on an appeal to the
Appeals Tribunal or to this Court by re-characterizing the issue as a question
of fact. [23] In
future, it is incumbent on the Appeals Tribunal to review the Commission’s
reasons for rejecting a claim to determine whether the appeal raises any
question of law, including the interpretation of any pertinent legislation.
That obligation places the Commission on notice that it may want to participate
in the hearing before the Appeals Tribunal if it wishes to defend its
interpretation or application of the relevant legislation. After all, there can
be no assurances that the claimant’s employer will be able to address legal
questions effectively. The present case is on point. [24] Once
the Appeals Tribunal has identified and resolved any question of law, it may
turn to the evidence adduced by the parties, make the necessary findings of
fact and apply those facts against the relevant legal framework. Even in cases
where the Commission’s ruling hinges on factual matters, the Appeals Tribunal
may well find it instructive to understand the general basis on which the
Commission rejected a claimant’s application for compensation benefits.

[25] Returning
to the present case, it is undeniable that the Commission’s published policies
governing work-related stress lay down a framework for assessing such claims.
That framework consists of a tri-partite objective test and definitions of key
terms. Whether or not that framework is in keeping with the legislative intent
underscoring the exception to the general rule is of critical significance. Had
the Appeals Tribunal dealt with this issue, this Court would have had to
identify the proper review standard by applying the pragmatic and functional
approach outlined in the Supreme Court jurisprudence. As this Court has stated
on numerous occasions, the review standard applicable to decisions of the
Appeals Tribunal involving questions of law is generally correctness (see Gallant
v. Workplace Health, Safety and Compensation Commission (N.B.) (2000), 228
N.B.R. (2d) 98 (C.A.) at para. 27, and Keddy). Parenthetically,
I am not aware of any Supreme Court decision in which that Court has
applied a review standard other than correctness in cases involving a statutory
right of appeal on a question of law alone. At the same time, the Supreme Court
continues to recognize that the existence of a statutory right of appeal does
not of itself mean that correctness is the proper review standard. The other
factors that comprise the pragmatic and functional approach have to be
considered and in particular the nature of the legal issue (see Dr. Q v.
College of Physicians and Surgeons of British Columbia, [2003] 1 S.C.R. 226
at paras. 17, 21-25, and 33, and Law Society of New Brunswick v. Ryan,
[2003] 1 S.C.R. 247 at para. 21).

"accident" includes a wilful and intentional act, not being the act of a worker, and also includes a chance event occasioned by a physical or natural cause, as well as a disablement caused by an occupational disease and any other disablement arising out of and in the course of employment, but does not include the disablement of mental stress or a disablement caused by mental stress, other than as an acute reaction to a traumatic event; « accident » comprend un acte volontaire et intentionnel autre que celui du travailleur; il comprend aussi un événement fortuit dû à une cause physique ou naturelle de même que l'incapacité causée par une maladie professionnelle et tout autre incapacité survenant par le fait et à l'occasion de l'emploi, mais ne comprend pas l'incapacité de la tension mentale ni l'incapacité causée par la tension mentale, sauf en tant que réaction violente à un événement traumatique; [28] In brief, the right to
compensation benefits is dependent on the worker establishing that he or she
was involved in an accident that arose out of and in the course of employment.
In turn, accident is defined to include: (1) a wilful and intentional act, not
being the act of a worker; (2) a chance event occasioned by a physical or
natural cause; (3) a disablement caused by an occupational disease; and (4) any
other disablement arising out of and in the course of employment. To this point
the definition of accident is arguably broad enough to encompass a disablement
resulting from mental stress, provided the stress was work-related; that is to
say the stress arose out of and in the course of employment. However, in 1992
the definition of “accident” was amended by An Act to Amend the Workers’
Compensation Act, S.N.B. 1992, c. 34 to exclude “the disablement of mental
stress or a disablement caused by mental stress, other than as an acute
reaction to a traumatic event.” [Emphasis added.]

[29] It
is not difficult to identify the historical reasons underscoring the decision
of legislatures to address the question of whether disability claims tied to
work-related stress would be compensable. During the late 1980s the Appeals
Tribunal of Ontario took the bold step of including such claims: a position
that was at odds with the policy being applied by the board. The historical
background is discussed in Douglas Gilbert’s text, Workers’ Compensation In Ontario. It helps explain why,
in 1992, the New Brunswick Legislature decided to amend the definition of “accident”
so as to exclude stress-related claims, subject to one exception. [30] Prior
to 1998 the Ontario board had no explicit
policy dealing with compensation for mental stress alone. It did have a policy
covering “psychotraumatic disability” which applied in situations where mental
stress resulted from a physical injury or disability. There was no policy in
place for cases in which stress originating in the workplace lead to an
employee’s inability to work. The Board’s practice was to award benefits only
where the stress claim was connected to a specific traumatic event in the
workplace. The board did not recognize stress claims associated with typical
workplace pressures. Subsequently, the Appeals Tribunal expanded the boundaries
of entitlement by allowing claims for stress reactions to normal workplace
events based on a modified reasonable person test. In the tribunal’s view,
chronic stress claims should be compensated in the same way as other gradual
process injuries. For example, in 717/88, [1992] O.W.C.A.T.D. No. 713 (QL)
the worker claimed that a diagnosed psychiatric condition of phobic anxiety and
severe clinical depression was the result of work-induced stress. In allowing
the appeal, the Appeals Tribunal held that the workplace stressors need not be
unusual or unexpected and that the test would be based on objective evidence of
work stressors that a “reasonable person” could plausibly find stressful. The
majority concluded that while there were personal stressors and a disposition
to a stress-related disability, the evidence did not negate the fact that work
was a “significant contributing factor.” In a later decision, 363/91,
[1994] O.W.C.A.T.D. No. 83 (QL), the tribunal adopted a modified objective
reasonable person test which required balancing objective evidence of stress in
the workplace against the worker’s perceptions of and subjective reaction to
workplace conditions.

[31] Understandably,
the divergent approaches taken by the Ontario board and the Appeals Tribunal generated
uncertainty, leading to substantial litigation. In 1996, the Ontario government commissioned
a report covering the issues of chronic stress and chronic pain. The report
recommended exclusion of compensation for chronic stress claims for the reason
that “there can be little assurance that, in any one case, the employment has
in fact caused a psychological disability that has so many other potential
non-work causes” (see Cam Jackson, New Directions for Workers’ Compensation
Reform: A Discussion Paper (Toronto: Minister Without Portfolio Responsible
for Workers’ Compensation Reform, 1996)). In 1997, the Ontario government
responded by amending its legislation to exclude claims for mental stress,
except where the disability arose from an acute reaction to a traumatic event (see
An Act to Secure the Financial Stability of the Compensation System for
Injured Workers, to Promote the Prevention of Injury and Disease in Ontario
Workplaces and to Revise the Workers’ Compensation Act and Make Related
Amendments to Other Acts, S.O. 1997, c. 16). However, the amendments go
further. They state that a worker is not entitled to benefits for mental stress
caused by the employer’s decisions or actions relating to the employment. The
amendment refers specifically to management decisions involving a change of
work or work conditions, a decision to discipline an employee or to terminate
the employment (see Workplace Safety and Insurance Act, S.O. 1997, c.
16, Sched. A, s. 13(5)). Together, the amended provisions confirmed the Ontario board’s traditional
approach to compensation for mental stress.

[32] With
the amendments to the Ontario legislation the board adopted a new policy which
distinguishes between gradual reactions to general workplace conditions, which
are not compensable, and delayed acute reactions to sudden and unexpected
traumatic events. For example, an employee who, weeks after the event, feels
stress related to witnessing a serious work accident would be entitled to
benefits, while an employee who becomes disabled by stress following weeks of
severe pressure in the workplace does not have an entitlement. The policy also
calls for a “reasonable person” standard to be applied in determining whether
an event is “traumatic.” The policy goes on to state that such events are
“usually horrific, or have elements of actual or threatened violence to the
worker.” The event must be uncommon in the normal course of the worker’s
employment. The “thin skull” principle does not apply. The event must be
traumatic on an objective basis. A worker who, due to personality or psychological
history, reacts strongly to a relatively innocuous incident has no entitlement
under the policy. On the other hand, an event may still be considered traumatic
even if others in the workplace do not share the worker’s reaction, or if the
worker had witnessed similar events in the past without experiencing a stress
reaction (e.g. ambulance driver). In 2002, the board adopted a policy with
respect to workplace harassment. Under that policy, harassment may be viewed as
a series of traumatic events giving rise to injury. In a related policy change,
persons working in stressful jobs such as health care, firefighting and
policing are entitled to claim a stress injury due to the cumulative effects of
events which occur on the job.

[33] Manitoba was the first province
to amend its workers’ compensation legislation for purposes of adopting a
general rule excluding stress claims. In 1991, its legislation was amended to
define “occupational disease” to exclude stress other than an acute reaction to
a traumatic event (see The Workers Compensation Amendment and Consequential
Amendments Act, S.M. 1991, c. 36). New Brunswick followed suit in 1992, but the wording of
the amendment differs from the other provinces in that the exclusion clause
states that the term “accident” does not include “the disablement of mental
stress or a disablement caused by mental stress” before acknowledging the
traumatic event exception. Newfoundland amended its legislation in 1998 to define
“injury” as excluding stress other than stress which qualifies as an acute
reaction to a traumatic event (see Act to Amend the Workers’ Compensation
Act, S.N. 1998, c. 19). By contrast, the other Acts simply exclude
“stress”, subject to the traumatic event exception. This is true of the Nova Scotia amendment adopted in
1995 (see An Act to Reform the Law Respecting Compensation for Workers,
S.N.S. 1995, c. 10). Prince Edward Island’s amending legislation of 2001 uses
the same language as does the British Columbia amendment adopted in 2002 (see An
Act to Amend the Workers Compensation Act, S.P.E.I. 2001, c. 20 and Workers
Compensation Amendment Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 56). However, the British Columbia amendment goes further
than any other. It imposes a requirement that stress claims be supported by a
physician’s or psychologist’s diagnosis that the mental stress fell within the
American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of
Mental Disorders, 4th ed. (Washington, D.C.: American
Psychiatric Association, 1994) (DSM-IV). Finally, Saskatchewan and Alberta are the only Provinces
that have not adopted amending legislation to deal with stress-related
claims.

agree that the question of whether the claimant experienced an “acute reaction

fact only. To persist with the view that the decision-maker is entitled to
exercise an informed but personal judgment as to whether an event is traumatic
and the reaction acute is to invite arbitrariness. There is no assurance that similarly
situated claimants will be treated alike or that future claimants will be able
to evaluate the merits of pursuing a claim. The Commission’s two policies
covering stress-related claims commend themselves, if only for the reason that
they introduce an element of objectivity and certainty into the decision-making
process. This is true for both the Commission’s adjudicators and claimants.
However, the law is clear that neither this Court nor the Appeals Tribunal is
bound by Commission policies (see Green v. Workplace Health, Safety and
Compensation Commission (N.B.) (1998), 201 N.B.R. (2d) 93 (C.A.) at para.
14; Melanson v. Workers’ Compensation Board (N.B.) (1994), 146 N.B.R.
(2d) 294 (C.A.); Dwyer v. Workplace Health, Safety and Compensation
Commission (N.B.) (1996), 179 N.B.R. (2d) 348 (C.A.) and Myles v.
Workplace Health, Safety and Compensation Commission (N.B.) (1996), 181
N.B.R. (2d) 183 (C.A.)). Ultimately, it is the responsibility of this Court to
interpret the provisions of the legislation in a manner that is in keeping with
interpretative principles.

[35] The
first of the two Commission policies dealing with stress-related claims is
Policy No. 21-103. It has the stated purpose of establishing “guidelines” for
the adjudication of stress-related claims. It begins with definitions for the
following terms: acute reaction, traumatic event and post-traumatic stress
disorder: Acute Reaction – An acute reaction is one that can be
established as being sharp in effect, serious or critical. It is not chronic. Traumatic event – A ‘traumatic’ event involves a physical
injury or wound caused by external force or violence, or an emotional or
psychological shock that may produce disordered feeling or behaviour. Post-traumatic stress disorder – According to the American Psychiatric
Association, “Post-traumatic Stress Disorder is a disorder which arises
following a psychologically distressing event that is outside the range of
usual human experience (i.e. outside the range of such common experiences as
simple bereavement, chronic illness, business losses and marital conflict). The
stressor producing this syndrome would be markedly distressing to anyone, and
is usually, [but not always], experienced with intense fear, terror and
helplessness.” [36] The
policy goes on to outline three criteria to be applied by staff when assessing
mental stress claims: (1) the disability must not be due to chronic stress; (2)
the event must directly produce a condition which meets established diagnostic
criteria; and (3) the event (the accident) arose out of and in the course of
employment. The policy goes on to exclude stress-related claims caused by
ongoing personal or employment conditions or normal workplace discipline and
management labour relations. In turn, the policy’s definition of acute reaction
excludes a chronic or gradual onset reaction. A traumatic event is defined to
involve a physical injury or wound caused by external force or violence or an
emotional shock that may produce disordered feelings or behaviour. The requirement
that the event must produce a condition which meets established diagnostic
criteria is further addressed in Policy No. 21-103.01. That policy provides
Commission staff with “guidelines” to be considered in cases involving
post-traumatic stress disorder as described in the third revised edition of the
American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of
Mental Disorders, 3rd ed. (Washington, D.C.: American
Psychiatric Association, 1987).

[37] The
second of the two Commission policies dealing with stress-related claims is
Policy 21-103.01. It describes the essential feature of a post-traumatic stress
disorder as “the development of characteristic symptoms following a
psychologically distressing event that is outside the range of usual experience.”
It goes on to state that for compensation purposes the event must be acute, not
cumulative, and extraordinary in nature in comparison with those events in the
normal scope of the worker’s employment. The disability must not arise out of
the usual activities of employment or events inherent in the job. Policy
21-103.01 also states that a traumatic event must be demonstrated by “clear and
concise evidence” and is to be measured by “objective standards and actual
events”, rather than the worker’s perceptions. That requirement is followed by
the direction to Commission staff that the event must directly produce a
condition which meets established diagnostic criteria and, in turn, the
diagnosed condition must produce a disability which is demonstrable based on
appropriate testing. The policy outlines in detail the symptoms of one
suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder. [38] In
summary, the Commission’s policies lay down the following directives for
assessing stress-related claims. First, the traumatic event must have arisen
out of and in the course of employment. Second, a traumatic event is defined as
an event that is sudden and unexpected: one that is outside the range of usual
human experience. Third, an employment decision affecting the terms and
conditions of employment does not qualify as a traumatic event. Fourth, cases
of chronic or gradual onset stress, being cumulative in nature, do not qualify
as a traumatic event. Fifth, what is or is not a traumatic event must be
measured objectively. Sixth, a claim will only succeed if the worker is
diagnosed as having the symptoms of one who suffers from a post-traumatic
stress disorder. I am in general agreement with all of the propositions, save
the last. My formal reasoning is as follows.

[39] It
goes without saying that the traumatic event which precipitates the employee’s
inability to work must arise out of and in the course of the employment, as do
all injury claims. As the causation issue was addressed above, I will say no
more of this requirement. [40] It
is safe to conclude that the 1992 amendment to the Act’s definition of
accident was intended to curtail the willingness of administrative tribunals to
grant benefits for what are commonly referred to as either “chronic” or
“gradual onset” stress claims. Prior to the amendment, it was open to argument
that if a worker is entitled to compensation benefits because of a gradual
onset physical injury so too should that worker be entitled to compensation in
circumstances where work-related stress culminates in his or her inability to
work. This explains why the 1992 amendment begins with the general rule that
compensation is not available for “the disablement of mental stress or a
disablement caused by mental stress.” As noted, this aspect of the Act’s
definition of accident differs from that found in the other Provinces mentioned
above. [41] It
is easy to grasp the significance of a “disablement caused by mental stress.”
Stress is the product of the psychological or emotional pressure that we
experience in both our personal and work lives. Often it is difficult to
isolate the stress in one situation from that in the other and to determine the
impact that stress in one domain has on stress in the other. But there may come
a point that the “stressors” encountered in the workplace lead to the inability
to function in a work environment. The clearest manifestation of this involves
employees who suffer what is commonly referred to as “burnout.” A claim for
compensation benefits in such circumstances is outside the purview of the
definition of accident. This view is reinforced when one turns to the exception
to the general rule outlined in the definition of accident. The inability to
work must arise from a traumatic event which produces an “acute reaction.” The
notion that the event must induce an “acute” reaction displaces the notion that
a compensation claim based on “chronic stress” qualifies as a compensable
accident.

[42] As
easy as it may be to grasp the concept of a disablement resulting from stress,
the same cannot be said of the expression “disablement of mental stress.” No
where have I been able to find any reference to the meaning of that expression.
Perhaps the draftsperson was contemplating the situation in which “chronic
stress” would be advanced as the reason for the inability to work. Perhaps, it
was intended to reinforce the notion that work-related stress claims are
outside the purview of the definition of accident. Otherwise, it is difficult
to give meaning to this expression. This leads us to consider the scope of the
exception to the general rule, namely, an acute reaction to a traumatic event. [43] What
is a traumatic event within the meaning of s. 1 of the Workers’ Compensation
Act? Is that meaning consistent with the interpretation set out in the
Commission’s policy which is reproduced above? Frankly, the Commission’s formal
definition is unhelpful (“psychological shock that may produce disordered
feeling or behaviour”). However, the descriptive portion of the policy refers
to a traumatic event in terms of one that is sudden and outside the realm of
what is expected or usual within the workplace. Applying that understanding, it
necessarily follows that management decisions involving changes to terms and
conditions of employment do not qualify as traumatic events. The same is true
with respect to the decision to impose a lay-off or to terminate employment,
with or without just cause. Such decisions may well generate stress, but that
is to be expected.

[44] As
easy as it is to conclude that management decisions do not qualify as traumatic
events, it is universally accepted that employees who suffer from a
post-traumatic stress disorder qualify for compensation benefits, provided of
course the traumatic event arose out of and in the course of employment. Inevitably,
such a diagnosis is made according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual
of Mental Disorders, 4th ed. (DSM-IV). According to that manual
the essential feature of a post-traumatic stress disorder is that the
distressing event must be outside the range of usual human experience. It is
one that would be markedly distressing to any person and is usually, but not
always, experienced with intense fear, terror and helplessness. The worker may
be directly involved in the traumatic event or a witness thereto. The event
will be sudden as well as a frightening or shocking experience. Invariably, a
traumatic event involves actual or threatened death or serious injury or a
threat to one’s physical integrity. Examples of a traumatic event are the
employee who is a victim of a robbery or hostage-taking incident; the employee
who witnesses the death or severe injury of a co-worker or who is the first to
respond to victims of severe physical trauma or fatalities. [45] I
pause here to note that the Commission’s Policy Directive 21-103.01 states
that: “[m]erely being a witness to an event does not qualify the occurrence as
being a traumatic event.” If the intent of that statement is to establish the
proposition that a witness to a traumatic event cannot be diagnosed with a
post-traumatic stress disorder, that statement is in error. As well, the
following statement from that policy directive must be read with caution:
“[f]or compensation purposes, the event must be acute, not cumulative, and
extraordinary in nature in comparison with those events in the normal scope of
the worker’s employment.” First, it is clear that it is the “event” that must
be “traumatic” and the reaction to the traumatic event which must be “acute.”
Second, the notion of cumulative events must be approached with caution. It is
true that the cumulative effects of stressors experienced within the workplace
do not qualify as a traumatic event. The cumulative effect of a series of
work-related events may lead to a worker’s inability to continue with employment,
in which case there is no right to compensation benefits. On the other hand,
there are cases where the worker is exposed to a series of traumatic events
which over time lead to a diagnosis of post-traumatic stress syndrome. Delayed
onset of the syndrome is not unusual for those who are required, for example,
to provide emergency care to accident victims. Thus, the cumulative effect of a
series of events is relevant, provided each occurrence qualifies as a traumatic
event.

[46] To
this point, I have identified the two categories of cases for which it is a
relatively simple task to predict whether or not the employee’s stress-related
claim will succeed. On the one hand, there are those cases where the employee
receives a professional diagnosis of a post-traumatic stress disorder or
syndrome, using the DSM-IV. On the other hand, stress claims tied to the
implementation of typical management decisions are doomed to failure. But not
all cases will fall neatly within either category. For example, case law reveals
that stress claims involving “harassment” in the workplace require further
consideration (see Canada Post Corp. v. Nova Scotia (Workers’ Compensation
Appeals Tribunal), [2004] N.S.J. No. 242 (C.A.) (QL)). [47] With
respect to the indeterminate cases, the crucial issue is whether the notion of
a traumatic event should be measured by either a subjective or objective test. The argument is as follows. The appellant does not accept the Commission’s
definition of traumatic event. That is to say, she does not agree that the
event must be one that is sudden and outside the realm of what is expected and
usual in the workplace. The appellant maintains that such a definition embraces
an objective test for gauging whether an event is or is not traumatic when, in
law, the test should be a subjective one. The appellant insists that a
traumatic event must be measured in terms of what is traumatic to the claimant
and not what the reasonable person would regard as traumatic. There is no doubt
that if we adopt the subjective test we will be effectively applying the “thin
skull” principle. What may be a traumatic event for one employee may not be for
another. An employee with a pre-existing emotional or psychological condition
may react differently to a precipitous event than an employee who is not so
burdened. In the present case, the appellant maintains that her pre-existing
mental condition arose from the poor working conditions which she had been
enduring for several months. The alleged traumatic event was the confrontational
exchange between the appellant and her supervisor.

[48] The
law should not readily embrace an entirely subjective test when adjudicating on
compensation claims. Typically what happens in the law is that an objective
test is adopted with a subjective component. At some point, the reaction of the
employee to the precipitous event must be measured against the reasonable
person standard. If that is so then the test would have to be reformulated as
follows: Would a reasonable person standing in the shoes of the claimant, and
possessing the same psychological profile, have reacted in the same way. In
law, this reformulation is labeled the “modified objective test.” By contrast,
a purely objective test imposes the reasonable person standard without
reference, for example, to the reasonable fears, concerns and circumstances of
the claimant. See generally Arndt v. Smith, [1997] 2 S.C.R. 539. [49] In
support of her argument, the appellant cites three administrative appeal
decisions emanating from Ontario. However, two of the
cases were decided prior to the adoption of the amending legislation in 1997.
The third case is not on point as it deals with the problem of psychotraumatic
disability (psychological injury arising from a physical injury) discussed
earlier in these reasons (see 916/94, [1995] O.W.C.A.T.D. No. 1116 (QL);
1763/99, [1999] O.W.S.I.A.T.D. No. 2233 (QL) and 576 02, [2002]
O.W.S.I.A.T.D. No. 1064 (QL)).

my view, the test for assessing whether an event is traumatic must be an
objective one. If it were a purely subjective test or even a modified objective
test, the most innocuous of management decisions could support a claim for
psychological injury. It would not be difficult for the skilled advocate to
turn a case of “chronic” or “gradual onset” stress into a claim of
psychological injury by focusing on a single incident; the one that broke the
camel’s back, so to speak. The overly sensitive employee who is experiencing a
severely stressful home or work life might well suffer an acute reaction to a
critical management decision. A decision to lay an employee off work or to
terminate employment, with or without just cause, may well lead to depression
and the inability to find alternative work. But are these the types of claims
for which the Legislature intended that compensation benefits would be
available? I think not. To hold otherwise would be to sanction a regime in
which the exception to the rule would become the rule. In my view, a subjective
or modified objective test would be incompatible with the object of the 1992
amendment and its wording. For these reasons, the Commission was correct in
imposing an objective test for deciding whether an event is a traumatic one.
The question properly formulated is whether the reasonable person would regard
the precipitous event as a traumatic one (out of the usual, expected or
ordinary) because it is the type of occurrence that could realistically result
in an employee being unable to continue with his or her employment.

[52] There
is one other aspect of the Commission’s policies that requires consideration.
The appellant challenges the understanding that the claimant’s acute reaction
to the traumatic event must manifest itself in the form of a post-traumatic
stress disorder. Commission Policy 21-103.01 supports the understanding that a
stress-related claim will only succeed if the claimant is able to lead evidence
that he or she has the symptoms of post-traumatic stress syndrome. This leads
me to ask whether a diagnosis of a post-traumatic stress disorder, as set out
in the DSM-IV, is a condition precedent to establishing a stress-related claim
under the Workers’ Compensation Act. I am not prepared to go this far.
Were that the intention of the Legislature it would have been easy for it to
adopt a provision to this effect as was done in British Columbia. In the absence of such
an express provision, I am willing to accept that, in theory, a worker may
suffer an acute reaction to a traumatic event even though he or she has not
been diagnosed as suffering from a post-traumatic stress disorder or syndrome.
This approach leaves open, for example, the possibility that the intentional
infliction of mental harm through harassment in the workplace may support a
stress-related claim whether or not it falls within the DSM-IV. Perhaps the
question of whether a DSM-IV diagnosis is a condition precedent to a claim for
compensation benefits for psychological injury is more of a theoretical
construct than a pragmatic one, once it is accepted that the test to be applied
in assessing whether an event is traumatic is an objective test. At the same
time, none of this should be taken to discourage claimants from seeking a
professional opinion as to whether they are suffering from a post-traumatic
stress disorder diagnosed in accordance with the criteria set out in the
DSM-IV. This is a question that all physicians and psychologists should address
when formulating their professional opinion as to whether the claimant suffered
a psychological injury following a work incident.

V. Application
of Legal Framework to Facts of Case [53] Applying
the legal framework outlined above, it is not difficult to conclude on the
facts of this case that neither the Commission nor the Appeals Tribunal erred
in dismissing the appellant’s claim for stress-related benefits. My reasons are
as follows. [54] To
establish a right to stress-related benefits the appellant had to show that the
alleged traumatic event arose out of and in the course of employment. On the
facts of this case that condition precedent has been satisfied. [55] The
next issue is whether the event in question qualifies as a traumatic event in
the objective sense. Accepting that a traumatic event is one that is sudden and
unexpected or outside the usual range of human experience, it must be asked
whether a reasonable person would regard a non-violent confrontation between
the claimant and her supervisor as capable of inducing an acute reaction
leading to the employee’s inability to work. I accept that confrontations in
which the employee is the recipient of a verbal rant are unacceptable. It is
one thing to wrongly discipline employees and quite another to do it in a
manner that infringes their sense of dignity and personal worth. But are such
confrontations outside the range of human experience in the workplace? I think
not. [56] Objectively
speaking, I do not believe that the reasonable person would regard the incident
in question as one that could realistically or plausibly lead to a
psychological injury that would prevent the employee from continuing with his
or her work. An isolated instance of management yelling at an employee does not
even support an allegation of harassment, which in appropriate circumstances,
might well support a claim of constructive dismissal. Admittedly, the employee
may feel ill at ease at returning to the workplace so long as the offending
supervisor remains in authority. But even if there are valid reasons for
refusing to return to work, those reasons cannot be transformed into a
psychological injury. Of course, if the real reason for not returning to work
is to avoid future confrontations, the claim for work-related stress benefits
has not been made out. The claimant should seek unemployment benefits under the
federal unemployment insurance regime or possibly file a grievance under a
collective agreement.

[57] If
there is doubt as to whether an incident qualifies as a traumatic event, it is
proper to ask whether it is more probable than not that the facts of the case
support a claim of chronic stress. In the present, the appellant’s psychiatrist
stated in his report that the appellant had been suffering from a “Major
Depression” prior to the incident in question and that the problem with “her
mood” started with the change to her new work environment and the problems
encountered with respect to the poor lighting and noise conditions. The report
goes on to state that as the appellant had no history of receiving psychiatric
care, “work-related stress is one of the major contributing factors toward her
problem with her mood.” In my view, this evidence supports the inference that
the appellant was suffering from chronic stress and that the confrontation with
her supervisor was simply the last of a series of cumulative events that
triggered the appellant’s inability to continue with her employment. In my
opinion, this is the true basis on which the Appeals Tribunal dismissed the
appellant’s appeal. [58] Finally,
I was able to find one Nova Scotia decision in which the Appeals Tribunal of
that Province held that a claimant was entitled to benefits following an
“intense meeting” with a supervisor. However, the Appeals Tribunal found that
the meeting was “personal”, “violent” and “aggressive.” There was also evidence
to support the Appeals Tribunal’s inference that there was “a real and imminent
threat that the meeting was about to become physically violent.” The claimant
also adduced a medical opinion that he had suffered a work-related
post-traumatic stress syndrome. The facts of that case are materially different
from those under consideration (see Children’s Aid Society of Cape
Breton-Victoria v. Nova Scotia (Workers’ Compensation Appeals Tribunal), [2005] N.S.J. No. 75
(C.A.) (QL)).

[59] In
conclusion, this is not a case where the claimant has established that she
comes within the exception to the general rule. In brief, the verbal tirade
directed at the appellant by her supervisor does not qualify as a traumatic
event. In these circumstances, it is unnecessary to determine whether the event
caused an acute reaction leading to her inability to work. VI. Two Issues
That Were Not Raised [60] I
have identified two issues that were not raised on this appeal that warrant a
passing comment or two. First, I am acutely aware of the Supreme Court’s ruling
in Nova Scotia
(Workers' Compensation Board) v. Martin; Nova Scotia (Workers' Compensation
Board) v. Laseur,
[2003] 2 S.C.R. 504. In that case, it was held that a provision of the Nova Scotia legislation denying
workers’ compensation benefits for “chronic pain” offended s. 15 of the Charter
and was not saved under s. 1. Specifically, it was found that those workers who
suffered from chronic pain following a physical and job-related injury were
being discriminated against, on the basis of disability, when compared to those
injured workers who did not suffer from chronic pain. This leads one to ask
whether the exclusion of “chronic stress” claims from the definition of
accident found in s. 1 of our Workers’ Compensation Act offends the Charter.
The difficulty I would have with such a challenge is in identifying the
relevant comparator group. The idea that employees who suffer from work-related
chronic stress are being discriminated against when compared to those who do
not suffer such an affliction appears nonsensical. Those who do not suffer from
chronic stress will not be in receipt of benefits and, hence, it is difficult,
if not impossible, to see how the issue of discrimination can arise.

[61] The
second non-issue stems from the fact that Via Rail is a federal employer. As I
understand the legislative scheme, federal employees may be entitled to file a
claim for workers’ compensation benefits under a provincial scheme pursuant to
the Government Employees Compensation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. G-5. The general
purpose of GECA is to provide compensation to federal workers on the same terms
and conditions as their provincial counterparts. For example, in Nova Scotia, the provincial scheme
governs claims submitted under GECA, provided two conditions are met. One of
those conditions is that a provision of the provincial legislation must not be
in conflict with GECA. In that regard the federal legislation does not
expressly exclude chronic or gradual onset stress from the definition of
“accident.” This leads one to ask whether their exclusion under the provincial
legislation applies to claims made under GECA, an issue touched on by the Nova
Scotia Court of Appeal in two decisions (see Morrison (Estate) v. Cape
Breton Development Corp., [2003] N.S.J. No. 353 (C.A.) (QL) and Canada
Post v. Nova Scotia). [62] The
applicability of GECA and the potential conflict with the Workers’
Compensation Act did not escape the appellant’s representative. Before
appealing the Commission’s decision to the Appeals Tribunal, he wrote to the
Commission asking whether the appellant’s eligibility for benefits arose under
the provincial legislation or under a tri-partite agreement entered into by the
federal and provincial governments and Via Rail [Whether or not such an
agreement exists is another question]. The Commission responded that as the
appellant worked for Via Rail, she was not considered a federal employee
governed by GECA. The Commission opined that as the appellant was a resident of
and worked in New Brunswick
she was covered under the provincial legislation. With great respect, the logic
employed eludes me. Furthermore, the Commission’s position appears to be at
odds with its position in Canada Post Corp. v. New Brunswick (Workplace Health,
Safety and Compensation Commission), [2003] N.B.J. No. 151 (C.A.). As the issue was not
raised before the Appeals Tribunal, or this Court, I will refrain from further
comment.

[2] The Applicant filed four affidavits in support of
the motions but the Respondent was unable to file the documents specified in
Rule 598 because of the short notice. [3] Notices of motion were filed in both actions
seeking a stay of proceeding pending a hearing on the merits. The stay was
granted after argument and these are the reasons for my decision. II. FACTS [4] The following facts are derived from the affidavits
of the Applicants and the statements of facts of the application briefs. [5] The Applicants own and operate a restaurant in
Iqaluit, Nunavut, under the name and style of the Kamotiq Inn Restaurant
(Kamotiq Inn). The business holds a dining room licence, issued by the
Respondent, authorizing the sale of alcohol to the customers of the business. [6] The Kamotiq Inn was the subject of an initial show
cause hearing under s.35 of the Liquor Act in 2004. The first hearing was
scheduled for December 9, 2004, and adjourned three times at the request of the
Applicants. A day-long hearing was finally held on June 8, 2005, where the
Kamotiq Inn was represented by legal counsel. The Respondent held that the
Kamotiq Inn had permitted drunkenness on six occasions in the restaurant
contrary s.98(2)(a) of the Liquor Act. The Respondent imposed a fine of $1000
for some incidents and $1500 for the others as well as a four-day licence
suspension. In addition, the Respondent ordered that the Kamotiq Inn provide
server training for all staff, along with satisfactory proof of compliance to
the Manager of Liquor Enforcement by August 15, 2005.

[7] On June 25, 2005, Marcel Mahe wrote to liquor
inspector, Ms. K. Pumphrey, and advised her that the server training ordered by
the Respondent had been completed by Loredana Mahe. [8] Loredana Mahe carried out the server training in
June and again in November 2005. [9] On March 16, 2006, the Chairperson of the
Respondent wrote to the Kamotiq Inn and advised that the renewal of the liquor
licence effective on April 1, 2006, was subject to providing proof of
compliance with health and fire regulations and the server training. The

with a show cause hearing if the necessary proof was not provided by March 31,
2006. [10] On March 30, 2006, the Kamotiq Inn alleges that it
sent a report to Simon Okpatauyak, the executive secretary of the Respondent,
containing documentation that provided proof of the completion of the server
training that had been ordered. Loredana Mahe alleges she telephoned Mr.
Okpatauyak on the same day and received confirmation from him that the report
was satisfactory. [11] The status of the Kamotiq Inn licence was on the
agenda of the June 2006 meetings of the Respondent, but was not discussed because
the Board ran out of time. [12] Around September 11, 2006, the Kamotiq Inn was
served with a notice of a show cause hearing scheduled for September 27, 2006. The notice specified that the Kamotiq Inn was required to show cause why its
licence should not be suspended because of the failure to provide proof of
compliance with the Order of the Respondent of June 5, 2005, to carry out the
server training before August 15, 2005.

[13] At the time of service of the notice of hearing,
the Applicants were in Gatineau P.Q. where Marcel Mahe was scheduled for cancer
biopsy surgery. He had waited six months for the appointment and wrote to the
chairperson of the Respondent on September 20, 2006, to explain the position of
the Kamotiq Inn. He indicated he could not afford to hire a lawyer and could
not attend the hearing because of his scheduled surgery. He also provided the
same documentation that had been sent to Simon Okpatauyak on March 30, 2006,
and informed him that Mr. Okpatauyak had confirmed that the Order of the
Respondent had been complied with. [14] Recognizing that there may have been a problem with
communications, Loredana Mahe contacted the Chief Liquor Inspector to find out
why the hearing had been scheduled and was informed that it was because she was
not qualified to conduct the server training. Then she spoke with Patrick
Galbraith, the Executive Director of the Respondent, who informed her that he
could not find the Notice of Hearing. Next she spoke with Simon Okpatauyak who
advised her to send someone to attend the hearing. Finally she telephoned Stu
Kennedy, who is a member of the Respondent, and provided him with a copy of all
the relevant documentation. He assured her that the documentation was
satisfactory to show cause to the satisfaction of the Respondent. [15] The Applicants sent Dana Mahe to represent the
Kamotiq Inn at the hearing on September 27. She is the daughter of the
Applicants and works in the restaurant as a waitress and manager. She
discovered that Stu Kennedy was not sitting on the Board panel. She put
forward the position of the Kamotiq Inn but was aggressively cross-examined by
the legal counsel for the Board and made some mistakes because she lacked
personal knowledge. She recognized that she needed some help and called
Loredana Mahe for advice.

[16] Loredana Mahe instructed her to ask for an
adjournment so that a lawyer could be retained. The adjournment was strongly
opposed by Counsel for the Respondent on the basis that the matter had been
outstanding for over a year and that the Kamotiq Inn was knowledgeable about
the procedures of the Respondent. After deliberation, the Board refused the
adjournment without reasons. [17] Simon Okpatauyak then testified that he did not
receive the materials about the server training on March 30, 2006. The
Respondent gave more weight to the evidence of Simon Okpatauyak than the
hearsay evidence of Dana Mahe but permitted her until noon the next day to
produce the necessary documentation. [18] The Respondent reconvened the next day and Dana
Mahe produced additional documentation but did not give any additional
evidence. The documentation did not include any fax confirmation sheets
proving the service of the documents on March 30, 2006, but did contain unsworn
statements from employees of the Kamotiq Inn indicating that they attended
server courses in June and November conducted by Loredana Mahe. [19] The Respondent, in written decisions of September
27 and 28, 2006, rejected the evidence of the Applicants and accepted the
evidence of Simon Okpatauyak. The Kamotiq Inn was fined $5000.00 and its
license was suspended until November 12. It was also ordered to provide server
training to its current employees from a qualified trainer by November 12 and
to provide proof of the payment of the expenses of the trainer. The licence
would remain suspended until the proof was provided to the Executive Secretary
of the Respondent.

[20] The licence suspension has caused bad publicity and
considerable economic damage to the Kamotiq Inn. Numerous employees have been
laid off and sales are very low. There is a risk that the business may close
permanently. III. ISSUES [21] The only issue in this interim application is
whether a stay of proceedings should be granted. The Respondent has raised
some preliminary issues on the admissibility of the affidavit evidence at the
hearing on the merits of the appeal and/or judicial review. Those objections do
not apply to the application for the stay but merit some comment to assist in
narrowing the issues at the hearing on the merits. IV. Affidavits A. Arguments [22] The Respondent argued that affidavit evidence is
not admissible to supplement the record that will be filed in the near future
on the appeal or judicial review. [23] The statutory appeal under s.23(2) of the Liquor
Act is restricted to errors of law and excess of jurisdiction. These grounds
create an appeal on the record of the Tribunal rather than a trial de novo. In
this type of appeal, new evidence is not generally admissible except under
stringent conditions. The Respondent opposes the admissibility of any
affidavit evidence but cited no authorities. [24] On the judicial review application, the Respondent
relied on R. v. Northumberland Compensation Appeal Tribunal, ex parte Shaw,
[1952] 1 All E.R. 122, [1952] 1 K.B. 338 (C.A.) (Northumberland), to argue that
the only evidence that was admissible was that contained in the record that
will be filed by the Respondent in the near future. The only exception to this
rule is evidence that pertains to due process and natural justice. The
Respondent argued that the facts deposed to, in the affidavits to support the
grounds alleged, did not reveal any errors of fact or law to ground an
assertion that the Board acted in excess of jurisdiction. As a result, the
Applicants failed to satisfy the exceptions to the rule. Admission of the
affidavits would only obscure the basic fact that the Applicants failed to
comply with an order of the Respondent.

[25] If the affidavits did fall within the exceptions,
the Respondent objects to a number of paragraphs and requests that they be
struck out because they are not in compliance with Rule 373(3) of the Rules. The offending paragraphs are 4, 10 and 11 of the affidavit of Marcel Mahe and
4, 7, 12, portions of 17 and 18, as well as 24, 26, 27, 29 and 30 of the
affidavit of Loredana Mahe. [26] The Applicants relied on Whitehouse v. Sun Oil.,
[1982] 6 W.W.R. 289, [1982] A.J. No. 656 (AB. C.A.), to support the admission
of the affidavits. In that case, the Court of Appeal asserted its right to
hear evidence and consider the merits of the decision of the tribunal. B. Analysis (i) Admission of Affidavits [27] Counsel for the parties chose not to address the
issue of the alternate remedies and the availability of certiorari when there
is a statutory right of appeal. However, consideration of this issue is an
essential prerequisite to determining the admissibility of the affidavits. [28] As noted at pages 3-6 and 3-7 of Judicial Review of
Administrative Action in Canada , the failure of an applicant to pursue a
statutory remedy will usually bar relief in judicial review proceedings if the
other remedy is considered to be an adequate alternative to judicial review. In each case, the reviewing court must determine whether the statutory
procedure provides an adequate remedy to the grievance of the applicant.

[29] The provision of a statutory remedy by way of an
appeal to the courts prima facie indicates a legislative intention to exclude
the courts’ exercise of their supervisory jurisdiction . Some courts have held
that the existence of an appeal right deprives them of jurisdiction because it
indicates a legislative judgment that it is better that a court’s consideration

a tribunal in good faith in interpreting or applying a provision of its

"23(1) Subject to this section, every order of the
Board is final. (2) A licence holder that is a party to a decision or
order of the Board may appeal the decision or order to the Supreme Court on the
ground that the Board has erred in law or exceeded its jurisdiction. (3) The Board or the Minister may state a case to the
Supreme Court in the manner provided for in the Criminal Code. (4) Where an appeal of a decision or order of the Board
has been made, a judge of the Supreme Court may by order stay the execution of
the decision or order on the terms that the judge considers just." [33] The appeal grounds for review by this Court
specified in s.23 are an error or law or excess of jurisdiction. These grounds
are broader than an "error of law raised before the board" and, in my
opinion, encompass all three types of error. As a result, the application for
judicial review should be refused. [34] Vertes J. also expressed the opinion that both
applications should not be sought for the same relief to prevent superfluous
litigation and possible conflicting judgments. The same view was expressed by
the Northwest Territories Court of Appeal in Baffin Plumbing & Heating Ltd.
v. Northwest Territories (Labour Standards Board), [1997] N.W.T.J. No. 26. However, in Marren v. Echo Bay Mines Ltd., 2000 NWTCA 6, [2000] N.W.T.J. No.
62, the Court of Appeal implicitly recognized the necessity to proceed in this
manner where the extent of the statutory jurisdiction was unclear. When both
proceedings are commenced, the Court should consider the statutory appeal first
and, if it provides the necessary jurisdiction and remedy, the judicial review
should be refused. Since there is limited administrative case law authority in
this jurisdiction, it was appropriate to launch both applications.

[35] The general rule on a judicial review application
is that the reviewing court should only look at the material that was before
the tribunal. The authority cited for the rule by the Respondents was the
classic case of Northumberland. An excellent summary of the application of the
Northumberland case in Canada appears in McFadyen v. Canada (Attorney General),
2005 FCA 360, [2005] F.C.J. No. 1817, where the Court stated: "[15] The principle that evidence outside the
administrative record, that is outside the record before the tribunal, can be
considered where the grounds for review are any of the various forms of
jurisdictional error is well-established: as Denning L.J. noted in an early
English leading case, "[w]hen certiorari is granted on the ground of want
of jurisdiction, or bias, or fraud, affidavit evidence is not only admissible,
but it is, as a rule, necessary" [Northumberland at 131] This principle has been approved by the Supreme Court of
Canada on numerous occasions... A breach of procedural fairness is also one of
the forms of jurisdictional error to which this principle applies…" [36] The documentation that constitutes the record
varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction. There are specific rules governing
the admission of new evidence in Newfoundland and under the Federal Court of
Canada. Nunavut does not have a comparable rule. Rule 598 requires the
tribunal to file a record that contains the judgment order or decision, the
process commencing the proceeding, the evidence and all exhibits filed, all
things touching the matter and the originating notice served on the
respondents. This Rule is identical to that used in Northwest Territories,
Alberta and Nova Scotia.
